Chapter-singular birth-aetiology → **overlay**. Claim_type *inferred*: the surface is the transliterated name + ASV-baseline vocabulary, the recorded substance is the two implicit etymologies.

**Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *zarach*, *shani*, *te'om*; BDB pp. 280, 1040, 1060; NIDOTTE 1:1158-1159 (zarach), 3:1303 (shani); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 271; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 453-454; on the twin-birth and the Gen 25 reprise: Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 219-220.

terms.translit: YHWH (the narrator's frame, vv 2, 3 [twice], 5 [twice], 21, 23 [twice]); Elohim (Yosef's own mouth, v 9)
terms.partOfSpeech: divine names (proper name / divine appellative)
terms.literal: YHWH (the Tetragrammaton, rendered 'YHWH' per corpus convention); Elohim ('God' / 'the Elohim')
terms.standardEnglish: the LORD (ASV/KJV/NRSV/NJPS, for YHWH); God (for Elohim)
terms.wohChoice: YHWH (vv 2, 3, 5, 21, 23) and Elohim (v 9), each rendered as the text has it; the chapter-distinctive YHWH/Elohim alternation across the Yosef cycle documented in commentary
terms.rationale:
**Genesis 39 is the ONLY chapter in the Yosef cycle (Gen 37-50) in which the divine name in the narrator's voice is the Tetragrammaton YHWH rather than Elohim.** The chapter's structural refrain is a YHWH-frame: *va-yehi YHWH et-Yosef* ('and YHWH was with Yosef', v 2; repeated v 21), *YHWH matzliach* ('YHWH made [it] to prosper', vv 3, 23), *va-yevarekh YHWH* ('and YHWH blessed', v 5), *birkat YHWH* ('the blessing of YHWH', v 5) — eight occurrences of YHWH at vv 2, 3, 5, 21, 23, all in the narrator's voice. Yet at v 9, in Yosef's own refusal-speech, the divine name switches to Elohim: *ve-eikh e'eseh ha-ra'ah ha-gedolah ha-zot ve-chatati le-Elohim* ('how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against Elohim?'). The alternation is not random: YHWH is the **narrator's** name for the deity in this chapter; Elohim is the name **on the character's lips**.

**The source-critical observation (named mainstream scholarship).** The Yosef novella (Gen 37-50) is, on the documentary analysis, predominantly an Elohistic and/or non-Yahwistic composition: across the cycle the deity is regularly *Elohim* (and, in characters' mouths, *Elohim* — e.g., Yosef at 41:16, 41:51-52, 45:5-9, 50:19-20). Genesis 39 stands out as a YHWH-saturated chapter and is widely assigned to the **J / Yahwistic source** (or read as a Yahwistic editorial framing inserted into an otherwise Elohistic novella). This is a classic datum of pentateuchal source-criticism: the divine-name distribution is one of the original Wellhausen-era criteria for source-division, and Gen 39's YHWH-frame against the cycle's Elohim-norm is a textbook case. The narrator-YHWH / character-Elohim split at v 9 is read either (a) as the J-narrator's own voice (YHWH) framing a scene in which the character, an Israelite speaking within an Egyptian household, naturally uses the more general *Elohim*; or (b) as a seam where Yahwistic framing (vv 2-6, 21-23) brackets an older novella-core. Standard treatments: Wellhausen *Prolegomena* (1883); S. R. Driver *Introduction to the Literature of the OT* (1913); von Rad *Genesis* OTL (1972) pp. 365-367; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* (1986) pp. 60-63; Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* (CBQMS 4, 1976); Redford *A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph* (VTSup 20, 1970) pp. 251-253 (on the divine-name distribution across the cycle).

**The translation choice.** The WoH translation renders the Tetragrammaton as **'YHWH'** (vv 2, 3, 5, 21, 23), per the confirmed corpus convention (verified across the stable chapters and re-confirmed at Gen 38:7, 10; 'Yahweh' is deferred to any future corpus-wide retransliteration pass), and renders **'Elohim'** at v 9 as the source has it. Both divine names stand exactly as the Hebrew distributes them; the translation does NOT harmonize them. The chapter-distinctive YHWH/Elohim alternation, and its source-critical reading, are documented in commentary (vv 2, 9). **No WoH synthesis about the divine names is imported** — the entry records the named documentary-critical observation only; any project-specific reading of the YHWH/Elohim distinction is wiki-reserved.

**Overlay housing.** This is a **chapter-distinctive structural observation** about Gen 39's place in the divine-name distribution of the Yosef cycle — a single-chapter literary/source-critical datum, not a lexical decision about a recurring lemma (the lemmas YHWH and Elohim are governed corpus-wide by their own established conventions). It is therefore housed in the **overlay**, anchored at the Gen 39 divine-name verses, and does not modify or extend any central YHWH/Elohim convention-entry. The claim_type is *inferred*: the distribution is grammatically explicit (direct), but the source-critical reading of it (the J-frame / Elohistic-novella analysis) is an interpretive observation, surfaced in commentary as named mainstream scholarship without adjudication.

**Scholarly literature.** Wellhausen *Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels* (1883); S. R. Driver *Introduction to the Literature of the OT* (9th ed. 1913); von Rad *Genesis* OTL (1972) pp. 365-367; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* (1986) pp. 60-63; Coats *From Canaan to Egypt: Structural and Theological Context for the Joseph Story* (CBQMS 4, 1976); Redford *A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph* (VTSup 20, 1970) pp. 251-253; Sarna *JPS Genesis* (1989) p. 271 (noting Gen 39's YHWH-distinctiveness); Friedman *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (2003) ad loc. (the J-assignment of Gen 39). // **Scope-extension to Gen 40:8 (the Elohim-default outside the Gen 39 YHWH-frame).** Genesis 40 contains a single divine-name occurrence, at v 8, on Yosef's own lips: *ha-lo le-Elohim pitronim* — 'Do not interpretations belong to Elohim?' This is **Elohim**, not YHWH — exactly the cycle's Elohim-default that this entry documents as the norm against which Gen 39's YHWH-frame stands out. Gen 40:8 is therefore a confirming scope-extension of the same cycle-wide divine-name observation, not a separate datum: it shows the Elohim-norm reasserting itself the moment the narrative leaves the YHWH-saturated Gen 39 (and it parallels Gen 39:9, where Yosef likewise says *le-Elohim* on his own lips). The entry's appliesTo is extended to add GEN-WOH-40:8; both divine names continue to be rendered exactly as the text distributes them ('Elohim' here), with no harmonization and no WoH synthesis. Yosef's claim at v 8 — that *pitronim* (interpretations) belong to Elohim — is the dream-cycle's theology of interpretation; the lexeme *pitron* itself is governed by the central `pitron-dream-interpretation-yosef-cycle` entry, and the dream-as-symbolic-puzzle (vs. dream-as-theophany) distinction is documented there.

terms.translit: yefeh-to'ar vifeh mar'eh (Gen 39:6, of Yosef); cf. yefat-to'ar vifat mar'eh (Gen 29:17, of Rachel)
terms.strongs: H3303 (yafeh, 'beautiful, fair') + H8389 (to'ar, 'form, shape, figure') + H4758 (mar'eh, 'appearance, look')
terms.partOfSpeech: double adjectival epithet (construct phrase: adjective + noun, twice)
terms.literal: beautiful of form and beautiful of appearance — fair in figure and fair to look upon
terms.standardEnglish: beautiful in form, and fair to look upon (ASV/KJV); well-built and handsome (NJPS); handsome and good-looking (NRSV); comely in features and comely to look at (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: beautiful in form, and fair to look upon (ASV-baseline; the verbatim Rachel cross-reference at Gen 29:17 documented in commentary)
terms.rationale:
**Gen 39:6 closes the prosperity-section and pivots to the seduction-scene with a description of Yosef: *va-yehi Yosef yefeh-to'ar vifeh mar'eh* — 'and Yosef was beautiful in form, and fair to look upon.' This double-epithet is VERBATIM the description of Rachel, Yosef's mother, at Gen 29:17: *ve-Rachel haytah yefat-to'ar vifat mar'eh* — 'and Rachel was beautiful in form, and fair to look upon' (the only difference being the feminine adjectival endings). These are the ONLY two people in Genesis described with this exact double-formula.**

**The literary cross-reference.** The verbatim repetition is a recognized deliberate narrative link. Three points are standardly made: (a) **inherited beauty** — Yosef, alone among Ya'aqov's sons, is given his mother Rachel's exact description; the beloved son of the beloved wife inherits her beauty, which the narrator flags by re-using her formula word-for-word. (b) **the gender-reversal of the seduction-plot** — the double-epithet is elsewhere a *woman's* beauty-formula (Rachel here; cf. the beauty-descriptions of Sarah, Rivkah, Avigayil, Tamar, Esther, all women); applying it to Yosef casts him, structurally, in the position a beautiful woman occupies in a seduction-narrative — the *object* of another's desire (here Potifar's wife's). The formula's placement is purposive: it stands immediately before *va-tissa eshet-adonav et-eineha el-Yosef* ('his master's wife cast her eyes upon Yosef', v 7), so the beauty-notice motivates the seduction-plot it introduces. (c) **the mother-son frame** — the formula binds Yosef to Rachel across the cycle (Rachel's death, Gen 35:18-19; Yosef and Binyamin as the Rachel-sons). Standard treatments: Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 272; Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 and *Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 223 (the gender-reversal observation); Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 64; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 462.

**The lexemes.** *to'ar* (H8389) is 'form, shape, figure, bodily-build' (cf. the *to'ar* of the captive woman, Deut 21:11; of Esther, Est 2:7); *mar'eh* (H4758) is 'appearance, look, the visual aspect'. The pair *yefeh-to'ar... yefeh mar'eh* names beauty of both *build* and *face/appearance* — a comprehensive beauty-formula. ASV 'beautiful in form, and fair to look upon' captures the build/appearance distinction; NJPS 'well-built and handsome' modernizes it.

**The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'beautiful in form, and fair to look upon'** (v 6), per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention, and — crucially — renders it **identically to the Gen 29:17 Rachel-description** so that the verbatim Hebrew echo is reproducible in English (a reader comparing 29:17 and 39:6 sees the same English formula, as the Hebrew intends). The inherited-beauty link to Rachel, the gender-reversal of the seduction-plot, and the formula's motivating placement before v 7 are documented in commentary.

**Overlay housing.** The double-formula describes only **Rachel and Yosef** in Genesis — a Genesis-internal, near-singular literary cross-reference (a mother-son beauty-link), not a corpus-wide lexical decision about a recurring lemma. Per the ratified split (chapter-singular / near-singular → overlay), it is housed in the **overlay**, anchored at Gen 39:6, with the Gen 29:17 Rachel-attestation documented in the rationale. (Should a corpus-wide beauty-formula pattern prove load-bearing across the HB — the *yafeh*/*to'ar*/*mar'eh* beauty-descriptions of Sarah, Rivkah, Avigayil, Tamar, Esther, etc. — this entry is the seed for a possible future central beauty-formula entry; for now it is the Rachel-Yosef link only.) The claim_type is *inferred*: the verbatim repetition is direct (a lexical fact), but the inherited-beauty / gender-reversal reading is the interpretive substance, surfaced in commentary.

**Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *to'ar*, *mar'eh*, *yafeh*; BDB pp. 1061, 909, 421; NIDOTTE 2:491-492 (to'ar), 3:1010-1015 (ra'ah/mar'eh); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 203 (Gen 29:17), 272 (Gen 39:6); Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 154, 223; Westermann *Genesis 12-36* 1985 p. 466 and *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 64; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 462.

terms.translit: le-tzachek (v 14, banu 'with us'; v 17, bi 'with me')
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Piel infinitive construct (with preposition le-) + prepositional object
terms.literal: to mock / make sport of / insult / dally-with (Piel of tz-ch-q, the laughter-root underlying the name Yitzchaq)
terms.standardEnglish: to mock (ASV/KJV); to dally with / insult (NJPS 'to dally with us' / 'to play with me'); to mock / to play with (NRSV); to play with (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: to mock us (v 14) / to mock me (v 17), ASV-baseline; the hostile / sexual-innuendo Piel sense and the tz-ch-q (Yitzchaq) wordplay documented in commentary
terms.rationale:
**This is the Genesis 39 sibling to the central tz-ch-q recognition entries, anchored in the central glossary at Gen 21:9 (*metzacheq-ishmael-debate*) and Gen 26:8 (*metzacheq-conjugal-vs-contested-disambiguation*). It is created as a SEPARATE sibling overlay entry — NOT by extending those central entries' appliesTo — per the ratified sibling-overlay-entries pattern (Gen 35): doublets/recurrences of a load-bearing polysemous lexeme get one entry per attestation-cluster, with cross-references.**

**The verse.** In Gen 39:14 Potifar's wife, after Yosef has fled leaving his garment, calls the household and accuses: *re'u hevi lanu ish Ivri le-tzachek banu* — 'See, he hath brought in a Hebrew unto us *le-tzachek* with us' — and repeats the charge to Potifar at v 17: *ba elai ha-eved ha-Ivri... le-tzachek bi* — 'the Hebrew servant... came in unto me *le-tzachek* with me.' The verb is the **Piel infinitive of tz-ch-q** (H6711), the same root that drives the laughter-and-name-play of the Avraham-Yitzchaq cycle (the name *Yitzchaq*, 'he laughs'; the *tzachoq* of Gen 21:6; the *metzacheq* of Gen 21:9 and 26:8).

**The sense here: hostile / sexual mockery.** The Piel of tz-ch-q is deliberately polysemous across the corpus (play, jest, sport, mock, caress, fondle, make-love, perform); the central entry *metzacheq-conjugal-vs-contested-disambiguation* maps the full range. At Gen 39:14, 17 the contextual disambiguator is the **accusation-frame**: the wife construes Yosef's presence as an *insult / outrage / sexual affront* against the household — *le-tzachek banu* / *bi* carries the hostile sense ('to make sport of us', 'to insult us', 'to mock me'), with a clear **sexual innuendo** (the accusation is that Yosef came 'to lie with me', v 14b). The verb thus sits in the *mockery* / *sexual-affront* register (range γ in the central polysemy-map: the erotic-mockery sense, explicitly cross-referenced there to 'Gen 39:14, 17 *l-tzacheq bi* in Potiphar's wife's accusation against Yosef'). The accusation is also tinged with **ethnic contempt** — *ish Ivri* ('a Hebrew', see *ha-ivri-hebrew-etymology*), the outsider's designation, is foregrounded: the household has been shamed by a *foreigner*.

**The rendering-traditions.** ASV/KJV 'to mock' (the hostile sense, neutral as to the sexual register); NJPS 'to dally with us' (v 14) / 'to play with me' (v 17) — foregrounding the sexual innuendo; NRSV 'to insult us' / 'to mock me'; Alter 'to play with us' / 'to play with me' (keeping the tz-ch-q wordplay visible). The sexual-mockery sense ('to dally with / fondle') is contextually present but the ASV 'mock' is the dominant English choice and keeps the hostility without over-committing the surface to the explicit sexual rendering.

**The Yitzchaq wordplay.** The choice of tz-ch-q is not incidental: the laughter-root underlying *Yitzchaq* is here turned to its darkest register — the patriarch's name-root ('laughter') deployed in a false accusation of sexual outrage. The verb's appearance here also echoes its other harsh-register uses: Gen 19:14 (Lot 'mocking' to his sons-in-law); Exod 32:6 (the golden-calf *le-tzachek*); Judg 16:25 (Samson made to 'make sport'). The cross-attestation map is fully documented in the central entry *metzacheq-conjugal-vs-contested-disambiguation*.

**Cross-reference (bidirectional).** This entry is the Gen 39 sibling of the central entries *metzacheq-ishmael-debate* (Gen 21:9, the contested Yishma'el participle) and *metzacheq-conjugal-vs-contested-disambiguation* (Gen 26:8, the conjugal participle + the full cross-corpus polysemy-map, which already names Gen 39:14, 17). The three are deliberately kept separate, each governing its own attestation; together they map the tz-ch-q polysemy across the patriarchal narratives. This entry does NOT extend those central entries' appliesTo.

**The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'to mock us'** (v 14) and **'to mock me'** (v 17), per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention — 'mock' carries the hostility without committing the surface to the explicit sexual rendering. The hostile / sexual-innuendo Piel sense, the ethnic-contempt foregrounding (*ish Ivri*), and the tz-ch-q (Yitzchaq) wordplay are documented in commentary. Genesis-internal sibling of a central polysemous-lexeme dossier → **overlay**. Claim_type *inferred*: the Piel is grammatically explicit (direct), but the disambiguation to the hostile/sexual register and the wordplay-reading are the interpretive substance, surfaced in commentary.

**Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *tz-ch-q* (Piel); BDB p. 850; NIDOTTE 3:797-798; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 273; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 64-65; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 463-464; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 223; on the tz-ch-q laughter-name-play arc: the cross-references in the central *metzacheq-conjugal-vs-contested-disambiguation* and *yitzchaq-name-etymology-laughter-pattern* entries.

terms.translit: zo'afim (qal participle plural, v 6); picked up at v 7 by penekhem ra'im, 'your faces look bad'
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, qal active participle, masculine plural
terms.literal: za'af — to be vexed / out of humor / dejected / agitated; participle: troubled-faced, downcast, vexed
terms.standardEnglish: sad (ASV/KJV); troubled (NJPS); dejected / downcast (NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: sad (ASV-baseline; the za'af 'vexation / agitation' register, debated against 'dejection', documented here)
terms.rationale: **Genesis 40:6 describes the cupbearer and baker the morning after their dreams: *ve-hinnam zo'afim* — 'and behold, they were* zo'afim'. The participle is from the root זעף (z-'-f), and its precise affective register is debated.** At v 7 Yosef glosses their state in his question *maddua penekhem ra'im ha-yom* ('why do your faces look bad/evil today?'), confirming a visibly disturbed countenance but not settling the exact emotion. // **The lexeme.** The root z-'-f and its noun *za'af* elsewhere in the HB connote **vexation, indignation, rage** more than simple sadness: of King Asa *za'af* (in a rage) at the seer (2 Chr 16:10); of King Uzziah *za'af* (furious) when struck with leprosy (2 Chr 26:19); of the *za'af* (raging) of the sea (Jonah 1:15); of the *za'af YHWH* (the indignation of the Lord, Mic 7:9; Isa 30:30; the *za'am*-adjacent register). On this evidence the participle here might mean the two officials were **agitated / out of humor / troubled** rather than merely 'sad'. But in the Gen 40:6 context — men who have had disturbing dreams they cannot decode, in prison — the affect is most naturally **dejection / distress / a troubled and downcast look**, and the older English tradition (KJV/ASV) renders 'sad'. The modern versions split: NJPS 'troubled', NRSV 'troubled / dejected', some 'distraught'. The vexation-vs-dejection ambiguity is the recorded crux. // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'sad'** (v 6) and 'why look ye so sad to-day' / 'your faces look bad' (v 7), per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention — 'sad' is defensible for the dejection-reading and is the dominant older-English choice. The fuller z-'-f 'vexation / agitation' register, attested by the 2 Chr / Jonah / Micah occurrences, is documented here so the reader can audit the affect-range. // **Overlay housing.** The participle's occurrence is **chapter-singular** within the WoH corpus (this is the only z-'-f form in Genesis; the vexation-occurrences cluster in Chronicles, the prophets, and Jonah, outside the current and near-term corpus). The decision is a single-verse affect-disambiguation, not a recurring-lemma decision with cross-corpus reach in the active corpus → **overlay**, per the ratified chapter-singular / near-singular split. (If a future Chronicles or prophets translation activates the *za'af* vexation-cluster, a central z-'-f entry could absorb this as a sibling-node; for now it stands in the overlay.) // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) both 'sad/dejected' and 'vexed/agitated' are lexically defensible; (b) the choice is interpretive (context favors dejection, the root's wider usage favors vexation); (c) the ASV-baseline 'sad' stands on the surface. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *za'af*; BDB p. 277; TDOT IV:106-109; NIDOTTE 1:1138-1139; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 277; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 75; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 479; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 306; von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972 p. 371.

terms.translit: sallei chori (v 16); sal — basket, plural sallim (v 18)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun phrase: construct plural noun (sallei) + noun (chori, of uncertain sense)
terms.literal: sallei chori — baskets of chori; chori (debated): white bread / fine white food / openwork (wicker) baskets / holes
terms.standardEnglish: baskets of white bread (ASV/KJV); baskets of white bread (NJPS); cake baskets / wicker baskets (NRSV margin); openwork baskets (various)
terms.wohChoice: three baskets of white bread (ASV-baseline; the chori hapax and its competing readings — white bread / white baskets / wicker — documented here, not adjudicated)
terms.rationale: **Genesis 40:16 reports the baker's dream: *shelosha sallei chori al-roshi* — 'three baskets of* chori *on my head'. The word *chori* (חֹרִי) is a hapax legomenon — it occurs ONLY here in the Hebrew Bible — and its sense is genuinely contested.** The basket-noun *sal* itself is secure (a wicker basket, also for the unleavened bread of the priestly ordination, Exod 29:3, 23; Lev 8:2, 26; Num 6:15, 17); the uncertainty is wholly in *chori*. // **The competing readings.** (a) **'white bread' / 'fine white food'** — the traditional reading, taking *chori* as related to חוּר (*chur*, 'white' / 'white stuff', cf. *chori* understood as 'white bread', the fine white bread of the Egyptian court; LXX χονδριτῶν, 'of fine/groats bread'; Vulgate *farinae*, 'of flour'). This yields ASV/KJV/NJPS 'baskets of white bread'. The reading suits the context (the *uppermost* basket holds *ma'aseh ofeh*, 'baked goods', v 17). (b) **'white baskets'** — taking *chori* (from *chur*, white) as modifying the *baskets* rather than their contents: 'three white baskets' (ASV margin). (c) **'openwork / wicker / perforated baskets'** — taking *chori* from חֹר / חוֹר (*chor*, 'hole'), so 'baskets full of holes' = open-weave wicker baskets (through which the birds of v 17 could the more readily get at the bread); this etymology is favored by several modern philologists and is reflected in NRSV-tradition 'cake baskets / wicker'. (d) a possibly defective or corrupt form, given the hapax-status. The principal/traditional reading is (a) 'white bread'; the entry does NOT adjudicate beyond noting it. // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'three baskets of white bread'** (the *chori*-as-white-bread reading; ASV margin 'white baskets'), per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention. The hapax-status and the competing readings (white bread / white baskets / wicker-openwork) are documented here; the lexeme is too uncertain to license any marked surface rendering, and per the report-don't-adjudicate posture the entry records the debate without resolving it. // **Overlay housing.** *Chori* is a hapax legomenon — by definition it has no cross-corpus reach (zero other occurrences) — and the basket-vision is chapter-singular → **overlay**, per the ratified split (hapax / chapter-singular → overlay). // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) 'white bread' is the traditional-and-dominant reading but is itself an interpretive reconstruction of an uncertain hapax; (b) the competing readings are all lexically arguable; (c) the ASV-baseline 'white bread' stands on the surface while the apparatus carries the full uncertainty. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *chori* (registering the uncertainty); BDB p. 360; NIDOTTE 2:288; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 277 (the white-bread reading, noting the difficulty); Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 75 ('the meaning is uncertain'); Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 480 n. (surveying white-bread vs wicker); Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 306; von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972 p. 371; for the LXX/Vulgate witnesses: J. W. Wevers *Notes on the Greek Text of Genesis* SBLSCS 35, 1993 ad loc.

terms.translit: achu (with preposition ba-achu, 'in the reed-grass'; vv 2, 18)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun (Egyptian loanword)
terms.literal: achu — Nile-bank reed-grass / reed-marsh vegetation / marsh-meadow (from Eg. *3ḫw* / *ahy*, 'reed, reed-marsh, Nile-vegetation')
terms.standardEnglish: meadow (KJV); reed-grass (ASV/NRSV); marsh (modern); reed-thicket (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: reed-grass (ASV-baseline; the Egyptian-loanword Nile-marsh-vegetation sense documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 41:2 and 41:18 describe the seven well-favored kine grazing *ba-achu* — *in the* achu. The noun *achu* (אָחוּ) is an Egyptian loanword (from Eg. *3ḫw* / *ahy*, 'reed, reed-marsh, Nile-bank vegetation') and a near-hapax in the HB: it occurs only here (vv 2, 18) and in Job 8:11 (*ha-yig'eh achu beli-mayim*, 'can the reed-grass grow without water?' — there in a wisdom-context about life's dependence on water). The Egyptian-loanword status and the Nile-marsh-vegetation sense are settled philology.** // **The lexeme.** *Achu* names the reed-grass and marsh-vegetation of the Nile-bank — the dense water-plant cover where cattle would graze along the river's edge. The Egyptian *3ḫw* refers specifically to the Nile-marsh ecology: the papyrus, reeds, and water-plants of the river's marshy fringes, which formed the natural grazing-ground for Nile-Delta cattle. The Hebrew *achu* preserves the Egyptian noun by direct loan. The Job 8:11 occurrence pairs *achu* with *gome* ('papyrus'), confirming the marsh-vegetation sense (papyrus and reed-grass together — the classical Nile-Delta plant-pair). // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'reed-grass'** at vv 2 and 18 — the philologically accurate rendering of the Nile-marsh-vegetation sense. The older KJV 'meadow' is functionally correct (a meadow is grazing-ground) but obscures the Egyptian Nile-marsh specificity; 'reed-grass' captures the dense water-plant cover the Egyptian original names. The Egyptian-loanword status and the cross-corpus reach (Job 8:11) are documented in commentary. // **Overlay housing.** The lemma is a near-hapax in the HB — only Gen 41:2, 18 + Job 8:11. Cross-corpus reach in the active corpus is limited (one Job occurrence, outside the near-term translation queue). The decision is therefore housed in the **overlay** per the ratified split (chapter-singular / near-singular → overlay). If a future Wisdom-corpus translation activates the Job 8:11 occurrence, the entry's appliesTo will extend, and promotion to central could be considered (though the cross-corpus reach is small enough that overlay-housing may remain the right call even after Job is drafted). // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the Egyptian-loanword etymology (*achu* < Eg. *3ḫw*) is settled philological consensus; (b) the Nile-marsh-vegetation sense is the standard reading; (c) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *achu*; BDB p. 28; TDOT I:227-228; NIDOTTE 1:351; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 283; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 89; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 489; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 312; for the Eg. *3ḫw* etymology and Nile-marsh-ecology: J. Vergote *Joseph en Égypte* 1959 pp. 50-52; D. B. Redford *A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph* VTSup 20, 1970 pp. 203-206; for Job 8:11: D. J. A. Clines *Job 1-20* WBC 17, 1989.

terms.translit: tzenumot (feminine plural participle; v 23, modifying shibbolim 'ears of grain' in Pharaoh's retelling)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, qal passive participle, feminine plural
terms.literal: tzenumot — withered / shrivelled / hard, dry (a hapax legomenon; cognates uncertain)
terms.standardEnglish: withered (ASV/KJV/NJPS/NRSV); shrivelled (modern); hard / dry (some)
terms.wohChoice: withered (ASV-baseline; the hapax-status and the lack of secure cognate evidence documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 41:23 introduces a feature absent from the narrator's first account of the dream (v 6): Pharaoh's retelling adds the participle *tzenumot* (צְנֻמוֹת) — 'withered / shrivelled' — to the description of the second set of ears. The form is a hapax legomenon in the Hebrew Bible (occurring only here) and the root *tz-n-m* is otherwise unattested in BH.** // **The lexical situation.** The root *tz-n-m* has no other HB occurrence and no securely-attested cognates in the cognate-Semitic languages. Proposed cognates include: (a) Arabic *ṣanama* ('to be hard, dry') — the most-frequently-cited proposal, supporting the 'withered / dry' rendering; (b) Aramaic *tznm* (proposed root with similar sense) — less securely attested; (c) Akkadian comparanda have been suggested but are debated. None of the proposed cognates is decisive. The hapax-status combined with the lack of secure cognate evidence makes the rendering genuinely uncertain — but the contextual sense (parallel to the v 6 *daqqot u-shedufot kadim*, 'thin and blasted with the east wind'; v 23's *tzenumot daqqot shedufot kadim*, 'withered, thin, and blasted with the east wind') strongly favors a withering / drying-out reading. // **Why the addition?** The variation between v 6 (narrator's account) and v 23 (Pharaoh's retelling) is part of the chapter's documented narrator-vs-character retelling-pattern. Pharaoh's retelling consistently adds affective intensifiers absent from the leaner narrator-account: *dallot* ('poor') at v 19 beyond v 3; the superlative *lo-ra'iti khahennah be-khol eretz Mitsrayim la-roa* ('such as I never saw in all the land of Mitsrayim for badness'); the not-be-known clause at v 21; *tzenumot* here. The retelling-variation pattern is a recognized literary observation (Sarna, Alter — Pharaoh's retelling registers his lingering distress; the narrator's account is clinical). // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'withered'** at v 23, per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention — 'withered' is the dominant English rendering across KJV/ASV/NJPS/NRSV, captures the contextual withering / drying-out sense, and is the principal traditional reading. The hapax-status and the lack of secure cognate evidence are documented in commentary so the reader can audit the philological uncertainty. Report-don't-adjudicate posture. // **Overlay housing.** A hapax legomenon has zero cross-corpus reach by definition → **overlay**. The lemma is unlikely ever to recur (no other HB occurrence of *tz-n-m*); a hapax cannot be promoted to central unless cognate-language scholarship establishes a recoverable lexical-decision-pattern, which is not the case here. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) 'withered' is the traditional-and-dominant reading but is itself an interpretive reconstruction of an uncertain hapax; (b) the proposed cognates are suggestive but not decisive; (c) the contextual reading is strong but rests on the v 6 parallel rather than on the word in isolation. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *tzanam* (registering the uncertainty); BDB p. 855; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 284; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 90; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 493; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 312; for the Arabic *ṣanama* cognate: HALOT s.v.; the standard philological dictionaries.

terms.translit: ve-chimmesh (Piel of ch-m-sh, v 34, Yosef's administrative-policy verb)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Piel perfect (consecutive), 3ms
terms.literal: ch-m-sh (Piel) — 'to fifth' (denominative); debated between (a) 'to take the fifth part' (institute a 20% tax), and (b) 'to organize / muster in five [divisions]' (cognate to chamushim, 'in battle-array', Exod 13:18)
terms.standardEnglish: take up the fifth part (ASV/KJV); organize / muster (less common); take a fifth (NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: take up the fifth part (ASV-baseline, the dominant tax-reading; the administrative-reading alternative documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 41:34 records Yosef's administrative-policy proposal: *ya'aseh Par'oh ve-yafqed peqidim al ha-aretz ve-chimmesh et-eretz Mitzrayim ba-sheva shenei ha-sava* — 'Let Pharaoh do this, and let him appoint overseers over the land, and* [chimmesh] *the land of Mitsrayim in the seven plenteous years.' The Piel verb *chimmesh* (וְחִמֵּשׁ) is a denominative from *chamesh* ('five') and is debated between two readings, with substantial implications for what Yosef's policy actually was.** // **The two readings.** // **(a) The tax-reading: 'take up the fifth part'.** The dominant English-tradition reading takes *chimmesh* as denominative of *chamishit* ('fifth part / fifth share'), yielding 'to take up the fifth part' — that is, to institute a **20% grain-tax** on the harvest during the seven plenteous years. The reading fits the chapter's storage-and-distribution narrative (vv 35-36, gathering food *tachat yad-Par'oh*, 'under Pharaoh's hand', as a national reserve), and the v 48 + v 49 description of Yosef's gathering. ASV / KJV / NJPS / NRSV uniformly follow the tax-reading. The reading also fits the Gen 47:24-26 *chomesh la-Par'oh* ('the fifth shall be for Pharaoh') — the institutionalized 20% land-tax that Gen 47 explicitly establishes as the ongoing post-famine tax-rate. On this reading Gen 41:34 is the policy-initiation of which Gen 47:24-26 is the permanent codification. // **(b) The administrative-reading: 'organize / muster in five [divisions]'.** A minority reading takes *chimmesh* as cognate to *chamushim* ('in battle-array', 'in fives' / 'arrayed-by-fives' — the Exodus march-formation, Exod 13:18, Josh 1:14, 4:12, Judg 7:11). On this reading the verb means 'to organize-by-fives / to muster / to deploy in administrative-fifths', and Yosef's proposal is an administrative restructuring of the country into five regional districts (or divisions) for tax-collection and grain-storage purposes. The reading is supported by the verb's morphology (a denominative Piel that more naturally yields the organizational-action sense than the tax-collection sense), by the *chamushim* cognate, and by some modern commentators (Speiser noting the alternative; some Egyptological readings linking it to the Egyptian regional-administrative-district system). On this reading Gen 47:24-26's *chomesh la-Par'oh* is a separate institution (a fifth-share-as-tax) not directly continuous with Gen 41:34's administrative-fives. // **Which reading is right?** The tax-reading is strongly supported by the Gen 47:24-26 cross-reference (the institutionalized fifth-share tax is the natural fulfilment of a 'take-the-fifth' policy), and is the dominant English-tradition reading. The administrative-reading has lexical support from the *chamushim* cognate and is the natural denominative-Piel sense. The two readings are not strictly incompatible: a tax-collection program of any kind would require administrative organization, and a 'fifth-share' policy fits naturally with regional administrative-fifths. The entry adopts the tax-reading on the surface (per ASV/KJV/dominant tradition) and documents the administrative-reading alternative. // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'take up the fifth part'** at v 34, per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention — the tax-reading is dominant, fits the Gen 47:24-26 cross-reference, and is the standard English. The administrative-reading and the *chamushim* cognate are documented in commentary. // **Overlay housing.** The lemma's specific Piel-of-ch-m-sh-as-administrative-policy-verb sense is chapter-singular in the active corpus. The cross-corpus *chamushim* ('in battle-array') is a different word-form and is governed by other contexts (Exodus, Joshua, Judges); the *chamishit* / *chomesh* ('fifth part') as a noun is governed by other entries when those contexts are drafted. The chapter-singular Piel-verb at issue here is housed in the **overlay**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) both readings are lexically defensible; (b) the choice is interpretive (driven by the Gen 47:24-26 cross-reference + dominant tradition vs the morphological *chamushim* cognate); (c) the ASV-baseline tax-reading stands on the surface while the apparatus carries the administrative-reading alternative. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *chamash* (Piel) — registering both readings; BDB p. 332; NIDOTTE 2:166-167; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 285; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 92; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 497; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 312 (noting the alternative); von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972 p. 376; for the Gen 47:24-26 cross-reference and the post-famine taxation-institution: M. Weinfeld 'The Counsel of the Elders to Rehoboam' in *Studies in Bible 1986* (S. Japhet ed.); for the Egyptian regional-administrative background: J. Vergote *Joseph en Égypte* 1959 pp. 117-120; D. B. Redford *A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph* VTSup 20, 1970 pp. 209-211.

terms.translit: ve-al pikha yishshaq kol ammi (v 40)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, qal imperfect, 3ms (with prepositional phrase al pikha 'upon thy mouth')
terms.literal: nashaq — to kiss / to render homage by kissing; (derived sense) to be ruled / governed by [a command]; (proposed sense) to arm / equip (cf. neshek, 'weapon')
terms.standardEnglish: shall be ruled (ASV/KJV); shall order themselves (NJPS); shall do homage (NRSV); shall kiss [thy mouth] (Alter — literal)
terms.wohChoice: shall be ruled (ASV-baseline; the homage-by-obedience reading documented in commentary alongside the literal kiss-reading and the arm/equip reading)
terms.rationale: **Gen 41:40 is the climactic line of Pharaoh's elevation-speech: *ata tihyeh al-beti ve-al pikha yishshaq kol-ammi raq ha-kisse egdal mimekka* — 'thou shalt be over my house, and according unto thy word shall all my people* [yishshaq]: *only in the throne will I be greater than thou.' The verb *yishshaq* — the third-singular imperfect of the root *n-sh-q* — is genuinely ambiguous, and the choice of reading bears on what authority Pharaoh is actually delegating.** // **The lexeme and the three readings.** The verb *nashaq* (נשק) has three attested senses in the HB: (a) **'to kiss'** — the primary literal sense (Gen 27:26-27, Yitzchaq kisses Ya'aqov; widely attested); (b) **derived from kissing as a gesture of homage / submission** — 'to render homage by kissing' (1 Sam 10:1, Shmuel kisses Sha'ul at his anointing; Ps 2:12, *nashku bar*, 'kiss the son'; Hos 13:2, kissing-calves as an idolatrous-homage gesture); (c) **'to arm / equip with weapons'** — a separate root or homonymous root *n-sh-q* II, attested in *neshek* ('weapon') and *nesheq* ('armament') and in the verbal sense at 1 Chr 12:2 (*noshqei qeshet*, 'archers, those-who-handle-the-bow') and Ps 78:9 (*noshqei romei-qashet*, 'shooters / armed-with-the-bow'). The three readings yield three different translations: // **(a) The homage-by-obedience reading: 'shall be ruled / shall do homage'.** The ASV/KJV tradition reads *yishshaq* as the homage-sense (derived from kissing-as-homage) and supplies the contextual sense 'shall be ruled by thy word' / 'shall render homage at thy command'. The reading takes *al pikha* ('upon thy mouth' = at / by thy word) as the instrumental of the homage. The reading has the advantage of being the dominant English tradition and giving a clean political sense (Yosef governs by word; the people submit at his command). // **(b) The literal kiss-the-mouth reading: 'shall kiss thy mouth'.** Some modern commentators (Alter) preserve the literal kissing-sense, reading *al pikha yishshaq* as 'shall kiss thy mouth' — the people kissing Yosef's mouth as the homage-gesture. The reading preserves the lexical primacy of *nashaq* and reads the *al pikha* as the literal location of the kiss. The reading has the advantage of literal-fidelity and registers the physical homage-gesture; its weakness is that 'kiss the mouth' is an unusual homage-formula (the standard homage-kiss is to the hand or to the ground, not to the mouth). // **(c) The arm/equip reading: 'shall arm themselves at thy command'.** A minority reading takes *yishshaq* as the homonymous *n-sh-q* II ('to arm / equip with weapons'), yielding 'shall arm themselves at thy command' — Yosef as commander-in-chief, the people arming themselves at his word. The reading has the advantage of fitting the *neshek* 'weapon' cognate; its weakness is that the military-sense fits the v 40 context less naturally than the political-administrative sense. // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'shall all my people be ruled'** at v 40, per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention — the homage-by-obedience reading is the dominant English tradition and fits the elevation-speech context. The literal kiss-reading (Alter) and the arm/equip reading (the *neshek* cognate) are documented in commentary. // **Overlay housing.** The lemma's specific construction at this verse — *al pikha yishshaq* in the elevation-context — is chapter-singular. Cross-corpus *nashaq* in its various senses (kissing, homage, arming) is governed by other contexts. The chapter-singular philological crux is housed in the **overlay**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the three readings are all lexically defensible; (b) the choice is interpretive (driven by tradition + context vs literal vs cognate-arming); (c) the ASV-baseline stands on the surface with the alternatives in apparatus. Report-don't-adjudicate posture. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *nashaq* I and II; BDB pp. 676-677; TDOT X:75-78; NIDOTTE 3:204-205; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 286-287 (surveying the readings); Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 95; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 506; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 313; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 238 (the literal kiss-reading).

terms.translit: mirkevet ha-mishneh (v 43, the chariot in which Yosef rides at his investiture-procession)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun phrase: feminine noun in construct + definite masculine noun
terms.literal: mirkevet ha-mishneh — 'the chariot of the second' or 'the chariot of the deputy' (depending on the reading of mishneh)
terms.standardEnglish: the second chariot (ASV/KJV — ordinal); his other chariot / second-best chariot (NJPS-style); the chariot of his second-in-command (some commentators — office-title)
terms.wohChoice: the second chariot (ASV-baseline, the ordinal reading; the office-title alternative — 'chariot of the deputy / vizier' — documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 41:43 records Yosef's investiture-procession: *va-yarkev oto be-mirkevet ha-mishneh asher lo* — 'and he made him to ride in* [mirkevet ha-mishneh] *which he had'. The construct *mirkevet ha-mishneh* turns on the reading of *mishneh* (מִשְׁנֶה), and the choice bears on whether the verse describes the chariot's *rank* (ordinal) or Yosef's *office* (deputy / vizier).** // **The two readings.** // **(a) The ordinal reading: 'the second chariot'.** *Mishneh* in the simple ordinal-sense — 'second, secondary, the second-of-its-kind'. *Mirkevet ha-mishneh* = 'the second chariot', i.e., the chariot ranked immediately after Pharaoh's own. On this reading Yosef rides in the king's second-best chariot in the investiture-procession — a high honor (riding in a royal chariot, second only to Pharaoh's own) without specifying a formal office-title. This is the ASV/KJV reading, supported by the broader sense of *mishneh* as 'second-of-its-kind' (Gen 43:12 *kesef mishneh*, 'double money'; the *mishneh torah* of Deut 17:18, 'a copy of the law'). // **(b) The office-title reading: 'the chariot of the deputy / second-in-command'.** *Mishneh* as the formal office-title of the **deputy / second-in-command / vizier**. Cross-corpus support: 2 Chr 28:7 (*Elqanah mishneh ha-melekh*, 'Elqanah the king's second-in-command'); Esth 10:3 (*Mordekhai... mishneh la-melekh Achashverosh*, 'Mordekhai... second to King Achashverosh'); 1 Sam 23:17 (David's promise that Yehonatan will be his *mishneh*, 'second-in-command'). On this reading *mirkevet ha-mishneh* is 'the chariot of the (office of the) deputy / the vizier's chariot' — and the verse marks Yosef's accession to the formal vizier-office (mirroring v 40 *ata tihyeh al-beti*, 'thou shalt be over my house'). The reading fits the chapter's elevation-narrative (Yosef now holds the formal second-in-command office; the chariot is the office's official transport) and is supported by the Egyptological evidence for the Egyptian vizier-office and its insignia (Vergote, Redford). // **Which reading is right?** Both are lexically defensible. The ordinal reading is the simpler grammatical default; the office-title reading is the more contextually-loaded narrative-reading. The cross-corpus evidence for *mishneh* as office-title is solid (2 Chr 28:7; Esth 10:3; 1 Sam 23:17), but those occurrences use *mishneh ha-melekh* / *mishneh la-melekh* explicitly (the office in relation to the king), not the standalone construct *mirkevet ha-mishneh* found here. The entry presents both readings without committing the surface to the office-title interpretation. // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'the second chariot'** at v 43, per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention — the ordinal reading is the dominant English-tradition rendering and is the simpler grammatical default. The office-title reading ('chariot of the deputy / vizier') and the cross-corpus *mishneh ha-melekh* parallels are documented in commentary. // **Overlay housing.** The specific construct *mirkevet ha-mishneh* in this verse is chapter-singular (the construct does not recur elsewhere in this form). Cross-corpus *mishneh* in its various senses is governed by other contexts (Esther, Chronicles, the Davidic narratives) and would warrant its own entry when those texts are drafted. The chapter-singular construct is housed in the **overlay**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) both readings are lexically defensible; (b) the choice is interpretive (driven by the simpler ordinal-default vs the contextually-loaded office-title reading); (c) the ASV-baseline ordinal stands on the surface. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *mishneh*; BDB p. 1041; TDOT XV:71-77; NIDOTTE 4:104-106; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 287; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 96; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 506; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 313; for the Egyptian vizier-office: J. Vergote *Joseph en Égypte* 1959 pp. 102-115; D. B. Redford *A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph* VTSup 20, 1970 pp. 187-192.

terms.translit: li-qmatzim (v 47, distributive prepositional-phrase with the noun qomets 'handful' in the plural)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun phrase: preposition le- + plural noun qmatzim (from qomets)
terms.literal: li-qmatzim — 'by handfuls / in handfuls / handful-by-handful' (distributive plural of qomets, the priestly grain-offering handful)
terms.standardEnglish: by handfuls (ASV/KJV); in abundance / abundantly (NJPS, NRSV); in heaps (modern paraphrase); copiously (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: by handfuls (ASV-baseline; the literal-distributive sense and the qomets cognate-context — the priest's handful of grain-offering — documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 41:47 records the abundance of the seven plenteous years in a rare distributive construction: *va-ta'as ha-aretz be-sheva shenei ha-sava li-qmatzim* — 'And in the seven plenteous years the earth brought forth* li-qmatzim'. The phrase is morphologically a distributive prepositional-phrase (preposition *le-* + plural noun *qmatzim*, from the singular *qomets*, 'handful'), and the rendering is genuinely debated between a literal-distributive sense and a metaphorical-intensive sense.** // **The lexeme.** *Qomets* (קֹמֶץ) — 'handful' — is from the verb *q-m-tz* ('to grasp a handful'), the action of closing the hand around a quantity. The noun's standard HB usage is in the **priestly grain-offering** instructions: Lev 2:2; 5:12; 6:8 [MT 6:1] — the priest takes a *qomets* of fine flour (with oil and frankincense) as the memorial-portion of the *minchah* (grain-offering), which is then burned on the altar while the rest goes to the priests. The 'handful' is the technical priestly measure for the memorial-portion. // **The two readings.** // **(a) The literal-distributive reading: 'by handfuls'.** The KJV/ASV reading takes *li-qmatzim* as the literal distributive plural — the earth brought forth grain *handful-by-handful*, each individual plant producing handfuls of grain. The image is of agricultural abundance imagined literally: the ground bringing forth grain in such quantity that each stalk gives a handful. // **(b) The metaphorical-intensive reading: 'in abundance / abundantly'.** The NJPS / NRSV tradition reads *li-qmatzim* metaphorically — 'in abundance', 'abundantly', 'in heaps', 'copiously' — the distributive plural functioning as an intensifier rather than a literal count. The reading explains the construction as an idiom for abundance rather than as a specific quantitative claim. // **Which reading is right?** Both are lexically defensible. The literal-distributive reading is the simpler grammatical default and preserves the *qomets* cognate-context (the priestly-handful associations). The metaphorical-intensive reading is the more idiomatic-modern reading and explains the construction as a stock abundance-idiom. The entry presents both. The ASV/KJV literal reading has the advantage of preserving the priestly *qomets* cognate-resonance (each priest's handful at the altar = each plant's handful at harvest, an unintended liturgical echo). // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'by handfuls'** at v 47, per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention — 'by handfuls' is the dominant English tradition, preserves the *qomets* cognate-context, and is the simpler literal reading. The metaphorical-abundance alternative is documented in commentary. // **Overlay housing.** The specific *li-qmatzim* construction is chapter-singular. Cross-corpus *qomets* in the priestly grain-offering sense is governed by Lev 2:2; 5:12; 6:8 (and would receive its own entry when Leviticus is drafted). The chapter-singular construction is housed in the **overlay**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) both readings are lexically defensible; (b) the choice is interpretive (literal-distributive vs metaphorical-intensive idiom); (c) the ASV-baseline literal reading stands on the surface. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *qomets*; BDB p. 888; TDOT XIII:75-77; NIDOTTE 3:957; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 289; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 98; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 510; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 314; for the priestly *qomets*-of-grain-offering: J. Milgrom *Leviticus 1-16* AB 1991.

terms.source: כִּי־נָכוֹן הַדָּבָר מֵעִם הָאֱלֹהִים וּמְמַהֵר הָאֱלֹהִים לַעֲשֹׂתוֹ
terms.translit: ki-nakhon ha-davar me-im ha-Elohim u-memaher ha-Elohim la'asoto (v 32, Yosef's articulation of the doubling-as-confirmation principle)
terms.strongs: H8138 (shanah, 'to repeat / double', Niphal hishshanot) + H3559 (kun, Niphal nakhon 'established') + H4116 (mahar, Piel memaher 'hastening')
terms.partOfSpeech: principle / interpretive-theological observation (named in narrative speech as the doubled-dream-meaning)
terms.literal: the dream-doubling-as-confirmation principle: a dream doubled to its dreamer signals that the matter is established (nakhon) by the Elohim and the Elohim is hastening (memaher) to do it
terms.standardEnglish: it is because the thing is established by God, and God will shortly bring it to pass (ASV/KJV); it shows that the matter has been determined by God and that God will soon carry it out (NJPS); it means that the matter is fixed by God and God will quickly do it (modern paraphrases)
terms.wohChoice: the matter is established by the Elohim, and the Elohim will shortly bring it to pass (ASV-baseline; the dream-doubling-as-confirmation principle articulated as a sibling node to the central pitron entry)
terms.rationale: **Gen 41:32 articulates explicitly the dream-doubling-as-confirmation principle: *ve-al hishshanot ha-chalom el-Par'oh pa'amayim ki-nakhon ha-davar me-im ha-Elohim u-memaher ha-Elohim la'asoto* — 'And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh, it is because the thing is established by the Elohim, and the Elohim will shortly bring it to pass.' The verse states the interpretive principle as Yosef's own teaching: **a dream doubled to its dreamer is a sign of (a) divine certainty (*nakhon*, 'established / fixed / determined') and (b) divine imminence (*memaher*, 'hastening')**. The principle is a sibling-node to the central `pitron-dream-interpretation-yosef-cycle` entry: where the central entry governs the lexical-keyword *pitron* (the dream-as-symbolic-puzzle, the act of decoding), this entry governs the principle by which a *particular feature* of the dream-form (its doubling) signals a *particular interpretive content* (certainty + imminence).** // **The principle in its narrative context.** The principle is articulated immediately after Yosef has decoded the two dreams as one (vv 25-31): the seven cattle and the seven ears are seven years; the seven good cattle/ears are seven years of plenty; the seven ill-favored / withered cattle/ears are seven years of famine. The doubled-dream signals that the famine will surely come and will come soon. The principle thus has explanatory work to do in the narrative: it justifies the urgency of Yosef's proposed policy (vv 33-36) and explains why Pharaoh should act immediately rather than waiting to see whether the dream's prediction holds. // **The principle's reach across the cycle and beyond.** The principle resonates as a node across several dream-doublings in the broader corpus: // **(a) Backward within Yosef's own dream-experience.** Gen 37 records Yosef's own *doubled* dreams (the sheaves-and-stars pair, 37:5-11) — exactly the doubled-dream-form whose meaning Yosef now articulates. The two Gen 37 dreams say one thing (the brothers will bow to Yosef), and the doubling — on the principle Yosef now states — would signal that the matter is *nakhon* (established) and *memaher* (imminent). The retrospective resonance is editorially deliberate: Yosef's articulation of the principle here illuminates his own opening dreams. // **(b) Backward within Gen 40.** Gen 40 records the *paired* dreams of the chief cupbearer and chief baker — not doubled to one dreamer, but paired across two dreamers in one night. The pairing is a related but distinct phenomenon; the doubling-to-one-dreamer of Gen 41 sharpens the principle's specificity. // **(c) Within Gen 41 itself.** The chapter doubles the cattle-dream with the ears-dream — Yosef's articulation explains the doubling as the certainty-and-imminence sign. // **(d) Forward to Daniel.** Dan 2 records Nebuchadnezzar's dream which Daniel decodes (the cross-corpus *chartumim* parallel; see central `chartumim-egyptian-lector-priests`); Dan 4 records a *second* Nebuchadnezzar dream (the great tree) — the two Nebuchadnezzar dreams function as a doubled-dream-across-time, both interpreted by Daniel, both fulfilled. The Daniel-Nebuchadnezzar narrative draws on the same dream-doubling-as-confirmation principle the Gen 41 verse articulates. Rabbinic and post-biblical dream-interpretation traditions explicitly cite the v 32 principle as the locus classicus for the doubled-dream theology. // **Cross-reference (bidirectional) to the central `pitron-dream-interpretation-yosef-cycle` entry.** The two entries are deliberate companions: the central *pitron* entry governs the **lexical keyword** of the dream-decoding (*pitron* / *p-t-r*) — the act, the office, the technical vocabulary; this overlay entry governs an **interpretive principle** articulated *within* the dream-decoding narrative — a stated theology of one particular dream-feature (the doubling). They are not duplicate entries: one is lexical, the other is principle-of-interpretation. Each names the other; the central *pitron* entry will be updated in a future scope-pass to reference this sibling-overlay (which the chapter-41 commentary at v 32 already does textually). // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline rendering at v 32: 'And for that the dream was doubled unto Pharaoh, it is because the thing is established by the Elohim, and the Elohim will shortly bring it to pass.' No surface rendering choice is at issue here — the verse is uncontested on the surface; the entry exists to record the interpretive principle the verse articulates and to cross-link it to the central pitron entry and to the dream-doubling-resonances across the cycle and into Daniel. // **Overlay housing.** The principle is articulated only here in the HB (Gen 41:32). The resonances across Gen 37 / Gen 40 / Dan 2-4 are interpretive cross-references, not lexical recurrences. The locus of articulation is chapter-singular → **overlay**, with the bidirectional cross-reference to the central pitron entry. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the principle is grammatically explicit in the verse (the *al hishshanot... ki-nakhon ha-davar... u-memaher* construction states it as Yosef's plain teaching); (b) the doublings within the Yosef-cycle and into Daniel are lexically verifiable; (c) the principle's documentation in named scholarship (Sarna, Alter, Husser; the rabbinic tradition explicitly) is settled. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 285 (on the doubling-as-confirmation principle); Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 236; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 92-93; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 495-496; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 313; for the cross-corpus dream-doubling resonances: A. L. Oppenheim *The Interpretation of Dreams in the Ancient Near East* 1956; J.-M. Husser *Dreams and Dream Narratives in the Biblical World* 1999; for the Daniel parallels: J. J. Collins *Daniel* Hermeneia 1993; for the rabbinic tradition on doubled-dreams: *b. Berakhot* 55a-57b (the dream-interpretation sections of the Berakhot dream-tractate).

terms.translit: ish asher ruach Elohim bo (v 38, Pharaoh's recognition of Yosef as a man in whom the spirit of Elohim is)
terms.partOfSpeech: construct phrase (ruach Elohim) deployed within a relative clause (ish asher... bo, 'a man in whom...')
terms.literal: ruach Elohim in a person — the spirit / breath of Elohim resident in an individual, in the sense of charismatic-wisdom, prophetic-craft capacity, or divinely-granted discernment (distinct from the cosmic ruach Elohim of Gen 1:2, the wind/breath/spirit hovering over the waters in creation)
terms.standardEnglish: the spirit of God (ASV/KJV/NJPS/NRSV); the divine spirit (modern); a man inspired by God (paraphrase)
terms.wohChoice: the spirit of Elohim (ASV-baseline; the in-a-person sense documented in commentary as a sibling-node to the cosmic-creation ruach Elohim of Gen 1:2)
terms.rationale: **Gen 41:38 records Pharaoh's recognition of Yosef after the dream-decoding: *ha-nimtza kazeh ish asher ruach Elohim bo* — 'Can we find such a one as this, a man in whom the spirit of Elohim is?' The phrase *ruach Elohim* (רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים) here is the same lexical construct as Gen 1:2 (*ruach Elohim merachefet al-penei ha-mayim*, 'the spirit of Elohim was moving over the face of the waters'), but the phenomenological category is distinct: Gen 1:2 is the **cosmic-creation** ruach (the breath/wind/spirit at the threshold of creation), Gen 41:38 is the **in-a-person** ruach (the spirit / charisma / discernment resident in an individual). The entry documents this distinction as a sibling-node to the central `ruach-elohim` (Gen 1:2) entry — both renderings preserved, no harmonization, no WoH synthesis.** // **The in-a-person ruach Elohim — a distinct phenomenological category.** Across the HB, the in-a-person ruach Elohim (or ruach YHWH) is a standard register for divinely-granted capacities — charismatic-leadership, prophetic-utterance, craft-skill, judgment-discernment. The construction is *ruach + X bo* (the spirit X is in him), or *ruach + X yarad / haytah / labshah al X* (the spirit X came down / was / clothed X). The major HB attestations: // - **Exod 31:3** + **35:31** — Betzalel filled with *ruach Elohim be-chokhmah u-vitvunah u-veda'at u-ve-khol-melakhah* ('the spirit of Elohim in wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all craftsmanship'); for the construction of the tabernacle. // - **Num 11:17, 25, 29** — Moshe's *ruach* taken and shared with the seventy elders; the explicit charismatic-leadership extension. // - **Num 24:2** — Bil'am *va-tehi alav ruach Elohim*; the prophetic-utterance Spirit. // - **Judges** — repeatedly: Otniel (Judg 3:10), Gideon (6:34, *labshah et-Gid'on*), Yiftach (11:29), Shimshon (13:25; 14:6, 19; 15:14). The charismatic-leadership Spirit on the judges. // - **1 Sam 10:6, 10** — Sha'ul; **16:13** — David at his anointing. // - **Isa 11:2** — the messianic Spirit (*ruach YHWH... ruach chokhmah u-vinah... ruach etzah u-gevurah...*) — the in-a-person Spirit at its most theologically loaded. // - **Ezek 2:2, 3:24** — Ezekiel; **36:27, 37:14** — the eschatological in-a-person Spirit. // - **Dan 4:5 [MT 4:8], 5:11, 5:14, 6:4 [MT 6:3]** — Daniel: *ruach Elohin qaddishin bo* ('the spirit of the holy gods is in him'; Aramaic) — the closest verbal parallel to Gen 41:38 (Babylonian-court setting, foreign-king's recognition of a divinely-endowed Israelite interpreter; the explicit Yosef-Daniel literary parallel). // **The Gen 41:38 occurrence sits at the head of this in-a-person tradition.** Yosef is the first HB character of whom another character (Pharaoh) explicitly says *ruach Elohim bo* — the recognition-formula that becomes a structural feature of later narratives. Pharaoh's recognition is **functional**: based on the discernment Yosef just displayed in the dream-decoding. The recognition is not a theophany-claim about Yosef's nature; it is a court-observer's attribution of a charismatic capacity. The Daniel-Belshazzar parallel (Dan 5:11) is the closest verbal echo and the most explicit literary continuation. // **Distinction from the Gen 1:2 cosmic ruach.** The Gen 1:2 *ruach Elohim* operates at a different category: it is the breath/wind/spirit at the threshold of cosmic creation, *merachefet al-penei ha-mayim* ('hovering over the face of the waters'). The phenomenology is cosmic, not personal; the action is hovering-over-water, not residing-in-a-person; the context is creation, not court-recognition. The central `ruach-elohim` entry (anchored at Gen 1:2) records the breath/wind-of-Elohim reading and the WoH 'breath of Elohim' choice for the surface there. The Gen 41:38 in-a-person sense is **not the same category** and a single appliesTo extension would conflate two distinct phenomenological uses. The sibling-overlay-entries pattern (the ratified architectural pattern; cf. the *tz-ch-q* polysemy-cluster, the Yisrael-renaming P-doublet, the Esav-wives-list, etc.) is the appropriate response: a sibling entry for the in-a-person sense, with bidirectional cross-reference, governing the specific phenomenological category. // **Cross-reference (bidirectional) to the central `ruach-elohim` entry.** This entry names the central entry (which it is sibling to); the central entry will be updated in a future scope-pass to reference this sibling (the chapter-41 commentary at v 38 already does so textually). The two entries together map the *ruach Elohim* construction across its two phenomenological registers — cosmic-creation (Gen 1:2) and in-a-person (Gen 41:38, and the cross-corpus tradition). // **The translation choice.** The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline **'the spirit of Elohim'** at v 38 ('a man in whom the spirit of Elohim is'), per the accuracy-above-lens / ASV-baseline convention — 'spirit' here captures the in-a-person charismatic-capacity sense (where 'breath / wind' would be unnatural in English for the in-a-person register). Note: the surface rendering here ('spirit') differs from the WoH choice at Gen 1:2 ('breath of Elohim'), and the difference is principled: the two phenomenological categories take different English-natural renderings (the in-a-person sense is 'spirit'; the cosmic-hovering sense allows 'breath' or 'wind'). The central `ruach-elohim` entry governs Gen 1:2; this overlay entry governs Gen 41:38. // **Overlay housing.** The Gen 41:38 occurrence is chapter-singular in the *narrator-and-Pharaoh*-court-recognition register within the corpus. The wider in-a-person *ruach Elohim* tradition (Exod 31:3 etc.) is governed by other contexts and would receive its own entries when those texts are drafted. The locus of articulation is the Gen 41:38 verse, with the cross-corpus tradition documented as a node-cluster → **overlay**, with the bidirectional cross-reference to the central `ruach-elohim` (Gen 1:2). // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexical construct (*ruach Elohim*) is grammatically explicit; (b) the in-a-person phenomenological category is established as a distinct HB tradition by the cross-corpus distribution (Exod 31:3; Num 11:17 + 24:2; Judges; Isa 11:2; Daniel); (c) the distinction from the Gen 1:2 cosmic sense is documented across the standard commentaries and theological lexica. Named scholarship only; no WoH synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *ruach*; BDB pp. 924-926; TDOT XIII:365-402 (the major dictionary-article on ruach across its semantic range); NIDOTTE 3:1073-1078; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 286; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 95; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 504-505; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 313; Alter *Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 238; for the in-a-person ruach tradition: D. I. Block 'The Prophet of the Spirit: The Use of RWḤ in the Book of Ezekiel' JETS 32 (1989) 27-49; J. R. Levison *The Spirit in First-Century Judaism* AGAJU 29, 1997; for the Daniel parallels: J. J. Collins *Daniel* Hermeneia 1993; for the Yosef-Daniel typological parallels: M. J. Smith 'Daniel and the Joseph Story' in *The Book of Daniel: Composition and Reception* (J. J. Collins and P. W. Flint eds., 2001).

terms.translit: titra'u (Hithpael 2mp imperfect of ra'ah, 'to see')
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Hithpael (reflexive / reciprocal-reflexive) imperfect 2mp
terms.literal: ye look at one another / ye show yourselves / ye gaze upon yourselves
terms.standardEnglish: look one upon another (ASV/KJV); stare at one another (sharper register); show yourselves / stand about (Hithpael-as-display reading)
terms.wohChoice: look one upon another (ASV-baseline; the reciprocal-reflexive Hithpael reading preserved; the 'show yourselves / stand about helplessly' alternative documented)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:1 records Ya'aqov's opening rebuke: *va-yomer Ya'aqov le-vanav lammah titra'u* — *and Ya'aqov said unto his sons, Why do ye* [titra'u]. The Hithpael of *ra'ah* ('to see') is rare in this sense and admits two principal readings; the surface rendering is the ASV-baseline 'look one upon another', with the philological alternatives documented.** // **The lexeme.** The Hithpael of *ra'ah* ('to see') is rare in classical Hebrew. The dominant reading takes the Hithpael as **reciprocal-reflexive**: 'to look at one another, to gaze upon one another' (HALOT s.v. *ra'ah* Hithpael, sense 1: 'sich gegenseitig ansehen / see one another'). This is the ASV/KJV reading: the brothers are 'looking one upon another' — gazing helplessly at each other rather than acting. Ya'aqov's rebuke is at their inaction, not at any specific gaze-content. A secondary reading takes the Hithpael as **display-reflexive**: 'to show oneself, to stand exhibited, to make oneself visible' (HALOT sense 2; cf. the Hithpael of related visual verbs in the 'display oneself' sense). On this reading the rebuke is 'why do ye show yourselves / stand about', referring to the brothers' inactive presence rather than to their inter-gazing. A third reading takes the Hithpael as **iterative-frequentative**: 'why do ye keep looking / why do ye look-and-look' (the Hithpael as habitual-aspect intensifier). The three readings are not mutually exclusive — Ya'aqov's exasperation is conveyed in all three — and the philological literature does not adjudicate. // **The cross-corpus reach.** The Hithpael of *ra'ah* in the reciprocal-reflexive sense recurs at 2 Kgs 14:8, 11 (= 2 Chr 25:17, 21) in Amatzyah of Yehudah's challenge to Yo'ash of Yisra'el: *lekhah nitra'eh fanim* — 'come, let us look one another in the face' — a formal military-challenge formula for face-to-face confrontation (the verb here in the 1cp cohortative). The 2 Kgs / 2 Chr occurrence is the closest verbal parallel to Gen 42:1 and supports the reciprocal-reflexive reading. The cross-corpus reach is otherwise limited (the Hithpael of *ra'ah* is rare). // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular construction in Genesis with limited cross-corpus reach; the 2 Kgs / 2 Chr parallel does not extend the lemma's reach beyond a single additional occurrence; → **OVERLAY**. The lemma's literary point is the chapter-opening rebuke; the central glossary does not need to house it. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the Hithpael-of-*ra'ah* reciprocal-reflexive reading is the dominant lexicographic analysis but the alternatives are defensible; (b) the surface rendering is the ASV-baseline 'look one upon another'; (c) the choice between readings is interpretive. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *ra'ah* (Hithpael); BDB p. 906; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 105-106; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 515; on the 2 Kgs 14:8 parallel: J. Gray *I & II Kings* OTL 1970; on the Hithpael's reciprocal-reflexive analysis: GKC §54e.

terms.translit: ason (here at v 4 in pen-yiqra'enu ason, 'lest harm befall him'; at v 38 in u-kra'ahu ason ba-derekh, 'and harm befall him by the way')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular
terms.literal: ason — fatal mischance, calamity, lethal-injury (the marked term for a fatal accident or calamity that 'befalls' someone, typically on a journey)
terms.standardEnglish: mischief (KJV — archaic); harm (ASV-modernized / NRSV / Alter); disaster (NJPS)
terms.wohChoice: harm (ASV-baseline modernized; the KJV-archaic 'mischief' has drifted in modern English toward 'misbehavior' and is replaced; the lethal force documented in commentary via the Exod 21:22-23 cross-corpus parallel)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42 contains two of the HB's five occurrences of the noun *ason* ('fatal mischance, lethal calamity'). At v 4, Ya'aqov's reason for withholding Binyamin from the journey: *ki amar pen-yiqra'enu ason* — *for he said, Lest peradventure harm befall him*. At v 38, the climactic refusal of the second journey: *u-kra'ahu ason ba-derekh asher tel'khu vah* — *and harm befall him by the way in which ye go*. The lexeme recurs at Gen 44:29 (Ya'aqov's third use, in the brothers' retelling to Yosef of the same fear), and across the corpus only at Exod 21:22-23 (the law of injury to a pregnant woman, where the *ason*/no-*ason* distinction explicitly names fatal vs non-fatal outcomes — the law of damages for accidental injury hinging precisely on whether *ason* occurs).** // **The lexeme.** The noun *ason* is rare and marked. HALOT s.v. *ason* registers the sense 'fatal accident / lethal calamity', with the Exod 21:22 parallel as the decisive evidence (the law's *ve-haya ason* / *im lo yih'yeh ason* distinction names fatal-injury vs non-fatal-injury outcomes, fixing the term's lethal force). The Genesis occurrences are the lexeme's only narrative-prose attestations; the Exodus occurrence is the lexeme's only legal-prose attestation; the lexeme is otherwise absent from the corpus. The five-occurrence distribution makes the lexeme a near-hapax confined to two contexts. // **The Yosef-cycle Ya'aqov-internal deployment.** The three Genesis occurrences (42:4, 42:38, 44:29) are ALL on Ya'aqov's lips and ALL about Binyamin and ALL about the journey-to-Mitsrayim. The lexeme is therefore a **Ya'aqov-internal repeated fear-formula** — the patriarch's specific term for the calamity he fears will befall the last Rachel-son on the road. The repetition is itself a literary signature: the same word three times across the same character's lips across the same fear, binding the chapter 42-44 sequence into a single anxiety-arc. // **The Exod 21:22-23 parallel and the rendering decision.** The Exod 21:22-23 legal text fixes *ason* as fatal: *ki yinnatzu anashim ve-nagfu ishah harah ve-yatze'u y'ladeha ve-lo yih'yeh ason* (*if men strive, and hurt a pregnant woman, so that her fruit depart, and yet no* [ason] *follow*) vs *ve-im ason yih'yeh ve-natata nefesh tachat nafesh* (*but if any* [ason] *follow, then thou shalt give life for life*). The distinction is between fatal-injury (the *nefesh tachat nafesh* lex talionis applies, Exod 21:23-25) and non-fatal-injury (a fine, Exod 21:22). The *ason* is the fatal-injury outcome. The Genesis occurrences inherit this lethal force: Ya'aqov fears Binyamin's *death*, not a generic 'mischief'. The KJV's 'mischief' has drifted in modern English toward the trivial sense ('misbehavior, mischievous prank'); the ASV-baseline modernized to 'harm' (with the Exod 21:22 cross-reference making the lethal force explicit in commentary) is the appropriate rendering. NJPS 'disaster'; Alter 'harm'; NRSV 'harm'. The 'harm' rendering is preserved across the two chapter-42 occurrences and will be carried forward to Gen 44:29 when that chapter is translated. // **Overlay housing — with promotion-path note.** The lemma's distribution is five occurrences in two contexts (Genesis Ya'aqov / Exodus law-of-injury); the cross-corpus reach to Exod 21:22-23 is the lemma's one external parallel. If the cross-corpus reach were three or more contexts the entry would warrant central housing; with only one external context, the Genesis-Ya'aqov anchor predominates and **OVERLAY** is the appropriate housing for now. **Promotion-path note**: when Exodus is translated, the Exod 21:22-23 occurrence will activate the entry's only cross-corpus reach; the editorial decision then will be whether to promote the entry to central or to create a separate Exod-21 entry for the law-of-injury context. The decision can be deferred. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the Exod 21:22-23 lethal-force definition is grammatically and lexically explicit; (b) the Genesis occurrences inherit that lethal force unambiguously (Ya'aqov is fearing death, not 'mischief'); (c) the ASV-modernized 'harm' is the direct rendering; (d) the Ya'aqov-internal three-fold deployment is textually verifiable. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *ason*; BDB p. 62; TDOT I:236-237; NIDOTTE 1:485; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 106; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 516; on the Exod 21:22-23 *ason* / no-*ason* distinction: B. S. Jackson 'The Problem of Exod xxi 22-25 (*Ius Talionis*)' VT 23 (1973) 273-304; S. E. Loewenstamm 'Exodus 21:22-25' VT 27 (1977) 352-360; C. Houtman *Exodus* HCOT 1996.

terms.translit: ervat ha-aretz (Yosef's spy-accusation idiom at vv 9 and 12)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun phrase: feminine noun in construct + definite feminine noun
terms.literal: the nakedness of the land — (transferred from sexual-shame sense to geopolitical sense) the land's undefended places, exposed vulnerabilities, weak points
terms.standardEnglish: the nakedness of the land (ASV/KJV/NJPS/Alter — literal preserved); the weakness / undefended places of the land (functional gloss)
terms.wohChoice: the nakedness of the land (ASV-baseline literal; the spy-idiom's transferred-geopolitical sense documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:9 and 42:12 record Yosef's spy-accusation: *lir'ot et ervat ha-aretz batem* — *to see the nakedness of the land ye are come*. The idiom *ervat ha-aretz* takes the noun *ervah* ('nakedness, exposed/shameful part') from its standard sexual-shame register (the Lev 18 / 20 *galah ervah* incest-prohibition formula, 'uncover the nakedness of') and transfers it to the geopolitical register: the land's undefended places, vulnerabilities, weak points — a spy's-eye view, looking for the gaps in the territorial fabric the way a man looks for what is shamefully uncovered.** // **The lexeme.** The noun *ervah* (עֶרְוָה) primarily denotes 'nakedness, the exposed/shameful parts of the body' in the cultic-sexual register: Lev 18:6-19 (the long list of *galah ervah* incest-prohibitions: *ervat avikha*, *ervat ish ve-ishto*, etc.); Lev 20:11-21 (the parallel-penalty list); Deut 24:1 (the divorce-cause *ervat davar*, 'something shameful'); Ezek 16:36-37; 23:10, 18, 29 (the prophetic deployment of nakedness-imagery for unfaithful-city Yerushalayim). The Lev 18 / 20 incest-list use is the lexeme's structural-cultic anchor. // **The transferred geopolitical sense at Gen 42:9, 12.** The Gen 42 occurrence takes the sexual-shame *ervah* and transfers it to the territorial register: the land has *ervah* — undefended places, weakness-points — that spies might come to see. The transfer is intelligible because both senses share the structure of *something-shamefully-exposed-that-was-meant-to-be-covered*: the body's *ervah* is its sexually-shameful parts that should be covered; the land's *ervah* is its strategically-vulnerable parts that should be defended/concealed. The metaphor is precise: a spy looks for the *ervah* of the land the way a violator looks for the *ervah* of a body. The transferred sense is restricted to Gen 42:9, 12 within the HB — the geopolitical *ervat ha-aretz* construction does not recur elsewhere — though the related idiom *ervat sin'ah* ('shameful enmity') appears at Ezek 23:18. // **The rendering-traditions.** ASV/KJV preserve the literal 'the nakedness of the land'; NJPS likewise; Alter 'the land's nakedness'; NRSV likewise (some moderns gloss 'the weakness of the land' or 'the defenseless places'). The literal preservation keeps the spy-trope intelligible and preserves the transferred metaphor's force; the functional glosses ('weakness', 'undefended places') sacrifice the metaphor for clarity.
