The ASV-baseline literal is preferable here because the metaphor is interpretively load-bearing — the brothers' protest at v 11 (*kenim anachnu*, 'we are honest men') is partly a rejection of the implied violation in the *ervah* accusation. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-internal construction (Gen 42:9, 12 only); the cross-corpus *ervah* in the sexual-shame register is governed by Lev 18 / 20 (when Leviticus is translated, the cultic-sexual *ervah* will receive its own central entry); the Gen 42 transferred-geopolitical sense is a chapter-specific metaphor → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexical construction is grammatically explicit; (b) the transferred-from-sexual-to-geopolitical sense is documented across the standard commentaries; (c) the 'nakedness of the land' literal rendering is the direct sense; (d) the chapter-internal pair (vv 9, 12) is textually verifiable. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *ervah*; BDB pp. 788-789; TDOT XI:343-349; NIDOTTE 3:528-530; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 107-108; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 519; on the *ervah* sexual-shame cultic register: J. Milgrom *Leviticus 17-22* AB 2000; on the transferred geopolitical sense: Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 242.

terms.translit: kenim (substantival plural of the adjective ken, 'right, true, honest, upright'; here at vv 11, 19, 31, 33, 34)
terms.partOfSpeech: adjective, masculine plural, substantivally used ('honest men, men of integrity')
terms.literal: kenim — right ones, true ones, honest ones; the substantival plural of the adjective ken ('right, true, honest, upright')
terms.standardEnglish: true men (ASV/KJV — archaic register); honest men (NJPS / NRSV / Alter — modern register); men of integrity (interpretive)
terms.wohChoice: true men (ASV-baseline; applied consistently across the five chapter-internal occurrences vv 11, 19, 31, 33, 34, preserving the protest-formula refrain)
terms.rationale: **Genesis 42 deploys *kenim* (כֵּנִים) five times as the brothers' running self-designation in their protest against Yosef's spy-accusation: v 11 (*kenim anachnu*); v 19 (*im kenim atem*, Yosef's conditional pickup); v 31 (the brothers retelling to Ya'aqov); v 33 (the brothers retelling Yosef's words back); v 34 (Yosef's final conditional). The five-fold repetition is the chapter's deliberate protest-formula refrain — the brothers' self-defense against the accusation of being *meraglim* (spies, the chapter's counter-keyword).** // **The lexeme.** The adjective *ken* III (כֵּן, 'right, true, honest, upright') is morphologically the homonymous form of *ken* I ('thus, so', the adverb of manner) and *ken* II ('base, pedestal', the noun) — three homonyms in HALOT distinguished by syntactic-role and context. *Ken* III in its predicative-adjective sense is well-attested: 'right, true' applied to speech (Num 27:7; 36:5: *ken benot Tzelofchad doverot*, 'the daughters of Tzelofchad speak right'; Exod 10:29 *ken dibbarta*; 2 Kgs 7:9 *lo ken anachnu osim*, 'we are not doing right'; Eccl 8:10 *lo ken*); to action (Prov 11:19 *ken tzedaqah le-chayim*, 'so righteousness tends to life'); to attestation (Job 5:27 *hineh zot chaqarnuha ken hi*, 'lo this, we have searched it, so it is'). The substantival-plural-of-persons sense *kenim* ('honest men, persons-of-integrity') is RARE — Gen 42 is the principal locus (the five chapter-internal occurrences plus its retelling-recurrence) — and is itself a chapter-specific deployment of the lexeme: the brothers are using the adjective as a noun, applying it to themselves as a class. The cross-corpus substantival-plural sense recurs at 2 Sam 14:18 (Avshalom's intermediary woman to David) and a few wisdom-attestations; the chapter-internal five-fold deployment dominates. // **The chapter's protest-formula structure.** The five occurrences form a literary structure: v 11 the brothers' initial self-designation (*kenim anachnu*); v 19 Yosef's conditional acceptance of the self-designation (*im kenim atem*, 'if ye be honest men'); v 31 the brothers retelling to Ya'aqov (*kenim anachnu*, 'we are honest men'); v 33 the brothers retelling Yosef's verification-condition (*be-zot eda ki kenim atem*, 'hereby shall I know that ye are honest men'); v 34 Yosef's closing conditional (*ki kenim atem*, 'that ye are honest men'). The refrain binds the brothers' protest, Yosef's test, the retelling to Ya'aqov, and the test-condition into a single rhetorical structure. The chapter's dramatic irony is sharp: the brothers' self-designation as *kenim* is precisely what the chapter is testing — whether they are honest about *what they did to Yosef*, the past that the v 21 confession is about to expose. The Gen 42:21 confession (*aval ashemim anachnu al achinu*) is the chapter's answer to its own *kenim*-claim: in the matter of Yosef, the brothers are NOT *kenim* but *ashemim* — guilty, not honest. The lexical contrast *kenim* (vv 11, 19, 31, 33, 34) ↔ *ashemim* (v 21) is one of the chapter's deepest literary-theological structures. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV 'true men' (the archaic English register that retains the moral-uprightness force of *ken* — 'true' in the sense of 'morally true, of integrity', not the modern 'factually true'); NJPS / NRSV / Alter 'honest men' (modern register, sacrificing the *ken* etymological resonance for clarity). The ASV-baseline 'true men' is preserved for two reasons: (i) consistency across the five occurrences (the refrain is preserved); (ii) the etymological resonance with *ken*'s moral-uprightness sense (the archaic 'true' carries 'morally true' more clearly than modern 'true'). // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-internal five-fold refrain; the substantival-plural-of-persons *kenim* sense is chapter-specific (the adjective *ken* in its predicative-adjective sense is cross-corpus, but the substantival 'honest men' deployment as a self-designating protest-formula is chapter-singular); → **OVERLAY**. The lemma's cross-corpus reach in other senses is governed elsewhere; the chapter-specific protest-refrain is here. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit (adjective *ken* III, substantival-plural form); (b) the chapter's five-fold deployment is textually verifiable; (c) the *kenim* ↔ *ashemim* lexical contrast is grammatically explicit; (d) the ASV-baseline 'true men' is the direct rendering. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *ken* III; BDB p. 467; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 107; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 518-519; on the *kenim* / *ashemim* lexical contrast: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 242.

terms.translit: mishmar (v 17, 'ward'); beit mishmarkhem (v 19, 'your prison-house')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular (mishmar — 'guard, custody, place of detention'); in construct beit mishmar — 'house of custody, prison-house'
terms.literal: mishmar — the general 'guard / custody / place of detention'; beit mishmar — 'house of [the] custody', the construct-noun-phrase 'prison-house'
terms.standardEnglish: ward (ASV/KJV — archaic register); guardhouse / prison (NJPS); prison (NRSV); ward / prison (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: ward (v 17) / prison-house (v 19 in the beit mishmarkhem construct) — ASV-baseline; the chapter's mishmar terminology distinguished from the Gen 39-40 beit ha-sohar in commentary
terms.rationale: **Genesis 42 deploys *mishmar* (v 17) and the construct *beit mishmarkhem* (v 19) as the chapter's terms for the place where Yosef detains the brothers (v 17, the initial three-day detention of all ten) and the place where Shim'on will be held (v 19, the conditional-pending-Binyamin detention). The terminology is distinct from the Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar* (the 'round-house / prison' that is governed by the central [`beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house`](#beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house) entry); whether the *mishmar* of Gen 42 names the same facility as the *beit ha-sohar* of Gen 39-40 or a different one is undecidable from the texts alone.** // **The lexeme.** The noun *mishmar* (from the root *sh-m-r* 'to guard, keep, watch') has three documented senses: (i) the **guarding-act** (a watch, a guard-duty: 2 Chr 8:14 *mishmerot* — 'guard-divisions'; Neh 7:3); (ii) the **guarded persons** (those in custody: Gen 40:3-4, 7 — Yosef and the cupbearer/baker held in the *mishmar* of the *sar ha-tabbachim*; Gen 41:10; 42:17, 19; Lev 24:12; Num 15:34); (iii) the **guarding-personnel** (the guards themselves: Neh 4:3, 9; 7:3 [MT 13:30]). The sense at Gen 42:17 is (ii) — the place of custody / detention. The construct *beit mishmar* ('house of custody') at v 19 specifies the building / facility — the construct-form *beit + noun* is the standard 'building-of-X' construction (cf. *beit ha-sohar*, *beit ha-bor* — 'house of the prison', 'house of the pit'). // **The Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar* / Gen 40 *mishmar* relation.** The central entry [`beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house`](#beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house) governs the *beit ha-sohar* — the Gen 39-40 Egyptian prison (likely a fortress-prison; the Egyptian *sohar* possibly from Eg. *s-h-r-y* 'fortress-tower'). Within Gen 40 the same facility is called both *beit ha-sohar* (vv 3, 5) AND *mishmar* (vv 3, 4, 7 — the cupbearer and baker placed in the *mishmar*; Yosef the *na'ar* serving them). The Gen 40 dual-naming establishes that *mishmar* can name the same facility as *beit ha-sohar*. Gen 42 uses only *mishmar* / *beit mishmar* (not *beit ha-sohar*), suggesting that the editor / narrator either: (a) names the same Egyptian prison-facility (the Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar*) using the alternate *mishmar* terminology — consistent with Gen 40's dual-naming; (b) names a different facility — perhaps a separate detention-area at Yosef's official residence, distinct from the prison Yosef himself was kept in; (c) the lexical-variation is stylistic and not referential. Sarna and Westermann both treat the Gen 42 *mishmar* as functionally the Egyptian prison; the question is undecidable from the texts alone. The English translation cannot recover the question and renders the Hebrew's lexical-variation: *mishmar* → 'ward' (v 17); *beit mishmar* → 'prison-house' (v 19). // **The three-day detention.** Gen 42:17 places the brothers in the *mishmar* for *sheloshet yamim* ('three days'). The three-day period is a marked literary threshold across the corpus: Gen 22:4 (the Aqedah's three days to Moriyah); Gen 40:12, 13, 18, 19, 20 (the cupbearer/baker dreams' three days, the *sar ha-mashqim*'s restoration and the *sar ha-ofim*'s execution both at three days; the dreams' three-day pivot); Gen 42:17 (the brothers' three-day detention); Exod 5:3 (the three-day wilderness journey); Josh 1:11; 2:16, 22; 3:2; 9:16; 2 Sam 1:2; 1 Kgs 12:5; Esth 4:16 (Esther's fast); Jonah 2:1 (Jonah in the fish). The three-day threshold marks transition from one state to another — captivity to resolution, dream to interpretation, journey to destination. The Gen 42:17 three-day detention is itself the threshold between the brothers' arrest and Yosef's conditional release. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-internal *mishmar* / *beit mishmar* terminology; the cross-corpus *mishmar* lexeme is multivalent and broadly distributed (governed by other contexts when those texts are translated); the chapter-specific deployment-as-Egyptian-detention-vocabulary, distinct from Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar*, is here. The cross-reference to the central [`beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house`](#beit-ha-sohar-prison-round-house) documents the relation. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the lexeme's multivalent sense-range is direct but the chapter-specific reading is interpretive; (b) the Gen 39-40 *beit ha-sohar* / Gen 40 *mishmar* same-or-different-facility question is undecidable; (c) the 'ward' / 'prison-house' rendering is the ASV-baseline but the choice between the lexemes preserves Hebrew's lexical-variation. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *mishmar*; BDB p. 1038; TDOT IX:281-285; NIDOTTE 4:191-193; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 109; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 521; on the three-day-threshold motif: G. F. Hasel 'The Significance of the Cosmology in Genesis 1' AUSS 10 (1972) 1-20; on the *mishmar* / *beit ha-sohar* relation: D. B. Redford *A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph* VTSup 20, 1970 pp. 17-19.

terms.translit: va-yakkirem (Hiphil 3ms perf w/ 3mp suff, 'and he recognised them'); va-yitnakker (Hithpael 3ms perf, 'and he made himself strange / disguised himself / feigned to be a stranger') — paired in a single verse at Gen 42:7
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, in paired Hiphil (recognise / identify) and Hithpael (make oneself strange / feign-unrecognisability) stems
terms.literal: va-yakkirem — and he recognised / identified them; va-yitnakker — and he made himself strange / disguised himself unto them, feigned not to be the one they would have known
terms.standardEnglish: knew them ... made himself strange unto them (ASV/KJV); recognized them ... acted like a stranger toward them (NJPS); recognized them ... but disguised himself (NRSV); recognized them ... feigned to be a stranger (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: knew them ... made himself strange unto them (ASV-baseline preserved; the Hiphil/Hithpael paired-deployment as the recognition-motif culmination documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:7 stages the chapter's recognition-motif at its culmination by deploying the root *nakar* (נכר) in two opposite stems back-to-back within a single verse: the Hiphil *va-yakkirem* ('and he recognised them' — the same Hiphil that Gen 37:32-33 used at the *haker-na* / *va-yakkirah* exchange between the brothers and Ya'aqov) and the Hithpael *va-yitnakker* ('and he made himself strange / disguised himself / feigned to be a stranger'). The juxtaposition of the recognition-verb and its anti-form within a single verse is rare in the HB and pointed: the verb of recognition is the very verb whose Hithpael Yosef adopts to conceal himself.** // **The Hithpael of *nakar*.** The Hithpael of *n-k-r* ('to make oneself strange / unrecognisable / feign-the-strangeness-of-a-stranger') is rare; the only other HB occurrence of the Hithpael in this specific sense is **1 Kgs 14:5-6** — the prophet Achiyah of Shilo, blind in his old age, is told by YHWH that Yarov'am's wife is coming to inquire of him about their sick child: *ve-hi mitnakkerah* ('and she will make herself strange / will be in disguise', v 5). Yarov'am has sent his wife in disguise to receive an oracle about their son's fate. Achiyah, alerted by YHWH despite his blindness, addresses her at her arrival: *boi eshet Yarov'am, lammah zeh at mitnakkerah* ('come in, wife of Yarov'am; why dost thou feign to be another?', v 6). The 1 Kgs 14:5-6 scene is structurally parallel to Gen 42:7: in both, a person of authority is approached by someone who *should* recognise them but who has been deceived by the visitor's disguise; in both, the addressed party (Achiyah / Yosef) is in fact aware of the visitor's identity and disguise. The verbal parallel is sharp: *mitnakkerah* (1 Kgs 14:5) / *va-yitnakker* (Gen 42:7). The two occurrences exhaust the HB's Hithpael-of-*nakar* in the feigning-unrecognisability sense. // **The chapter's culmination of the Gen 27 / 37 / 38 recognition-arc.** The recognition-motif binds the patriarchal narratives: (a) **Gen 27:23** *ve-lo hikkiro* ('and he recognised him not' — the blind Yitzchaq failing to identify the disguised Ya'aqov, the deception by exploiting recognition's failure); (b) **Gen 37:32-33** *haker-na* / *va-yakkirah* (the brothers' bloodied-tunic deception of Ya'aqov, the deception by demanding recognition); (c) **Gen 38:25-26** *haker-na le-mi* / *va-yakker Yehudah* (Tamar's pledge-items to Yehudah, the deception caught by demanding recognition); (d) **Gen 42:7-8** *va-yakkirem ... va-yitnakker ... ve-hem lo hikkiruhu* (Yosef's controlled recognition combined with concealed identity, the culmination-and-reversal: the brothers, who once exploited Ya'aqov's misrecognition of a bloodied tunic, are themselves misrecognising the brother they sold). The four-stage *nakar*-arc resolves at Gen 42:7-8 with the chapter's exact role-reversal: Yosef holds the recognition-knowledge that Ya'aqov in Gen 27 lacked, and uses it to *feign* the non-recognition that the brothers in Gen 37 created. The Hithpael *va-yitnakker* is the structural counterpart of Gen 27's *ve-lo hikkiro* — not failed-recognition but **deliberate concealment**, the choice to perform non-recognition. // **The cross-reference to `haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif`.** The companion overlay entry [`haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif`](#haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif) governs the Gen 37 *haker-na* / *va-yakkirah* anchor of the recognition-motif (with the Gen 27 + Gen 38 cross-references documented in its rationale), and has had its appliesTo extended to include Gen 42:7 + 42:8 as the motif's culmination-occurrences. This sibling entry is anchored at the Gen 42:7 paired Hiphil-and-Hithpael deployment specifically (the chapter's Hithpael-of-*nakar* is the motif's anti-form, distinct from the Gen 37 Hiphil-only deployment); the two entries are deliberate companions per the ratified sibling-overlay pattern with bidirectional cross-reference. The motif entry names this sibling by id in its rationale; this entry names the motif entry by id in this paragraph — a true bidirectional sibling link. The pair governs the recognition-arc's full lexical-stem range (the Hiphil disclosure-by-demand at Gen 37; the Hithpael concealment-by-feigning at Gen 42); together they map the motif as it culminates in Gen 42:7-8. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular Hithpael-of-*nakar* construction (the only other HB Hithpael-of-*nakar* occurrence is the 1 Kgs 14:5-6 Achiyah scene); the Gen 27 + 37 + 38 + 42 recognition-arc is Genesis-internal; the chapter-specific Hithpael-pair deployment is here. The companion `haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif` (also overlay-housed) is the Gen 37 anchor. → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional sibling-link to the companion entry. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the paired Hiphil + Hithpael deployment is morphologically explicit; (b) the Hithpael-of-*nakar* feigning-unrecognisability sense is well-attested at the 1 Kgs 14:5-6 parallel; (c) the recognition-motif's Gen 27 / 37 / 38 / 42 cross-chapter structure is textually verifiable; (d) the ASV-baseline 'knew them ... made himself strange unto them' is the direct rendering. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *nakar* (Hithpael); BDB p. 649; TDOT IX:423-432; NIDOTTE 3:107-110; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 290; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 107; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 518; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 242; Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1 (the foundational reading of the recognition-arc); on the 1 Kgs 14:5-6 parallel: J. Gray *I & II Kings* OTL 1970 pp. 333-336; on the Yosef-cycle recognition-motif: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975 pp. 130-152. // **Cross-reference (the Gen 45:1 *hitvadda* sibling-overlay link).** The recognition-and-feigning Hithpael-pair structure documented in this entry is completed by the SIBLING overlay-entry [`hitvadda-yosef-self-disclosure-recognition-pair-gen45`](#hitvadda-yosef-self-disclosure-recognition-pair-gen45), anchored at Gen 45:1's *be-hitvadda Yosef el-echav* ('while Yosef made himself known unto his brethren'), the marked Hithpael of *yada*. The cycle's recognition-arc deploys the two Hithpael-stems at structurally-opposed moments: at Gen 42:7 *va-yitnakker* (Hithpael of *nakar*) marks Yosef's deliberate-concealment from the brothers as the recognition-withheld stem; at Gen 45:1 *be-hitvadda* (Hithpael of *yada*) marks Yosef's deliberate-self-disclosure to the brothers as the recognition-disclosed stem. The Hithpael-pair *hitnakker / hitvadda* maps the recognition-arc's full reflexive-stem range — the deliberate-concealing (Gen 42) and the deliberate-disclosing (Gen 45). The two entries are deliberate companions per the sibling-overlay-entries pattern with bidirectional cross-reference: this entry names the Gen 45 sibling by id; the sibling entry names this one by id. Together they govern the recognition-arc's Hithpael-stem structure (Gen 42 → 45). Both Hithpaels are chapter-singular within Genesis in their respective scenes; both are rare across the corpus; both stand at structurally-load-bearing moments of the cycle's recognition-and-disclosure architecture.

terms.translit: ha-melitz (the participle of l-w-tz in the 'interpreter / translator' sense, at v 23)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb participle (Hiphil of l-w-tz), here substantivally: 'the interpreter / one who interprets / spokesman / mediator'
terms.literal: ha-melitz — the one who interprets / mediates / speaks-between; here in the 'court interpreter / translator' sense (effectively a hapax in this specific register within the HB)
terms.standardEnglish: an interpreter (ASV/KJV/NJPS/NRSV/Alter — uncontested)
terms.wohChoice: an interpreter between them (ASV-baseline; the lexeme's rare 'interpreter / translator' sense — distinct from the dominant 'scoffer / mocker' sense — documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:23 contains a narrator's parenthetical disclosure: *ve-hem lo yad'u ki shomea Yosef ki ha-melitz beinotam* — *and they knew not that Yosef understood them; for there was an interpreter between them*. The noun *melitz* (מֵלִיץ) here is in the 'court interpreter / translator' sense, which is effectively a hapax in this specific register within the HB. The lexeme's standard senses are quite different — *l-w-tz* otherwise generates the 'scoffer / mocker' (the dominant biblical sense) and the 'mediator / spokesman / advocate' (a secondary sense). The Gen 42:23 'interpreter' deployment is rare and pointed.** // **The lexeme.** The verb *l-w-tz* (or *lits*) has a complex distribution. The Qal participle *letz* and the Hiphil participle *melitz* both appear, with overlapping but distinguishable senses: (i) the dominant **'scoffer / mocker'** sense — Ps 1:1 *u-ve-moshav letzim lo yashav* ('nor sitteth in the seat of the *letzim* / scornful'); Prov 9:7-8 (the *letz* — scorner — who hates correction); Prov 13:1; 14:6, 9; 15:12; 19:25, 29; 20:1; 21:11, 24; 22:10; 24:9; 29:8 — the Proverbs wisdom-literature deploys *letz* as the foil to the wise. The Hiphil *halitz* in this register is 'to scorn / deride' (Ps 119:51 *zedim helitzuni*, 'the arrogant scorn me'; Prov 14:9; 19:28). (ii) The **'mediator / spokesman / advocate'** sense — Job 33:23 (the *malakh melitz*, 'an angel, a mediator', the heavenly advocate in Elihu's speech); Isa 43:27 (*meliteikha pashe'u bi*, 'thy mediators / spokesmen / interpreters have transgressed against me' — possibly the prophets, possibly the priestly intercessors); 2 Chr 32:31 (*melitzei sarei Bavel*, 'the spokesmen / envoys of the princes of Bavel' come to inquire of Hizqiyahu). (iii) The Gen 42:23 **'interpreter / translator'** sense — distinct from the mediator-as-advocate sense by being specifically the language-mediator (the one who renders Egyptian speech into Hebrew or vice versa, the cross-linguistic court interpreter). The Genesis 42 occurrence is the lexeme's only HB attestation in this language-translation register. The semantic relation across the three senses: all share the structure of *one who stands between* — the scoffer stands between truth and the audience (interposing mockery); the mediator stands between two parties (interceding); the interpreter stands between two languages (translating). The Hebrew lexeme captures the 'standing-between' structurally; English distinguishes the three senses by separate words. // **The court-interpreter institution.** The 'interpreter / dragoman' role is well-attested in ancient Near Eastern royal administration. Egyptian-court protocol of the Middle and New Kingdom employed *targumannu*-class language-mediators (the Akkadian term is *targumannu* / *tergumannu*, the Hebrew cognate *targuman*, later Aramaic *targum* — the LXX of Gen 42:23 uses ἑρμηνευτής, the Greek 'interpreter'); the Amarna letters extensively document the use of court-interpreters in royal diplomacy. The Gen 42:23 *melitz* is the Genesis Hebrew rendering of this institutional role. Yosef, the *shallit*, would maintain his Egyptian-court persona by routing his speech to the brothers through the official interpreter — the brothers see only the Egyptian-court-protocol-mediation and do not know that the *shallit* understands their Hebrew directly. // **The narrative disclosure.** The narrator's parenthetical at v 23 is precisely placed: it follows the brothers' v 21-22 confession in Hebrew (the *aval ashemim anachnu al achinu* and Re'uven's *dam nidrash* exchange) and precedes Yosef's v 24 weeping. The reader is told *now* — at the moment the brothers' confession-in-Hebrew has just been recorded — that Yosef has heard everything directly. The brothers, speaking unguardedly in Hebrew, do not know that Yosef has understood; the v 24 weeping follows from the v 21-22 confession Yosef has just overheard. The narrative-architecture is precise: the disclosure of the interpreter's presence makes Yosef's emotional reaction at v 24 narratively grounded. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular 'interpreter / translator' sense; the cross-corpus *melitz* in the 'mediator / spokesman' sense (Job 33:23, Isa 43:27, 2 Chr 32:31) is governed by other contexts when those texts are drafted; the chapter-specific court-interpreter register is here. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit; (b) the chapter-specific 'interpreter' sense is grammatically and contextually clear; (c) the cross-corpus other-senses are documented; (d) the ASV-baseline 'an interpreter between them' is the direct rendering; (e) the court-interpreter institution is well-attested in the ANE-comparative material. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *lutz* (the verb) and *melitz*; BDB pp. 539-540; TDOT VII:547-552; NIDOTTE 2:801-803; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 291; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 111; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 523; on the ANE court-interpreter institution: A. F. Rainey 'The Scribe at Ugarit' *Proceedings of the IAJS* 1969; W. L. Moran *The Amarna Letters* 1992 (the *targumannu* documentation); on the polysemy of *l-w-tz*: M. V. Fox *Proverbs 1-9* AB 2000 pp. 39-43 (on *letz* in wisdom-literature). // **Cross-reference (the Gen 45:12 *fi ha-medabber* sibling-overlay link).** The chapter's interpreter-mediation construction is structurally reversed at Gen 45:12 by Yosef's *ki fi ha-medabber aleikhem* ('it is my mouth that speaketh unto you'), governed by the SIBLING overlay-entry [`fi-ha-medabber-aleikhem-direct-speech-reversal-melitz-gen45`](#fi-ha-medabber-aleikhem-direct-speech-reversal-melitz-gen45). The cycle's speech-mediation literary structure: at Gen 42:23 the *melitz* stands between Yosef and the brothers as the institutional court-language-mediator (the brothers see Egyptian-court-protocol-mediation, not the *shallit*-who-understands-Hebrew-directly); at Gen 45:12 the *melitz*-mediation is dispensed-with, and the marked emphasis falls on Yosef's *mouth* speaking directly. The Gen 42:23 mediated-speech / Gen 45:12 direct-speech literary pair is one of the cycle's neatest narrative arcs (the disclosure-scene's signature gesture: the dropping of the interpreter-mediation in favor of unmediated Hebrew-from-the-brother's-mouth). The two entries are deliberate companions per the sibling-overlay-entries pattern with bidirectional cross-reference: this entry names the Gen 45 sibling by id; the sibling entry names this one by id. Together they govern the cycle's speech-mediation literary structure.

terms.translit: kelim ('vessels', v 25); saq ('sack', vv 25, 27, 35); amtachat ('sack-pouch', vv 27, 28; pervasively across Gen 43-44)
terms.partOfSpeech: three nouns alternating across the Gen 42-44 grain-purchase narrative-arc: keli ('vessel, utensil, container'); saq ('sack, cloth-bag'); amtachat ('sack-pouch', restricted to Gen 42-44)
terms.literal: kelim — the general 'vessels / utensils / containers / equipment'; saq — the specific cloth-sack; amtachat — also 'sack', but a distinct lexeme confined within the HB to the Gen 42-44 grain-purchase narrative (Gen 42:27, 28; 43:12, 18, 21, 22, 23; 44:1, 2, 8, 11, 12)
terms.standardEnglish: vessels / sack / sack (ASV/KJV — the alternation flattened in English); bags / sack / sack / bag (NJPS — likewise flattened); generally undistinguished in translation
terms.wohChoice: vessels (kelim) / sack (saq) / sack (amtachat) — ASV-baseline retained; the lexical-distinctness and the possible referential differentiation documented in commentary
terms.rationale: **Gen 42-44 deploys three distinct sack-lexemes — *kelim*, *saq*, *amtachat* — across the brothers' two journeys to Mitsrayim. The alternation is striking and lexically marked, but English translations uniformly flatten the distinction. The third lexeme *amtachat* is the most striking: it is restricted within the HB to the Gen 42-44 grain-purchase narrative (twelve occurrences across Gen 42:27, 28; 43:12, 18, 21, 22, 23; 44:1, 2, 8, 11, 12 — and NOWHERE ELSE in the HB), making it a narrative-arc-specific lexeme.** // **The three lexemes.** (i) *keli* (כְּלִי, plural *kelim*) is the general 'vessel / utensil / container / equipment / weapon' lexeme — extensively distributed across the corpus, covering everything from kitchen utensils (Gen 27:3 Esav's hunting-*keli*; Exod 22:6-7 [MT 22:5-6] vessels lent out) to sacred objects (Exod 25-27, the tabernacle *kelim*) to weapons (1 Sam 17:54 *kelei zeino*, 'his armor'). The lexeme is broad and unspecific. (ii) *saq* (שַׂק) is the specific 'cloth-sack / coarse-cloth-bag' (the same lexeme as the 'sackcloth' of mourning — Gen 37:34 Ya'aqov's *saq*; 2 Sam 3:31; 1 Kgs 21:27; Joel 1:8, 13). The Gen 42-44 *saq* is the brothers' cloth-sack for grain transport. (iii) *amtachat* (אַמְתַּחַת) — the rare lexeme confined to Gen 42-44 — is etymologically obscure; the root has been variously proposed as *m-t-ch* ('to stretch out, to extend') with the *a*-prefix denoting place or means (HALOT registers the etymological obscurity). The lexeme appears to denote a specific kind of sack — possibly a stretched-out / extended cloth-bag, possibly a sub-pouch within a larger container, possibly simply a synonym for *saq*. // **The three explanations of the alternation.** (a) **Referential differentiation**: the lexemes name different containers. The *kelim* are the general travel-vessels (perhaps including jars, leather-bags, etc.); the *saq* is the cloth-sack (the bag); the *amtachat* is a sub-pouch within the bag — supporting v 27's *be-fi amtachto* ('in the *mouth* of his *amtachat*') as referring to a distinct internal compartment, and v 35's *tzeror kasp-o be-saqqo* (his bundle of money in his *saq*) as distinguishing the *saq*-level location from v 28's *amtachti*-level. On this reading the silver was put *in* the *amtachat* (a sub-pouch) which was *in* the *saq* (the outer bag), the bag itself being one of the *kelim* (the general travel-equipment). The reading is supported by Sarna and Westermann as the most likely if a referential distinction is to be drawn. (b) **Stylistic synonymy without referential differentiation**: the alternation is poetic-stylistic variation, the three lexemes being functionally synonymous; the choice between *saq* and *amtachat* at vv 27-28 is variatio for its own sake. The reading is supported by the difficulty of cleanly mapping each lexeme to a distinct referent (especially v 25's *vessels with grain ... money into his sack* — *kelim* and *saq* used in the same sentence for what seems to be the same container). (c) **Source-critical seams**: some commentators (Skinner ICC; Eissfeldt) have read the *saq*/*amtachat* alternation as a documentary-source split (the *saq* the J-source term; the *amtachat* the E-source term, restricted to the E-novella's grain-purchase narrative). The reading depends on the wider source-critical analysis of Gen 42-44 and is not adopted by all commentators. // **The lexeme's restriction to Gen 42-44.** *Amtachat*'s twelve-occurrence distribution exclusively within Gen 42:27, 28; 43:12, 18, 21, 22, 23; 44:1, 2, 8, 11, 12 is one of the corpus's most striking lexical-restriction phenomena. The lexeme is not used elsewhere in Genesis, not used in Exodus or anywhere in the rest of the Pentateuch, not used in the prophets, not used in the wisdom or poetic literature, not used in Chronicles or Ezra-Nehemiah. The restriction is exhaustive. This is the strongest single piece of evidence for either reading (b) the source-critical seam (suggesting the lexeme belongs to one documentary source whose contribution is limited to the Gen 42-44 grain-narrative) or reading (a) the referential-distinction (suggesting the lexeme names a specific sub-container peculiar to the Mitsrayim grain-purchase context). // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV / NJPS / NRSV / Alter all flatten the alternation: *kelim* → 'vessels' (ASV) or 'bags' (NJPS); *saq* → 'sack'; *amtachat* → 'sack' (ASV) or 'bag' (NJPS) — the English distinction between *saq* and *amtachat* is uniformly lost. The WoH translation preserves the ASV-baseline ('vessels' / 'sack' / 'sack'), with the lexical-distinctness documented in this overlay entry and the per-verse commentary at v 25, v 27, v 35. The English text cannot reproduce the Hebrew's three-lexeme variation without inventing distinctions ('sack-pouch' for *amtachat*) that the standard English translation tradition does not support; the conservative ASV-baseline preservation is preferred, with the apparatus carrying the philological observation. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-arc-specific lexical-alternation (Gen 42-44); the *amtachat* lexeme is exhaustively restricted to this arc; the *saq* and *kelim* lexemes are broadly distributed but the chapter-arc-specific alternation pattern is what is documented here. → **OVERLAY** (the chapter-arc-specific phenomenon; the broader *saq* and *kelim* lexemes would be governed by other contexts in central entries if and when such are warranted). // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the three-lexeme alternation is grammatically and lexically explicit, but (b) the three explanations (referential differentiation / stylistic synonymy / source-critical seam) are interpretive and not decisively resolved; (c) the ASV-baseline rendering flattens the alternation (the philologically more transparent rendering would distinguish, but English convention does not); (d) the *amtachat* lexeme's exhaustive Gen 42-44 restriction is the strongest piece of evidence but does not by itself adjudicate between the three readings. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *keli*, *saq*, *amtachat* (the *amtachat* entry notes the etymological obscurity and the Gen 42-44 restriction); BDB pp. 479 (*keli*), 974 (*saq*), 607 (*amtachat*); TDOT VII:169-175 (*keli*); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 112 (favoring the referential-distinction reading); Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 524; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 320; on the source-critical reading of the *saq*/*amtachat* alternation: J. Skinner *Genesis* ICC 1910 p. 472; O. Eissfeldt *Hexateuch-Synopse* 1922; on the J/E source-analysis of Gen 42-44: G. von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972 pp. 380-385; for the *amtachat* etymology and the *m-t-ch* root: HALOT s.v. *m-t-ch*; G. R. Driver 'Hebrew Roots and Words' WO 1 (1947-52) 406-415.

terms.translit: malon (here at v 27 in ba-malon, 'in the lodging-place')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular (from the root l-w-n / lin, 'to lodge / pass the night')
terms.literal: malon — a place of lodging / overnighting / passing-the-night; a wayfaring stopover (caravanserai, way-station, or night-camp)
terms.standardEnglish: the inn (KJV — anachronistic); the lodging-place (ASV / NRSV); the place where they spent the night (NJPS / Alter)
terms.wohChoice: the lodging-place (ASV-baseline; the wayfaring-stopover / caravanserai sense documented in commentary; the KJV 'inn' anachronism noted)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:27 records the brother's discovery of the restored silver: *va-yiftach ha-echad et saqo lateit mispo la-chamoro ba-malon* — *and as one of them opened his sack to give his ass provender in the* [malon] — he sees the silver in the mouth of his *amtachat*. The noun *malon* names the place where the brothers stopped to spend the night on the return journey to Kena'an.** // **The lexeme.** *Malon* (מָלוֹן) derives from the root *l-w-n* / *lin* ('to lodge, to spend the night, to overnight'), with the *ma-* prefix indicating place or means. The standard formation is *ma- + verbal-root* generating a noun-of-place: *malon* = 'the place of lodging / overnighting'. The lexeme denotes the institutional wayfaring stopover — variously a caravanserai (a roadside enclosure with provision for travelers and beasts), a way-station (a fortified or semi-fortified stop on a trade route), or simply the customary night-camp location for caravans on a given route. The lexeme is NOT 'inn' in the modern Western sense — there were no commercial inns in the modern sense in ancient Near Eastern trade; travelers stopped at caravanserai-style way-stations (often associated with springs, oases, or fortified posts), guest-houses (private or village-provided hospitality), or simply customary camp-sites. The KJV's 'inn' (here and at Exod 4:24, Luke 2:7) is anachronistic and has misled readers; the ASV-baseline 'lodging-place' is the philologically appropriate rendering. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The lexeme recurs at: **Gen 43:21** — the brothers' second-journey *malon* (the same return-journey *malon* type, possibly the same physical location as the Gen 42:27 occurrence); **Exod 4:24** — *va-yhi ba-derekh ba-malon va-yifgeshehu YHWH* — the bridegroom-of-blood encounter (the obscure scene where YHWH meets Mosheh at the *malon* on the way to Mitsrayim, with the Tzipporah-circumcision-and-blood ritual; one of the corpus's most contested passages); **Josh 4:3, 8** — the twelve-stone memorial at Yisrael's *malon* on the night after crossing the Jordan (the camp-site at Gilgal); **2 Kgs 19:23 = Isa 37:24** — Sancheriv's boast of reaching the *malon qitzo* ('the lodging of his border / the night-camp of his furthest extremity', a poetic geographical metonym); **Jer 9:1 [MT 9:2]** — *mi-yittenenni va-midbar melon orchim* ('Oh that I had in the wilderness a *malon* of wayfarers' — Jeremiah's wish for a desert way-station to retreat to away from his people). The cross-corpus distribution is consistent: the lexeme always denotes the institutional wayfaring stopover, never the modern 'inn'. // **The Gen 42:27 narrative context.** The *malon* is presumably a customary night-camp on the route between Mitsrayim and Kena'an — possibly at one of the Negev oases or at a way-station on the desert margin. The brothers stop, one of them opens his *saq* to give the ass its *mispo* (provender), and discovers the silver. The discovery's location at the *malon* is narratively significant: only one brother makes the discovery (vv 27-28), and the dread is collective only later (the full collective discovery at v 35 when they unload their sacks at home). The *malon*-discovery is the first crack in the test, before the home-discovery that completes it. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach (Gen 43:21; Exod 4:24; Josh 4:3, 8; 2 Kgs 19:23 = Isa 37:24; Jer 9:1) but limited distribution; the lexeme is chapter-anchored at the Gen 42:27 discovery-scene narrative point; the cross-corpus reach is documented as a promotion-path. → **OVERLAY** (the lexeme is well-distributed enough that central housing might be warranted on cross-corpus reach grounds; the editorial decision here is to overlay-house with promotion-path noted, since the chapter-narrative-point is what the entry documents). When Exodus is translated, the Exod 4:24 *malon* is the most significant cross-corpus parallel; promotion to central could be reconsidered then. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit; (b) the wayfaring-stopover sense is well-established across the standard lexica; (c) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable; (d) the ASV-baseline 'lodging-place' is the direct rendering; (e) the KJV-anachronism critique is documented in the standard reference works. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *malon* and *lin*; BDB p. 533; TDOT VII:553-555; NIDOTTE 2:790-792; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 524; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 320; on ANE caravan-routes and way-stations: V. H. Matthews 'Hospitality and Hostility in Judges 4' BTB 21 (1991) 13-21; W. F. Albright 'The Egyptian Empire in Asia in the Twenty-First Century B.C.' JPOS 8 (1928) 223-256; on the KJV 'inn' anachronism: J. Jeremias *Jerusalem in the Time of Jesus* 1969 (Luke 2:7 context).

terms.translit: va-yetze libbam (literally 'and their heart went out', at v 28)
terms.partOfSpeech: verbal idiom: verb yatza (Qal 3ms wayyiqtol) + noun lev (with 3mp possessive suffix) — 'their heart went out'
terms.literal: and their heart went out — (idiomatic) the sudden onset of dread / fear / dismay; the courage / life-force draining away
terms.standardEnglish: their heart failed them (ASV/KJV/NRSV); their hearts sank (NJPS / Alter); their heart went out (literal)
terms.wohChoice: their heart failed them (ASV-baseline; the striking literal 'their heart went out' physiological-emotional idiom documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:28 records the brothers' reaction to the discovery of the restored silver at the *malon*: *va-yetze libbam va-yecherdu ish el achiv* — *and their heart went out, and they trembled one to another*. The idiom *va-yetze libbam* (literally 'and their heart went out') is a striking physiological-emotional construction for the sudden onset of dread, fear, or dismay. The construction is rare in the HB and admits two principal readings.** // **The idiom.** The construction 'the heart goes out' (*lev yatza*) is a near-hapax in the HB in this specific physiological-emotional sense. The dominant rendering tradition reads the construction idiomatically as 'the heart failed / the courage drained away' — the heart conceived as the seat of resolve, its 'going out' as the draining of life-force or determination. The reading is supported by the immediate context (the brothers *charadu* — 'trembled'; their fear is the dominant register) and by the parallel idiom *va-yafag libbo* at Gen 45:26 (Ya'aqov, on hearing Yosef is alive, 'his heart fainted'; literally 'his heart grew faint / became cold') — both idioms describe the heart's sudden-shock response to overwhelming news. A more literal reading takes 'the heart went out' as a striking physical image: the heart leaving the body in shock, the imagined-physiological-departure of the life-force at the moment of dread. The literal preservation 'their heart went out' would render the Hebrew image faithfully; the ASV-baseline 'their heart failed them' renders the idiom into the conventional English-equivalent. // **The cross-corpus parallels (the heart-as-seat-of-courage idioms).** The Hebrew Bible deploys several heart-going-out / heart-failing idioms for shock-and-dread: (i) *yatza lev* at Gen 42:28 (this entry); (ii) *pug lev* at Gen 45:26 (the *va-yafag libbo* of Ya'aqov hearing Yosef lives); (iii) *namos lev* ('the heart melts', Deut 20:8; Josh 2:11; 7:5; Isa 13:7; 19:1; Nah 2:11 [MT 2:10] — the most common heart-failing idiom in the corpus); (iv) *namog lev* ('the heart faints', Ps 22:15 [MT 22:14]); (v) *ne'esfu chayyei lev* ('the life of the heart was gathered up', a related sudden-shock construction). The idioms share the structural pattern of *the heart's vital-function ceasing* as the bodily-correlate of sudden-dread. The Gen 42:28 *yatza lev* is the most striking of the cluster — the heart not melting or fainting but going out, leaving the body. The nearest extra-Genesis parallel is **Cant 5:6** *nafshi yatz'ah ve-dabro* — *my soul went out at his speaking* — also a sudden-shock idiom, with *nefesh* ('soul') instead of *lev* ('heart') as the departing-entity. The Cant 5:6 parallel suggests the idiom-type is the *X yatza* (a vital-entity goes out) form. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV/NRSV 'their heart failed them' renders the idiom into the conventional English-equivalent (the 'heart failing' idiom is itself an English-language convention for sudden-dread, e.g., 'his heart failed him at the sight'). NJPS / Alter 'their hearts sank' moves further toward modern register. The literal 'their heart went out' is preserved-in-spirit by the ASV-baseline (the 'failed' captures the failure-of-courage that 'went out' encodes); the literal preservation would be defensible but is rarely adopted because it reads as awkward in English. The ASV-baseline is retained. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular *yatza lev* construction (the only HB occurrence of this specific idiom is Gen 42:28; the cross-corpus parallels are with different vital-entity nouns — *pug lev*, *namos lev*, etc. — and are separate idioms); → **OVERLAY**. The wider heart-failing idiom cluster could receive a future central entry if a cross-corpus collection of the sudden-dread heart-idioms warrants it; the chapter-specific *yatza lev* is here. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the idiom is grammatically and lexically explicit; (b) the heart-as-seat-of-courage sense is direct in the Hebrew physiological-emotional register; (c) the ASV-baseline 'their heart failed them' is the direct idiom-equivalent rendering. The literal-preservation reading is documented as a defensible alternative. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *yatza* (the heart-idiom uses); BDB p. 422; TDOT VI:225-250; NIDOTTE 2:498-502 (yatza); on *lev* in idiomatic constructions: HALOT s.v. *lev*; TDOT VII:399-437 (lev); F. Stolz 'lev Herz' THAT I:861-867; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 113; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 525; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 245; on the Cant 5:6 *nafshi yatz'ah* parallel: M. Pope *Song of Songs* AB 1977; on the heart-failing idiom cluster more broadly: H. W. Wolff *Anthropology of the Old Testament* 1974 pp. 40-58 ('Lev — The Reasonable Man').

terms.translit: tzeror kesef ('bundle of money / pouch of silver', at v 35 in tzeror kaspo and tzeroрот kaspeihem)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun phrase: masculine noun in construct + noun ('bundle of money / pouch of silver')
terms.literal: tzeror kesef — a bundle / pouch / bag of silver; the small money-pouches in which silver coin or weight was carried for commercial transactions
terms.standardEnglish: bundle of money (ASV/KJV/NJPS); bag of money (NRSV); bundle of silver (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: bundle of money (ASV-baseline; the literal 'pouch / bag of silver' sense and the cross-corpus tzeror-cluster documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:35 records the final shock of the chapter: as the brothers empty their sacks at home before Ya'aqov, each finds *tzeror kaspo be-saqo* — *his bundle of money in his sack* — and the brothers and Ya'aqov collectively see *tzeroрот kaspeihem* — *their bundles of money* — and are afraid. The noun *tzeror* (צְרוֹר, 'bundle, pouch, bag') derives from the root *tzarar* I ('to bind up, tie in a bundle'); the construct *tzeror kesef* names the small money-pouches in which silver was carried for mercantile transactions.** // **The lexeme.** *Tzeror* I (from *tzarar* I, 'to bind up') denotes the bundled / tied-up form of whatever is wrapped or pouched. The construct-form *tzeror + (substance)* generates 'bundle of X' compounds: *tzeror kesef* ('pouch of silver'), *tzeror ha-mor* (Cant 1:13, 'sachet of myrrh'), etc. The lexeme is distinguished from *tzeror* II (from *tzarar* II, 'to be narrow / press / oppose'), which gives 'enemy / adversary' senses. The two lexemes are homonymous but etymologically distinct (HALOT registers them separately). // **The cross-corpus *tzeror*-cluster (Gen 42 occurrence and the four parallels).** The lexeme recurs in four notable HB attestations: (i) **1 Sam 25:29** *ve-haytah nefesh adoni tzerurah be-tzeror ha-chayim et YHWH Elohekha* — *and the soul of my lord shall be bound up in the bundle of the living with YHWH thy Elohim* — Avigail's blessing of David. The phrase *tzeror ha-chayim* ('bundle of the living') has entered Jewish liturgical and funerary tradition (the blessing-of-the-departed prayer includes the phrase *te'urar nafsho be-tzeror ha-chayim*, 'may his soul be bound up in the bundle of the living'). The theological-poetic image: the souls of the righteous bound together in YHWH's care, like precious items in a treasure-pouch. (ii) **Prov 7:20** *tzeror ha-kesef laqach be-yado le-yom ha-kese yavo veito* — *he has taken a* tzeror ha-kesef *in his hand; he will come home at the day of the full moon* — the adulteress's husband's traveling money-pouch. The Prov 7:20 *tzeror ha-kesef* is the closest cross-corpus parallel to Gen 42:35: both use the construct *tzeror ha-kesef* for the merchant's traveling money-pouch. The Proverbs occurrence confirms the lexeme's mercantile register. (iii) **Hag 1:6** *u-ha-mishtakker mishtakker el tzeror naquv* — *and he who earns wages earns them into a pouch with holes* — the prophetic indictment of mismanaged commerce; the *tzeror naquv* ('holed pouch') as the image of vain-labor. (iv) **Cant 1:13** *tzeror ha-mor dodi li* — *my beloved is a bundle / sachet of myrrh unto me* — the love-poetry deployment, with *tzeror ha-mor* as the perfume-sachet held between the breasts. The four cross-corpus occurrences plus the Gen 42:35 mercantile occurrence form a tight five-occurrence *tzeror*-cluster: the lexeme covers (a) the mercantile pouch (Gen 42:35; Prov 7:20; Hag 1:6); (b) the metaphorical-poetic bundle (1 Sam 25:29 *tzeror ha-chayim*; Cant 1:13 *tzeror ha-mor*). The Gen 42:35 occurrence is the corpus's earliest narrative-prose mercantile *tzeror* and is the structural anchor of the mercantile-register cluster. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV 'bundle of money' (preserving the literal *tzeror* — the 'bundle' as the bound-up pouch); NJPS 'bundle of money'; NRSV 'bag of money'; Alter 'bundle of silver'. The 'bundle' rendering is awkward in modern English (a 'bundle of money' suggests a sheaf of bills rather than a pouch of silver-weight) but preserves the *tzeror* etymological force; 'pouch of silver' would be philologically more transparent but loses the cross-corpus echo to *tzeror ha-chayim* and *tzeror ha-mor*. The ASV-baseline 'bundle of money' is preserved for the cross-corpus consistency. // **Overlay housing — with promotion-path note.** Cross-corpus reach to 1 Sam 25:29 (the *tzeror ha-chayim* blessing-formula), Prov 7:20 (the mercantile-pouch parallel), Hag 1:6 (the holed-pouch prophetic-indictment), and Cant 1:13 (the love-poetry sachet); the lexeme's reach is genuine. The editorial decision here is to overlay-house the chapter-specific mercantile occurrence, with a promotion-path note: when Samuel or Proverbs or Haggai or Canticles is translated, the lexeme's cross-corpus reach will activate, and promotion to a central *tzeror-bundle-pouch-vocabulary* entry could be considered. The cluster is borderline — five occurrences in five distinct contexts is the cross-corpus threshold; the central-vs-overlay decision is judgment-dependent. For now → **OVERLAY**, with the promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit; (b) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable; (c) the 'bundle / pouch of silver' rendering is the direct sense; (d) the mercantile-register cluster is documented across the standard commentaries.
