K. McCarter *I Samuel* AB 1980 pp. 396-397; on the Prov 7:20 mercantile-pouch parallel: M. V. Fox *Proverbs 1-9* AB 2000.

terms.translit: seivah (here at v 38 in seivati, 'my gray hair / my old age', in the descent-to-She'ol grief-formula ve-horadtem et seivati be-yagon She'olah)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, feminine singular (from sav, 'gray-haired one, elder')
terms.literal: seivah — gray-haired old age, the metonymic noun for old age figured through its bodily marker (the gray hair); 'my gray hairs' figures the patriarch's aged person and life
terms.standardEnglish: gray hairs (ASV/KJV/NRSV); white head (NJPS); gray head (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: gray hairs (ASV-baseline; the metonymic 'gray-haired old age' sense and the Yosef-cycle grief-formula documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 42:38 records Ya'aqov's striking concrete embodiment of his aged-mourning in the descent-to-She'ol formula: *ve-horadtem et seivati be-yagon She'olah* — *and ye shall bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to She'ol*. The noun *seivah* (שֵׂיבָה) is the metonymic noun for old age figured through its bodily marker (gray hair) — the patriarch's gray hairs standing for his whole aged person and life. The lexeme recurs at Gen 44:29 and 44:31 in the same descent-to-She'ol grief-formula, forming a Ya'aqov-internal repeated grief-arc across Gen 42:38 → 44:29 → 44:31.** // **The lexeme.** *Seivah* (שֵׂיבָה) derives from *sav* (שָׂב, 'gray-haired one, elder'); both lexemes denote the bodily-and-social condition of aged-ness, the *seivah* the abstract / metonymic noun, the *sav* the substantive person. The metonymy is precise: the gray hairs as the visible marker of advanced age stand for the whole aged person. The lexeme is distinct from *zaqen* (זָקֵן, 'old man / elder', the general lexeme for advanced age) and from *yashish* (יָשִׁישׁ, 'aged one', a rarer lexeme); the *seivah* / *sav* pair carries specifically the gray-haired marker, with the social-honor register of the elderly-as-honored that the gray hair calls forth. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The lexeme recurs across the corpus in the standard 'gray-haired old age' register: **Gen 15:15** — Avraham's *titqaver be-seivah tovah* ('thou shalt be buried in a good old age', the patriarchal promise of a long life); **Gen 25:8** — Avraham's death *zaqen ve-saveya yamim*... *be-seivah tovah* ('an old man and full of years... in a good old age'); **Gen 42:38, 44:29, 44:31** — Ya'aqov's *seivah*-and-She'ol grief-formula (three Yosef-cycle occurrences); **Lev 19:32** — *mipnei seivah taqum ve-hadarta penei zaqen* — *before the gray head thou shalt rise up, and honor the face of the old man* — the honoring-the-aged commandment; **1 Kgs 2:6, 9** — Shelomoh's deathbed-instructions about Yo'av (*ve-lo toreid seivato be-shalom she'olah*, 'and let not his gray head go down to She'ol in peace' — the lexical-parallel to Gen 42:38's *horadetem et seivati ... She'olah*, the only HB *seivah* + She'olah cross-corpus parallel) and the parallel about Shim'i; **Deut 32:25** (the Song of Mosheh, lexically related); **Judg 8:32** — Gid'on's death *be-seivah tovah*; **Ruth 4:15** — Naomi's promised restoration *u-khalkel et-seivatekh* ('and a nourisher of thy gray hairs'); **1 Chr 29:28** — David's death *be-seivah tovah*; **Job 41:24 [MT 41:32]** (the Leviathan-and-the-deep poetic deployment); **Ps 71:18** *ve-gam ad-ziqnah ve-seivah Elohim al ta'azveni* — *now also when I am old and grayheaded, O Elohim, forsake me not* — the elder's prayer; **Ps 92:15 [MT 92:14]**; **Prov 16:31** *ateret tif'eret seivah* — *the gray head is a crown of glory* — the wisdom-tradition's honor-formula; **Prov 20:29** *ve-hadar zekenim seivah* — *and the glory of old men is the gray head*; **Isa 46:4** *ve-ad seivah ani esbol* — *and even to your gray hairs will I carry* — the deity's promise; **Hos 7:9** — *gam-seivah zarqah bo* — *gray hairs are sprinkled upon him* — the prophetic indictment of unaware aging. The lexeme is one of the corpus's standard honor-and-age vocabulary nodes. // **The Yosef-cycle Ya'aqov-internal three-fold deployment.** The three Yosef-cycle occurrences (Gen 42:38, 44:29, 44:31) are ALL on Ya'aqov's lips, ALL in the descent-to-She'ol formula (*ve-horadetem et seivati ... She'olah*), and ALL about the fear-of-losing-Binyamin context. The construction is a fixed lament-formula: *seivah* + *She'olah* + descent-verb. The formula's three occurrences (one in Gen 42, two in Gen 44) form a Ya'aqov-internal grief-arc that the 1 Kgs 2:6 cross-corpus parallel echoes lexically (Shelomoh's 'let not his gray head go down to She'ol in peace' uses the same *seivato* + *She'olah* construction in a deathbed-curse register). The Yosef-cycle grief-formula and the 1 Kings cross-corpus parallel are the lexeme's only attestations in the descent-to-She'ol construction. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach (Gen, Lev, Deut, Judg, Ruth, 1 Kgs, 1 Chr, Job, Ps, Prov, Isa, Hos) but Yosef-cycle-anchored grief-formula deployment; the lexeme's cross-corpus reach is genuine and the entry could plausibly be central, but the editorial decision here is to overlay-house the Yosef-cycle-anchored entry (since the chapter-narrative-point is the three-fold grief-formula recurrence in Ya'aqov's mouth), with a promotion-path note: when the Levitical (19:32), Davidic/Solomonic (1 Kgs 2:6, 9), and wisdom (Prov 16:31, 20:29) occurrences are translated, the lexeme's broader honor-and-age vocabulary reach will warrant central housing. → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit; (b) the 'gray-haired old age' metonymic sense is well-established; (c) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable; (d) the ASV-baseline 'gray hairs' is the direct rendering; (e) the Yosef-cycle three-fold deployment is textually verifiable; (f) the 1 Kgs 2:6 *seivah* + *She'olah* construction parallel is documented. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *seivah* and *sav*; BDB pp. 966-967; TDOT XIV:209-217; NIDOTTE 4:1190-1191; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 292-293; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 114; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 527; on the Yosef-cycle *seivah* + *She'olah* descent-formula: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on the 1 Kgs 2:6 parallel: J. Gray *I & II Kings* OTL 1970; on the honoring-the-aged Lev 19:32 commandment: J. Milgrom *Leviticus 17-22* AB 2000 pp. 1664-1667; on *seivah* in the wisdom-tradition: M. V. Fox *Proverbs 10-31* AB 2009.

terms.translit: einennu (negative-existential particle + 3ms suffix: 'he is not [here / present / extant]'; here at vv 13 ve-ha-echad einennu; 32 ha-echad einennu; 36 Yosef einennu ve-Shim'on einennu)
terms.partOfSpeech: negative-existential particle ayin + 3ms suffix; the construction means 'he is not / he is no longer (here / present / extant)'
terms.literal: einennu — 'he-is-not'; the negative-existential 'he is not [here / present / extant]', a charged euphemism for the absence-of-a-person (typically by death or by unexplained disappearance)
terms.standardEnglish: is not (ASV/KJV — literal); is no more (NJPS); is no longer (Alter); is gone (looser)
terms.wohChoice: is not (ASV-baseline literal; the chapter's einennu-refrain across vv 13, 32, 36 documented; the cross-cycle echo to Gen 37:30 and the forward Gen 44:20, 26, 30 noted)
terms.rationale: **Genesis 42 deploys *einennu* (literally 'he is not') four times across the chapter as a deliberate refrain: v 13 (*ve-ha-echad einennu*, 'and one is not' — the brothers' first deployment, in their initial response to Yosef's questioning); v 32 (*ha-echad einennu* — the brothers retelling to Ya'aqov); v 36 (*Yosef einennu ve-Shim'on einennu* — Ya'aqov's climactic double deployment, applying the formula to two missing brothers at once). The refrain echoes Re'uven's anguished *ha-yeled einennu* at Gen 37:30 (the moment Re'uven returned to the empty pit and discovered Yosef gone) and forward-echoes the brothers' Gen 44:20 (*ve-achiv met ... ve-hu levado nishar*), 44:26, and 44:30 deployments before Yosef's final disclosure.** // **The construction.** *Einennu* (אֵינֶנּוּ) is the negative-existential particle *ayin* (אַיִן, 'there is not / is not') with the 3ms pronominal suffix *-ennu*: 'he is not' — denoting the absence-or-non-existence of the referent. The construction is grammatically equivalent to *lo hi shams* ('he is not present') or *einennu po* ('he is not here'). The semantic force is the negative-existential statement of a person's absence, with the particular force of CHARGED EUPHEMISM: the construction does NOT commit to *why* the referent is absent (death? departure? unexplained disappearance?), only that the referent is currently *not*. This deliberate ambiguity is what makes the refrain a literary device in the chapter. // **The chapter-internal refrain's literary force.** The brothers' deployment of *einennu* in vv 13 and 32 is a charged euphemism: they neither admit the sale (the truth) nor state the conventional 'dead' (the false-but-conventional reading they have allowed Ya'aqov to accept). The deliberate non-committal *einennu* preserves the brothers' deception: they say 'he is not' without saying *what happened to him*. Ya'aqov, who has accepted the Gen 37:33 bloodied-tunic evidence, will be the one to state the conventional *met* ('dead') at v 38 (*ki achiv met*) — the brothers will not use the word *met* of Yosef in this chapter. The lexical-restraint is precise: the brothers say *einennu*; Ya'aqov says *met*; the truth (Yosef is alive in Mitsrayim) is known to none of the speakers. // **Ya'aqov's climactic double-deployment at v 36.** Ya'aqov picks up the brothers' refrain and doubles it: *Yosef einennu ve-Shim'on einennu* — 'Yosef is not, and Shim'on is not'. The formula applied to two missing brothers at once (Yosef presumed dead; Shim'on currently bound in Mitsrayim) and threatened toward a third (Binyamin) is the chapter's most concentrated grief-construction. The deployment shifts the refrain's register: the brothers used *einennu* as a euphemistic concealment-device; Ya'aqov uses it as the language of accumulating bereavement — each *einennu* counting another missing son. The threefold count (Yosef + Shim'on + the threatened Binyamin) is the patriarch's grief-arithmetic, and the *alai hayu khullanah* ('all these things are against me') closure seals the lament. // **The cross-Genesis arc Gen 37:30 → 42 → 44.** The refrain begins at Gen 37:30 — Re'uven, returning to the pit to retrieve Yosef and finding it empty, cries out *ha-yeled einennu, va-ani anah ani-va* ('the child is not, and I, where shall I go?'). The Gen 37:30 *einennu* is the first deployment of the refrain in the cycle, in Re'uven's anguished discovery. The refrain returns in Gen 42 (vv 13, 32, 36, four occurrences) as the brothers' deployment and Ya'aqov's double-deployment, and continues forward into Gen 44 (vv 20, 26, 30 — the brothers' deployment before Yosef in the second journey, retelling the same absence-and-loss to the *shallit*-Yosef who is in fact the missing one). The cross-cycle arc Gen 37:30 → 42:13, 32, 36 → 44:20, 26, 30 is one of the corpus's tightest lexical-refrain structures. The arc resolves at Gen 45:3 when Yosef discloses himself: the chapter that has run on the *einennu* refrain is silenced at the *ani Yosef achikhem* disclosure, with *einennu* never again applied to Yosef. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV literal 'is not' preserves the negative-existential force and the deliberate non-committal euphemism; NJPS 'is no more' and Alter 'is no longer' modulate to modern register but lose the construction's stark force. The ASV-baseline literal is preserved across the four chapter-internal occurrences, the Gen 37:30 anchor, and the Gen 44 forward-echoes — the refrain's lexical-keyword status requires uniform rendering. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-internal refrain (four deployments in Gen 42) plus the Gen 37:30 anchor and the Gen 44:20, 26, 30 forward-echoes — the literary arc is Genesis-internal (the Yosef-cycle); → **OVERLAY**. The lemma *einennu* (and the broader *ayin* + suffix construction) is a common Hebrew construction across the corpus; the chapter-specific deployment as the Yosef-cycle missing-brother refrain is what is documented here. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the chapter-internal four-fold deployment is textually verifiable; (c) the Gen 37:30 anchor and the Gen 44 forward-echoes are textually verifiable; (d) the deliberate-euphemism reading is documented across the standard commentaries; (e) the ASV-baseline literal 'is not' is the direct rendering. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *ayin*; BDB pp. 34-35; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 290-292; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 109, 113-114; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 519, 526; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 243-245 (on the *einennu* refrain); on the Yosef-cycle missing-brother arc: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; G. W. Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* CBQMS 4, 1976.

terms.translit: anokhi e'ervennu (Gen 43:9, Qal imperfect 1cs + 3ms suffix of arav, 'I will be surety for him'); avdekha arav et ha-na'ar (Gen 44:32, the Yehudah-speech repetition)
terms.strongs: H6148 (arav I, 'to pledge, give in pledge, be surety for')
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Qal (with the cognate noun eravon, 'pledge, surety', registered separately in the Gen 38 sibling-overlay entry)
terms.literal: arav — to pledge oneself, to be surety for (another); the verbal action of standing as the pledge-person for another's obligation or safety
terms.standardEnglish: I will be surety for him (ASV/KJV); I myself will be surety (NJPS); I will offer myself as pledge for him (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him (ASV-baseline; the Gen 38 eravon-pledge-triad cross-reference and the moral-literary fulcrum documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:9 stages one of the corpus's most concentrated character-arc moments: Yehudah's surety-pledge to Ya'aqov for Binyamin's safe return — *anokhi e'ervennu mi-yadi tevaqshennu, im lo havi'otiv elekha ve-hitzagtiv lefanekha ve-chatati lekha kol ha-yamim* ('I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him: if I bring him not unto thee, and set him before thee, then let me bear the blame for ever'). The verb *arav* (Qal *e'ervennu*, with the 3ms suffix referring to Binyamin) is the same root as the cognate noun *eravon* (the 'pledge / surety' that Tamar extracted from Yehudah at Gen 38:17-25, governed by the sibling overlay-entry [`eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff`](#eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff)). The Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44:18-34 Yehudah-arc is widely recognized as the corpus's moral-literary fulcrum: the man who once GAVE a pledge (the *eravon* triad of signet, cord, and staff) for a transaction now OFFERS HIMSELF as the *arav* (the surety-person) for his brother's life.** // **The lexeme.** The verb *arav* I (עָרַב) means 'to pledge oneself, give surety, stand as pledge for another'. The Qal-active is the standard stem for the act of becoming-surety; the cognate noun *eravon* (H6162) names the pledge-object (the security-deposit held until payment). The lexeme is forensically-precise: an *arav* (surety-person) takes responsibility for another's obligation, becoming legally liable if the obligation fails. The construction *anokhi e'ervennu mi-yadi tevaqshennu* — 'I will be surety for him; of my hand shalt thou require him' — is the technical surety-formula naming the surety-person and the demand-on-his-hand if the obligation fails. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The verb *arav* in the surety-sense recurs at: **Gen 43:9** (here); **Gen 44:32** (Yehudah's Gen 44:18-34 surety-speech repetition: *ki avdekha arav et ha-na'ar me-im avi le'mor, im lo avi'enu elekha ve-chatati le-avi kol ha-yamim* — 'for thy servant became surety for the lad unto my father'); **Ps 119:122** (*arov avdekha le-tov*, 'be surety for thy servant for good'); **Prov 6:1** (*beni im aravta le-re'ekha, taqa'ata la-zar kappekha* — 'my son, if thou be surety for thy friend'); **Prov 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26; 27:13** (the wisdom-tradition's repeated surety-warnings against the financial-and-relational risks of standing surety); **Job 17:3** (*sima-na orveni immakh*, 'lay down now, be surety for me'); **Isa 38:14** (Chizqiyahu's *orveni* lament); **Jer 30:21** (the Davidic eschatological figure who *arav et libbo* approaches YHWH). The cognate noun *eravon* in the pledge-object sense is restricted to Gen 38:17, 18, 20 (the Tamar pledge-triad). // **The Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44 Yehudah-arc.** The arc is one of the corpus's most-cited character-development structures. The Gen 38 scene stages Yehudah's *eravon*-giving: he hands Tamar his personal-identity tokens (the *chotam*, *petil*, *matteh*) as the pledge for the promised *gedi izzim*; Tamar later returns the items via the *haker-na* formula (Gen 38:25, the recognition-formula echoing the Gen 37:32 bloodied-tunic deception that Yehudah architected) and convicts him; Yehudah's *tzadqah mimmeni* verdict (Gen 38:26) names her righteousness. The Gen 38 chapter is therefore one of the corpus's first MAJOR Yehudah-character-development scenes: the man who gave the *eravon* learns from being convicted by it. The Gen 43:9 surety-pledge then re-deploys the same *arav* root in a transformed register: Yehudah now offers HIMSELF as the *arav*, not an external token but his own person. The Gen 44:18-34 surety-speech extends the pledge into the full speech-act that brings the Gen 45:1 recognition-scene: Yehudah's offer to substitute himself for Binyamin (44:33) — 'let thy servant abide instead of the lad a servant to my lord' — completes the transformation. The man who once gave the *eravon* now IS the *arav*; the pledge-taker has become the pledge-person; the man who orchestrated the Gen 37 deception (selling Yosef into slavery) now offers himself into slavery to save the surviving Rachel-line son. // **The bidirectional sibling-overlay link.** This entry is the Gen 43-44 sibling to the existing Gen 38 overlay entry [`eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff`](#eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff). Per the ratified sibling-overlay-entries pattern (Gen 35 / 38 / 39 / 41 / 42 precedents), the two entries are created as SEPARATE companions — NOT by extending one entry's appliesTo — with bidirectional cross-references in each rationale. The Gen 38 entry's rationale has been extended with a 'Cross-references (the Gen 43:9 / 44:32 Yehudah-surety-pledge sibling-overlay link)' paragraph that names this entry by id and documents the Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44 character-arc. This entry's rationale here cross-references the Gen 38 entry by id. The two entries together govern the *arav* / *eravon* root across the patriarchal narratives. // **The self-imprecatory closing.** *Ve-chatati lekha kol ha-yamim* — literally 'and I shall be sinful before thee all the days' — uses the verb *chatat* (here Qal-perfect-consecutive) in a rare self-curse register. The ASV-baseline 'let me bear the blame for ever' renders the legal-forensic 'bear the blame' force without surfacing the *chatat* lexeme. The literal 'I shall stand sinful before thee all the days' (NJPS variant) preserves the lexeme but reads stiltedly in English. The ASV rendering is preserved; the *chatat* lexeme's broader cross-corpus reach (the standard sin-vocabulary; central anchors at Gen 4:7 *chatat rovetz*, Gen 18:20 the Sedom *chatat*, etc.) is governed elsewhere. // **Overlay housing.** Patriarchal-narrative Yehudah-arc (Gen 38 / 43 / 44) — Genesis-internal sibling-doublet of a load-bearing character-development motif → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional cross-reference to the Gen 38 sibling. The cross-corpus reach into the wisdom-tradition (Prov 6:1 etc.) is genuine but the entry's editorial point is the Genesis-internal Yehudah-character-arc; a future Proverbs translation may justify central promotion if the surety-warnings are governed in unified fashion. → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the verb is morphologically explicit (Qal of *arav*), but (b) the recorded editorial substance is the Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44 character-arc reading and the moral-literary-fulcrum claim, both of which are interpretive observations between attested readings; (c) the self-imprecatory *chatati lekha kol ha-yamim* rendering is between attested alternatives (the ASV-baseline forensic 'bear the blame' vs. the literal 'I shall be sinful'); (d) the bidirectional-sibling-overlay claim is editorial. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *arav* I; BDB p. 786; TDOT XI:326-329; NIDOTTE 3:495-496; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 268-271, 298, 305-307; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 121-122, 135-137; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 543-545, 562-571; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 322; on the Gen 38 → Gen 43 → Gen 44 Yehudah-character-arc as the corpus's moral-literary fulcrum: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1 ('A Literary Approach to the Bible'); M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; G. W. Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* CBQMS 4, 1976; on the *arav*-as-surety lexeme in ancient-Israelite commercial law: R. Westbrook 'The Phrase 'His Heart Is Satisfied' in Ancient Near Eastern Legal Sources' JAOS 111 (1991) 219-224.

terms.translit: nikhmeru rachamav (Gen 43:30; Niphal of kamar I, 'to be hot / grow warm / burn', paired with the noun rachamim 'compassion / mercy / tender-feeling' with 3ms suffix)
terms.partOfSpeech: verbal idiom: Niphal perfect 3mp of kamar I + noun rachamim (in plural-abstract) with 3ms possessive suffix
terms.literal: nikhmeru rachamav — his rachamim (compassion-affections) burned / grew warm / were stirred — the visceral compassion-yearning construction figured through the burning / warming of the womb-affections
terms.standardEnglish: his heart yearned over (ASV/NRSV); his bowels did yearn upon (KJV — visceral-literal); his feelings for his brother had welled up (Alter); he was overcome with feeling toward (NJPS); his compassion was stirred (modern)
terms.wohChoice: his heart yearned over his brother (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:30; the visceral 'bowels did yearn' KJV-literal and the rachamim womb-root force documented in commentary; the cross-corpus 1 Kgs 3:26 and Hos 11:8 idiom-cluster surfaced)
terms.rationale: **The idiom *nikhmeru rachamav* — 'his rachamim burned / grew warm / were stirred' — is the corpus's most concentrated compassion-yearning construction. The Niphal of *kamar* I ('to be hot, grow warm, burn'; HALOT distinguishes from *kamar* II 'priest', the kemarim of idolatrous priests, a separate lexeme) paired with *rachamim* (the womb-compassion-noun derived from *rechem* 'womb', governed by the central entry [`rachamim-compassion-womb-root`](#rachamim-compassion-womb-root)) generates the idiom. The three HB occurrences (Gen 43:30, 1 Kgs 3:26, Hos 11:8) form a tight cross-corpus *nikhmar*+compassion idiom-cluster, and the Genesis 43 occurrence is the corpus's first.** // **The lexeme.** The verb *kamar* I (כָּמַר) in the Qal is rare; the Niphal (passive-reflexive) is the standard stem for the idiom and means 'to be heated / to grow warm / to become hot / to burn (internally)'. The semantic core is the visceral-physiological sensation of warmth-of-internal-organs: the womb-affections (the *rachamim*) growing-hot in response to a love-or-pity-object. The construction is therefore anatomical-and-affective: the *rachamim* (the womb-affections) burn (the visceral warming) toward (the object of compassion). The lexeme is psycho-physical: the action being described is felt as a warming-of-the-inner-being, the same physical metaphor English preserves in 'my heart went out to', though the Hebrew lexeme is anatomically more specific (the womb-affections, not the heart). // **The three-occurrence idiom-cluster (the cross-corpus parallels).** The construction is restricted to three HB occurrences, each load-bearing: // **(1) Gen 43:30 (here).** Yosef sees Binyamin (his mother's son, the only Rachel-line brother) for the first time in twenty-two years; the construction names the visceral compassion-burning that drives him from the room to weep in private. The deployment is the cycle's most concentrated emotional-marker — the only moment in the cycle Yosef's emotional state is named at this anatomical-visceral register. The compassion-burning is the inner-state; the outward-restraint (the *va-yit'appaq* of v 31, central entry [`yitappaq-emotional-restraint-yosef-arc`](#yitappaq-emotional-restraint-yosef-arc)) is the response. // **(2) 1 Kgs 3:26.** The famous Solomon-judgment scene: the two prostitute-mothers contest the living child, and Shelomoh threatens to cut him in half; the verse names the true mother's response: *va-tomer ha-ishah asher benah ha-chai el ha-melekh ki nikhmeru rachameha al benah va-tomer bi adoni* — 'and the woman whose son was the living child spoke to the king, for her *rachamim* burned for her son; and she said, Oh, my lord'. The construction is VERBATIM identical to Gen 43:30 (same Niphal-of-*kamar* + *rachamim*-with-suffix + *al* + child-object). The Solomon-judgment narrative deploys the construction to identify the true mother by the visceral physiological compassion-response; the false mother's willingness to see the child cut in half is the diagnostic absence-of-the-construction. The construction is therefore the corpus's lexical-anatomical test for the maternal compassion-bond. // **(3) Hos 11:8.** The prophetic deployment, in the divine voice: *eikh ettenkha Ephraim, amaggenkha Yisra'el, eikh ettenkha khe-Adamah, asimkha kitz'voyim; nehepakh alai libbi, yachad nikhmeru nichumai* — 'how shall I give thee up, Ephraim? how shall I deliver thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? how shall I set thee as Tzvoyim? my heart is turned within me, together my *nichumai* are burned'. The Hos 11:8 deployment uses the related noun *nichumim* ('compassions / consolations', cognate of *nicham* 'comfort') rather than *rachamim*; the Niphal-of-*kamar* construction is otherwise identical. The deployment names YHWH's compassion-burning-toward-Ephraim in the most concentrated divine-pathos passage of the prophet, and reads as the divine analog of the Solomon-judgment-mother and of Yosef-at-Gen-43:30: the deity's *nichumim* burn toward Ephraim as a mother's *rachamim* burn toward her child. The Hos 11 deployment is one of the corpus's deepest theological-anthropomorphisms; the lexical idiom anchors the maternal-divine compassion-identification. // **The womb-root link.** The *rechem* (womb) → *rachamim* (compassion-noun) derivation makes the construction's force anatomically-precise: it is the *womb-affections* that burn. The 1 Kgs 3:26 occurrence is therefore lexically the most-natural (a mother's womb-affections burning for her womb-born son); the Gen 43:30 occurrence transfers the maternal-anatomical register to Yosef's response to Binyamin (the brother who shares the mother — the only brother on the scene with whom Yosef shares the same womb); the Hos 11:8 occurrence transfers the maternal-anatomical register to the deity-toward-Ephraim. The three deployments draw on the womb-root link in slightly different ways but the construction's semantic-physiological core is consistent. // **The rendering question.** The KJV's 'his bowels did yearn upon his brother' preserves the anatomically-visceral force of the Hebrew (the *bowels* as the modern-anatomical-imprecise-but-visceral approximation of the womb-affections) but reads archaically. The ASV's 'his heart yearned over his brother' modernizes to the heart-as-emotional-organ but loses the womb-root specificity. NJPS 'he was overcome with feeling toward his brother' and Alter 'his feelings for his brother had welled up' are functional moderns that flatten the anatomical force entirely. The ASV-baseline 'his heart yearned over his brother' is preserved for register-consistency; the visceral-anatomical force and the womb-root link are documented in this entry and in the central [`rachamim-compassion-womb-root`](#rachamim-compassion-womb-root) entry. // **The bidirectional sibling-link.** This entry is the Gen 43:30 idiom-specific sibling to the central [`rachamim-compassion-womb-root`](#rachamim-compassion-womb-root) entry. The central entry governs the *rachamim* lexeme's full cross-corpus distribution (the divine-attribute formula Exod 34:6, the Deuteronomic restoration-promises, the prophetic compassion-language, the Psalter, etc.); this overlay entry governs the chapter-specific *nikhmeru rachamav* idiom-construction with its three-occurrence cross-corpus cluster (Gen 43:30, 1 Kgs 3:26, Hos 11:8). The bidirectional cross-reference is wired: the central `rachamim-compassion-womb-root` entry's rationale notes Gen 43:30 as the construction's first attestation; this entry cross-references the central entry by id. The two entries are companions: the central one for the lexeme; this overlay one for the idiom. // **Overlay housing.** The three-occurrence idiom-cluster is genuine cross-corpus reach but the editorial point at Gen 43:30 is the chapter-specific construction-deployment, with the 1 Kgs 3:26 and Hos 11:8 cross-corpus parallels documented as the idiom-cluster. → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional cross-reference to the central [`rachamim-compassion-womb-root`](#rachamim-compassion-womb-root) entry. The construction's three-occurrence restriction makes overlay housing appropriate for the idiom-specific entry; the broader *rachamim* lexeme is housed centrally. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit (Niphal of *kamar* I + *rachamim*); (b) the three-occurrence cross-corpus cluster is exhaustively verifiable; (c) the womb-root etymological link is documented; (d) the maternal-compassion-anatomical reading is established across the standard lexica; (e) the 1 Kgs 3:26 verbatim parallel is grammatically explicit. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *kamar* I (Niphal); BDB p. 485; TDOT VII:153-159; NIDOTTE 2:686-687 (kamar); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 124-125; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 545-546; on the 1 Kgs 3:26 Solomon-judgment lexical parallel: J. Gray *I & II Kings* OTL 1970; on the Hos 11:8 divine-compassion deployment: H. W. Wolff *Hosea* Hermeneia 1974 pp. 202-203; J. L. Andersen and D. N. Freedman *Hosea* AB 1980 pp. 585-589; on the womb-root anatomical-affective register: P. Trible *God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality* OBT 1978 ch. 2 ('Journey of a Metaphor').

terms.translit: hitmahmahnu (Hithpalpel of m-h-h, 'to tarry / delay / hesitate', here at Gen 43:10 in the lulei-counterfactual)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Hithpalpel (intensive-reflexive reduplicated stem) of the root m-h-h
terms.literal: hitmahmah — to tarry, delay, hesitate, linger; the reduplicated Hithpalpel intensifies the simple delaying-action
terms.standardEnglish: lingered (ASV/KJV); tarried (older); had we not dawdled (NJPS); had we not lingered (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: except we had lingered (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:10; the reduplicated Hithpalpel and the eschatological Hab 2:3 cross-corpus parallel documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **The verb *hitmahmah* (הִתְמַהְמַהּ) is the Hithpalpel (intensive-reflexive reduplicated stem) of the root *m-h-h* ('to tarry, delay, hesitate'). The reduplicated stem is a striking morphological feature: the verbal root is doubled (*m-h-m-h*) and conjugated in the Hithpael-with-reduplication pattern, intensifying the simple tarrying-action. Gen 43:10 deploys the Hithpalpel in Yehudah's reproach to Ya'aqov: *ki lulei hitmahmahnu ki ata shavnu zeh pa'amayim* — 'for except we had lingered, surely we had now returned a second time'. The counterfactual particle *lulei* ('except / had it not been that') frames the verb in the contrary-to-fact register: the brothers' delay caused the second journey not yet to have happened.** // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The Hithpalpel of *m-h-h* occurs at a small but pointed cluster of attestations: // **Gen 19:16** — *va-yitmahmah* of Lot at Sedom: the messengers seize Lot and his family because Lot is *tarrying* in the doomed city. The Gen 19:16 deployment is the canonical narrative-tarrying scene; the messengers' physical-seizing-of-the-tarrying-one is the structural counterpart of the warning-of-judgment. // **Judg 3:26** — Ehud's escape after assassinating Eglon: *ve-Ehud nimlat ad hitmahmeham* — 'and Ehud escaped while they tarried'. The verbal deployment names the courtiers' delay (whether out of confusion or out of protocol-respect for the king's chambers) that gives Ehud time to escape. // **2 Sam 15:28** — David fleeing from Avshalom, to the priests Tzadoq and Aviatar: *re'u anokhi mitmahmehah ba'avot ha-midbar ad bo davar me'immakhem le-haggid li* — 'see, I will tarry at the fords of the wilderness, until there come word from you to inform me'. The verbal deployment names David's planned tactical-delay at the wilderness-fords. // **Isa 29:9** — the prophetic indictment: *hitmahmehu u-temahu* — 'tarry ye and wonder' (or *hithmemehu u-temahu*; the verbal-form vocalization is debated; some manuscripts read a different root). The Isa 29:9 deployment is the prophets' invitation-or-indictment to the people to engage in their characteristic spiritual-delay. // **Hab 2:3** — the FAMOUS eschatological deployment: *ki od chazon la-mo'ed ve-yafe'ach la-qetz ve-lo yekhazev; im yitmahmah chakeh lo ki vo yavo lo ye'achar* — 'for the vision is yet for an appointed time, and it hasteneth toward the end, and shall not lie; though it tarry, wait for it, because it will surely come, it will not delay'. The Hab 2:3 *im yitmahmah chakeh lo* is the corpus's most-cited eschatological-patience formula — the prophetic instruction to wait-for-the-tarrying-vision. The verse is heavily-cited in the post-biblical Jewish messianic tradition (Maimonides' thirteen principles of faith echo it) and in early Christianity (Heb 10:37 cites it). The lexeme's reach into the prophetic-eschatological tradition is concentrated at this verse. // **Ps 119:60** — *chashti ve-lo hitmahmahti li-shmor mitzvotekha* — 'I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments'. The Psalter deployment names the worshipper's hastening-without-delay in obedience. // **The cross-corpus distribution is therefore moderate but pointed**: a single Pentateuchal occurrence (Gen 19:16 + Gen 43:10), two historical-narrative occurrences (Judg 3:26, 2 Sam 15:28), two prophetic occurrences (Isa 29:9, Hab 2:3 with the eschatological-patience formula), and one wisdom-psalmic occurrence (Ps 119:60). // **The Hithpalpel stem.** The reduplicated Hithpalpel is a relatively rare Hebrew stem-pattern, attested for a small number of roots with internal-iterative or intensive-reflexive force. The *m-h-m-h* reduplication of *m-h-h* names the back-and-forth, hesitating, repeatedly-delaying quality of the tarrying — not a single act of delay but the ongoing-state-of-being-in-delay. The morphological force is therefore precise: *hitmahmah* names the lingering-as-state, the hesitating-as-condition. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach into Pentateuch (Gen 19, 43), historical narratives (Judges, Samuel), prophets (Isaiah, Habakkuk), and psalms (Ps 119) — moderate distribution but limited scope; the chapter-specific Gen 43:10 deployment in the counterfactual-condition is what is documented; the Hab 2:3 eschatological reach noted as a promotion-path-seed. → **OVERLAY** (the lexeme's cross-corpus reach is moderate; central housing is plausible but the editorial point is the chapter-specific deployment with the cross-corpus distribution documented). // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the morphological Hithpalpel is grammatically explicit, but (b) the rendering between 'tarry' (older), 'linger' (ASV), and 'dawdle' (NJPS) is an interpretive choice between attested registers; (c) the eschatological Hab 2:3 cross-corpus parallel is interpretive (the Gen 43:10 mercantile-tarrying does not directly invoke the eschatological-patience register, but the lexical connection is documented). Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *mahmah*; BDB p. 554; TDOT VIII:1-5; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 298; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 121; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 544; on the Hab 2:3 eschatological deployment: J. J. M. Roberts *Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah* OTL 1991 pp. 110-112; on the Hithpalpel stem: J. Joüon and T. Muraoka *A Grammar of Biblical Hebrew* §59h.

terms.translit: mi-zimrat ha-aretz ('of the choice produce / praise-fruits of the land', Gen 43:11)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, feminine singular in construct (from zamar II 'to be choice / strong / praiseworthy', distinct from zamar I 'to sing / make music')
terms.literal: zimrah — choice-produce / pick-of-the-land / praise-worthy fruit; the lexically-distinct zimrah II (from zamar II), separate from the homophonous zimrah I (musical 'song / praise')
terms.standardEnglish: the best fruits in the land (KJV); the choice fruits of the land (ASV); the choice products of the land (NJPS); the bounty of the land (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: of the choice fruits of the land (ASV-baseline; the zimrah I / zimrah II homophonous-lexemes distinction documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **The construct phrase *mi-zimrat ha-aretz* in Gen 43:11 deploys the noun *zimrah* in a 'choice produce' sense that is effectively chapter-singular in this register. The lexeme's analysis is complicated by the existence of a homophonous lemma *zimrah* I ('song / music / praise' from *zamar* I 'to sing'), which is distinct from *zimrah* II ('choice produce / strength / praise-worthy thing' from *zamar* II, a separate root). HALOT registers the two as distinct lexemes; the Gen 43:11 deployment belongs to *zimrah* II.** // **The lexeme.** *Zimrah* II derives from the root *zamar* II — a separate root from the more common *zamar* I ('to sing, make music, praise with song'). The *zamar* II root carries the semantic core of 'to be choice / strong / praiseworthy'; the cognate noun *zimrah* II names that which is choice-or-praiseworthy. The homophonous *zimrah* I ('song / melody / praise' as musical-act) is etymologically unrelated. The two lemmas share the same triconsonantal form and are difficult to distinguish without context. // **The 'choice produce' sense at Gen 43:11.** Ya'aqov instructs his sons to take 'of the *zimrat ha-aretz*' (literally 'of the choice-produce-of-the-land') as the *minchah* for the disguised Yosef. The semantic context unambiguously requires the 'choice produce' sense: the items listed in the verse (balm, honey, spicery, myrrh, pistachios, almonds) are physical-luxury-produce, not songs. The lexeme is therefore the 'choice produce' / 'best of the land' sense. ASV/NJPS/Alter agree on the produce-reading. // **The Exod 15:2 ozzi ve-zimrat Yah debate.** The most-cited HB occurrence of *zimrah* / *zimrat* is at Exod 15:2 (the Song of the Sea: *ozzi ve-zimrat Yah va-yhi li li-shu'ah* — traditionally 'YHWH is my strength and song'). The Exod 15:2 *zimrat* is contested between two readings: (a) *zimrah* I — 'song / praise' (the traditional reading; YHWH as my-song); (b) *zimrah* II — 'strength / might' (some modern critical readings; YHWH as my-strength, doubling the parallel with *ozzi*). The Exod 15:2 occurrence is NOT the Gen 43:11 produce-sense; the two are different lexical-deployments. The Gen 43:11 produce-sense is essentially confined to this verse (with a possible cognate at 2 Sam 23:1 *u-ne'im zemirot Yisrael*, contested as 'pleasant in the songs of Israel' or 'pleasant in the strength of Israel'). The lexical-rarity of the produce-sense is what makes the Gen 43:11 deployment near-hapax. // **The translation choice.** The ASV-baseline 'choice fruits of the land' preserves the produce-reading and is the consensus modern rendering. The KJV's 'best fruits' is functionally equivalent; NJPS 'choice products' modernizes; Alter's 'bounty' loses the lexical specificity. The WoH translation retains ASV. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-near-hapax in the 'choice produce' sense; the Exod 15:2 contested-homophone is governed elsewhere when Exodus is translated. → **OVERLAY** (the chapter-specific produce-sense lexeme; no cross-corpus reach in the produce-register). // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the produce-sense at Gen 43:11 is grammatically explicit from context, but (b) the *zimrah* I / II distinction is interpretive (the lemma-analysis between the homophonous lexemes is a scholarly inference), and (c) the rendering between 'choice fruits' (ASV) and 'bounty' (Alter) is a choice between attested registers. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *zimrah* I and *zimrah* II (the distinct lemma-analysis); BDB pp. 275-276; TDOT IV:91-98; NIDOTTE 1:1116-1118; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 298; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 122; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 544; on the Exod 15:2 *zimrat Yah* contested-homophone: B. S. Childs *Exodus* OTL 1974 pp. 240-244; W. H. C. Propp *Exodus 1-18* AB 1999 pp. 511-513.

terms.translit: kesef mishneh ('double money / second-money', Gen 43:12, 15); mishgeh ('oversight / inadvertence', Gen 43:12, chapter-singular noun)
terms.strongs: H4932 (mishneh, 'double / second / repetition'); H4870 (mishgeh, 'inadvertent error', chapter-singular noun from shagah 'to err inadvertently')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular (mishneh in attributive-construct 'double money'); noun, masculine singular (mishgeh, from the root sh-g-h, 'to err inadvertently')
terms.literal: kesef mishneh — money-of-doubling / second-money / double-portion of silver; mishgeh — an inadvertent error / oversight / unwitting fault
terms.standardEnglish: double money (ASV/KJV); a double sum of money (NJPS); double the silver (Alter); peradventure it was an oversight (ASV)
terms.wohChoice: double money (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:12, 15); peradventure it was an oversight (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:12; the chapter-singular mishgeh and the commercial-mishneh sense documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:12 deploys two distinct lexical items in Ya'aqov's instructions about the silver: *kesef mishneh* ('double money', the doubling of the silver for the second journey; recurs at v 15) and *mishgeh* ('an oversight / inadvertence', the chapter-singular noun naming the possible explanation for the silver's return in the brothers' sacks).** // **(i) Kesef mishneh — double money.** The noun *mishneh* (מִשְׁנֶה) spans the corpus in two distinct registers: (a) the simple-doubling / numerical sense — 'double / twofold / second-amount-equal-to-the-first'; (b) the ordinal / office-title sense — 'second [in rank], deputy, vice-regent, substitute'. The Gen 43:12, 15 occurrences belong to register (a): the brothers take *double* the original silver, both to cover the silver mysteriously returned in their sacks AND to fund the second purchase. The doubling-sense recurs at: Gen 41:43 (the office-title *mirkevet ha-mishneh*, governed by the sibling overlay [`mirkevet-ha-mishneh-chariot-of-the-second-gen41`](#mirkevet-ha-mishneh-chariot-of-the-second-gen41) — distinct from the Gen 43 commercial sense); Exod 16:5, 22 (the double-portion of manna for the Sabbath — *lechem mishneh*, the commercial-doubling-as-cultic-provision register); Deut 15:18 (the double-wages-of-a-hired-servant); Deut 17:18 (the king's *mishneh ha-torah ha-zot* — 'a copy of this torah', the ordinal-as-copy register); 1 Sam 8:2 (Shemu'el's second-born son's name); 1 Sam 17:13; 23:17 (David and Yehonatan: *ata timlokh al Yisrael ve-anokhi ehyeh lekha le-mishneh*, 'and I shall be next to thee', the deputy-sense); 2 Kgs 22:14 = 2 Chr 34:22 (Hulda's *mishneh* / second-quarter location); 1 Chr 5:12; 15:18; Jer 17:18 (the prophetic double-destruction: *shivron mishneh shavrem*); Zech 9:12 (*mishneh ashiv lakh*). The lexeme's two registers (doubling vs ordinal/office-title) are differentiated by context; the Gen 43 commercial-doubling deployment is the corpus's first commercial-doubling occurrence. // **(ii) Mishgeh — oversight.** The noun *mishgeh* (מִשְׁגֶּה) is chapter-singular in the HB — it appears only at Gen 43:12. The verbal root *shagah* / *shagag* ('to err inadvertently, to go astray without intention') is the standard Levitical lexeme for inadvertent-sin (the *shogeg* who errs without intention is the subject of the inadvertent-sin sacrificial-rules at Lev 4:2, 13, 22, 27; 5:15, 18; Num 15:22-29). The cognate noun *shegagah* ('inadvertence', the standard Levitical noun) is well-attested in the HB; the *mishgeh* noun-form at Gen 43:12 is morphologically distinct (a different formation from the same root) and is here used in a non-cultic commercial register: Ya'aqov suggests the silver's return may be a *mishgeh* — an inadvertent error / oversight on the part of the Mitsrayim official who handled the transaction. The shift from the cultic-Levitical *shegagah* (inadvertent-sin) to the commercial *mishgeh* (commercial-oversight) is a lexical-register transfer; the same lexical-conceptual frame (unintentional error) is applied across two domains. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-Pentateuchal reach for *mishneh* (Gen, Exod, Lev/Deut, Sam/Kings) but the chapter-specific commercial-doubling deployment at Gen 43:12, 15 is what is documented; the cross-reference to the sibling overlay [`mirkevet-ha-mishneh-chariot-of-the-second-gen41`](#mirkevet-ha-mishneh-chariot-of-the-second-gen41) (which governs the Gen 41 office-title sense) bidirectionally distinguishes the two registers. The chapter-singular *mishgeh* is by definition overlay-housed. → **OVERLAY** for both. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the morphological items are explicit, but (b) the *mishneh* commercial-doubling vs ordinal/office-title distinction is interpretive (the lexeme spans both registers; the chapter-specific deployment is one of two attested senses), and (c) the *mishgeh* / *shegagah* morphological-distinction-but-same-root analysis is interpretive. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *mishneh*, *mishgeh*, *shagah*; BDB pp. 1041-1042 (mishneh), 993 (mishgeh), 993 (shagah); TDOT XIV:307-313; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 298; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 122; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 544; on the Levitical inadvertent-sin code: J. Milgrom *Leviticus 1-16* AB 1991 pp. 226-292.

terms.translit: asher al beito ('him who [is] over his house', Gen 43:16, 19; cf. 44:1, 4)
terms.strongs: H834 (asher, relative particle) + H5921 (al, 'over') + H1004 (bayit, 'house') + 3ms suffix
terms.partOfSpeech: relative-construct idiom: relative particle + preposition + noun-with-suffix; the standard office-title for the chief-of-household / steward / household-administrator
terms.literal: asher al beito — 'he who [is] over his house' — the technical-administrative office-title for the chief steward / household-manager
terms.standardEnglish: the steward of his house (ASV/NJPS); the one who was over his house (literal-functional); the steward (Alter); the chief of his house (some moderns)
terms.wohChoice: the steward of his house (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:16, 19; the cross-corpus royal-administration office-title distribution documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **The idiom *asher al ha-bayit* (or with possessive suffix, *asher al beito*) is the technical office-title for the chief steward / household-administrator across the HB. Gen 43:16, 19 introduces Yosef's chief steward in this technical register; the title recurs at Gen 44:1, 4 (the same official, in the cup-test scene). The idiom is not generic ('someone in his house') but technical (the chief-administrator of the household / palace).** // **The lexeme.** The construction *asher al + (the named entity)* is a standard Hebrew office-naming pattern: 'he-who-[is]-over-the-X' names the X-administrator, the chief-functionary responsible for the X. The *asher al ha-bayit* / *asher al beito* form names the household-administrator; the parallel *asher al ha-tabbachim* (the captain-of-the-guard) and *asher al ha-mashqim* / *ha-ofim* (the chief cupbearer / baker) parallel-constructions name analogous Egyptian-court offices. The lexeme is administrative-technical: it specifies an institutional role, not a casual functional description. // **The Yosef-cycle distribution.** The Gen 43-44 stewardship-scenes deploy the title repeatedly: **Gen 43:16** ('to him that was over his house' — the chief steward receiving Yosef's instructions about the noon-feast); **Gen 43:19** ('they came near to the steward of Yosef's house' — the brothers approaching at the door); **Gen 44:1** ('he commanded him that was over his house, saying' — the cup-test instruction); **Gen 44:4** ('Yosef said unto his steward' — the cup-test execution). The four-occurrence cycle-internal distribution names a specific named-character-by-office: Yosef's chief steward, a recurring figure in the cycle. The earlier Gen 39:4 *va-yifqideihu al beito* — Yosef himself appointed by Potifar 'over his house' — uses a verbal construction with the same al-beito phrase, marking Yosef's own ascent through the household-administration office before his elevation to the *shallit*. The Yosef-cycle's structural irony is that Yosef, who once was the *asher al beito* of Potifar, now has his own *asher al beito*. // **The cross-corpus royal-administration distribution.** The office-title extends across the HB into the royal-administration vocabulary as the chief-minister title under the Davidic-Solomonic and northern kingdoms: **1 Kgs 4:6** (Solomon's officers: *Achisar al ha-bayit*); **1 Kgs 16:9** (Zimri's coup: *Artza asher al ha-bayit*); **1 Kgs 18:3** (Achav's *Obadyah asher al ha-bayit*); **2 Kgs 10:5** (Achav's household-administrator surrendering Shomron); **2 Kgs 15:5** (Yotam *asher al ha-bayit*); **2 Kgs 18:18, 37; 19:2 = Isa 36:3, 22; 37:2** (the famous Elyaqim son of Chilqiyahu *asher al ha-bayit*, against Sancheriv); **Isa 22:15-25** (the prophetic indictment of Shevna *asher al ha-bayit* and the promise of his replacement by Elyaqim — the corpus's most concentrated single-passage treatment of the office, with the key-of-the-house-of-David imagery). The royal-administration deployments name the highest-ranking court official, second only to the king himself; the office carries the keys-of-the-house authority (Isa 22:22's key-of-the-house-of-David image). // **The Egyptian comparative context.** The Egyptian institutional parallel is the *jmj-r3 pr* ('overseer of the house') office attested across the Egyptian administrative corpus; the title was applied to Egyptian household-administrators of all ranks (private estates, royal palace, etc.). The Gen 43 deployment matches the Egyptian institutional context exactly: Yosef's household has an *asher al beito* — an Egyptian-style household-overseer — managing the daily-affairs of his Egyptian estate. The historical-ethnographic plausibility of the Gen 43-44 stewardship-scenes is well-documented in the Egyptological literature (Vergote, Redford). // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus royal-administration reach into the Kings and Isaiah corpus is genuine and substantial; the editorial point at Gen 43:16-19 is the chapter-specific Egyptian-household-context deployment; the Kings / Isaiah / Isa 22:15-25 cross-corpus reach noted as a promotion-path-seed (when those texts are translated, central promotion could be reconsidered for the royal-administration deployment). → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the office-title function is established across the standard lexica; (c) the cross-corpus royal-administration distribution is verifiable; (d) the Egyptian institutional parallel is documented; (e) the chapter-internal recurrence is grammatically explicit. N. D. Mettinger *Solomonic State Officials* CB OT 5, 1971 pp. 70-110; J. Begrich 'Sōfēr und Mazkīr' ZAW 58 (1940-41) 1-29; on the Isa 22:15-25 prophetic-treatment: H. Wildberger *Isaiah 13-27* CC, 1997 pp. 365-394; on the Egyptian *jmj-r3 pr* institutional parallel: P. Vergote *Joseph en Égypte* 1959 pp. 24-26; D. B. Redford *A Study of the Biblical Story of Joseph* VTSup 20, 1970.

terms.translit: le-hitgolel ... u-le-hitnafel (the Hithpael-infinitives, Gen 43:18, the brothers' fear-construction)
terms.strongs: H1556 (galal, Hithpael 'roll oneself / fall upon'); H5307 (naphal, Hithpael 'fall oneself / fall upon')
terms.partOfSpeech: two Hithpael infinitives in series; chapter-singular violence-and-pretext construction
terms.literal: le-hitgolel ... u-le-hitnafel — 'to roll [himself] upon us and to fall [himself] upon us' — the Hithpael of galal (rolling oneself / seeking-pretext) paired with the Hithpael of naphal (falling oneself / aggressive-assault) in the corpus's chapter-singular violence-idiom
terms.standardEnglish: that he may seek occasion against us, and fall upon us (ASV/KJV); so that he may seize us as slaves (NJPS — paraphrastic); to throw himself upon us, to fall upon us (Alter — literal)
terms.wohChoice: that he may seek occasion against us, and fall upon us (ASV-baseline; the chapter-singular Hithpael-of-galal + Hithpael-of-naphal violence-pair documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:18 records the brothers' fear-construction as they are brought into Yosef's house: they suppose they are being brought in *al devar ha-kesef ha-shav be-amtechoteinu ba-techillah* ('because of the money that was returned in our sacks at the first time') — *le-hitgolel aleinu u-le-hitnafel aleinu ve-laqachat otanu la-avadim ve-et chamoreinu* — 'to roll [himself] upon us and to fall [himself] upon us and to take us for bondmen, and our asses'. The two Hithpaels in series (Hithpael of *galal* 'roll' + Hithpael of *naphal* 'fall') compose a chapter-singular violence-and-pretext idiom-pair.** // **The lexemes.** (i) **Hithpael of galal** — *hitgolel* — names a 'rolling oneself against' or 'rolling oneself upon' someone, in the aggressive-pretext register. The cognate root *galal* in the Qal names physical-rolling (of stones, of bodies); the Hithpael-reflexive shifts to the metaphorical-aggressive deployment ('roll oneself upon someone' as in physical-or-legal aggression). Cross-corpus the Hithpael is rare in this aggressive sense: 2 Sam 20:12 has *mitgolel ba-dam* of Amasa's body rolling in his blood (a different context); the specifically-aggressive 'seek pretext' sense at Gen 43:18 is essentially chapter-singular. (ii) **Hithpael of naphal** — *hitnafel* — names a 'falling oneself' or 'casting oneself down', with two distinct semantic ranges: (a) the supplicatory-prostration register (Deut 9:18, 25 of Mosheh's intercessory prostration before YHWH; Ezra 10:1 of Ezra prostrating in supplication); (b) the aggressive 'fall upon (as attacker)' register, which is rare in the Hithpael and pointed to here at Gen 43:18. The Hithpael's two registers are differentiated by context; the Gen 43:18 deployment is aggressive. // **The chapter-singular violence-pair.** The two Hithpaels in series — both with the preposition *aleinu* ('upon us') — compose a stylistically-marked violence-idiom. The construction's rarity is precise: the two Hithpaels are individually rare in the aggressive-sense; their paired-series at Gen 43:18 is chapter-singular in the HB. The literary-rhetorical force of the pair is the brothers' compounded-fear: the first Hithpael names the 'rolling-of-pretext' (legal-or-rhetorical accusation), the second names the 'falling-upon' (physical-violent assault). The fear-construction therefore covers both the legal-and-physical violence-threat the brothers anticipate. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV 'that he may seek occasion against us, and fall upon us' captures the legal-pretext + physical-assault force with the conventional English 'seek occasion' for *hitgolel* (a functional gloss). NJPS 'so that he may seize us as slaves' paraphrastically collapses the construction into a single seizure-action, losing the lexical pair. Alter 'to throw himself upon us, to fall upon us' preserves the literal force but at the cost of redundancy in English (the two infinitives are functionally near-synonymous in Alter's rendering). The WoH preserves the ASV-baseline force-and-clarity. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular construction; the two Hithpaels in series do not recur elsewhere; cross-corpus reach for each lexeme is limited (the 2 Sam 20:12 *hitgolel* and the Deut 9:18, 25 / Ezra 10:1 *hitnafel* deployments are different registers). → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the morphological Hithpael pair is grammatically explicit, but (b) the precise semantic registers ('roll-as-pretext' for *hitgolel*; 'fall-upon-as-assault' for *hitnafel*) are interpretive (the lexemes' specifically-aggressive sense at Gen 43:18 is not paralleled elsewhere in the same register), and (c) the rendering between ASV's 'seek occasion' and Alter's literal 'throw himself upon' is a choice between attested approaches. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *galal* (Hithpael), *naphal* (Hithpael); BDB pp. 164-165, 656-658; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 299; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 122; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 545.

terms.translit: matmon ('treasure / hidden store', Gen 43:23; from taman 'to bury / hide')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular (from taman 'to hide / bury')
terms.literal: matmon — that-which-is-buried / hidden-store / cache; the standard noun for buried treasure
terms.standardEnglish: treasure (ASV/KJV); a treasure (NJPS); treasure (Alter); buried treasure (some literal)
terms.wohChoice: treasure (ASV-baseline; the buried-and-hidden-store sense and the cross-corpus Isa 45:3 / Jer 41:8 / Job 3:21 / Prov 2:4 distribution documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **The noun *matmon* (מַטְמוֹן) is the corpus's standard 'buried treasure' lexeme, formed from the verbal root *taman* ('to bury, to hide, to conceal') with the *ma-* prefix denoting place or means. The Gen 43:23 occurrence — the steward's reassuring explanation that *Elohekhem ve-Elohei avikhem natan lakhem matmon be-amtechoteikhem* ('your Elohim, and the Elohim of your father, hath given you treasure in your sacks') — is the corpus's first attestation.** // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The lexeme recurs at: **Gen 43:23** (here); **Isa 45:3** — the famous Cyrus-prophecy: *ve-natati lekha otzrot choshekh u-matmonei mistarim, lema'an teda ki ani YHWH ha-qore be-shimkha Elohei Yisrael* — 'and I will give thee the treasures of darkness, and hidden riches of secret places, that thou mayest know that I am YHWH, who calleth thee by thy name, the God of Israel'. The Isaian deployment is the lexeme's most-cited prophetic occurrence and names the hidden-divine-treasure given to the Persian conqueror as a recognition-of-divine-providence. The lexical-resonance with Gen 43:23 (the *matmon* given-by-Elohim) is striking. **Jer 41:8** — the *matmonim* hidden in the field: ten men from among the captives at Mizpah plead *al temitenu ki yesh-lanu matmonim ba-sadeh chittim u-se'orim ve-shemen u-devash* ('do not kill us, for we have *matmonim* in the field — wheat, barley, oil, and honey'). The Jeremianic occurrence is the post-destruction concealed-food-supply context. **Job 3:21** — Iyov's lament: *ke-tomenim li-matmonim* ('who dig for *matmonim* more than for hid treasures'). **Prov 2:4** — the wisdom-instruction to seek wisdom *ke-khesef u-kha-matmonim techappesennah* ('as silver, and search for her as for hid treasures'). // **The Gen 43:23 deployment.** The steward's reassurance reframes the silver's mysterious return as a *matmon* — a divine-given treasure, not a Mitsrayim-court accounting-mistake. The lexical choice is theologically loaded: the steward attributes the returned silver to *Elohekhem* (the brothers' deity) rather than to any accounting-explanation or Yosef's secret-instruction. Whether the steward is a Yosef-informed character (the rabbinic-reading) or simply diplomatic, the lexical-choice frames the silver as divine-provision. The construction echoes the broader Yosef-cycle's divine-providence theme (Gen 45:7-8, 50:20). // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach into Isaiah, Jeremiah, Job, Proverbs — moderate but limited; the lexeme's most-cited deployment is the Isa 45:3 Cyrus-prophecy, which a future Isaiah translation may make a cross-corpus node. → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-path noted at the Isa 45:3 cross-corpus parallel. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit (the standard *m-* + *taman* formation); (b) the buried-treasure sense is well-established across the standard lexica; (c) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable; (d) the ASV-baseline 'treasure' is the direct rendering. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *matmon*, *taman*; BDB p. 380 (matmon), 380 (taman); TDOT V:367-369; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 299; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 123; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 545; on the Isa 45:3 Cyrus-prophecy and the hidden-treasure motif: J. Blenkinsopp *Isaiah 40-55* AB 2000 pp. 247-253.

terms.translit: va-yitmehu ha-anashim ish el re'ehu (Gen 43:33; Qal imperfect 3mp of tamah, 'to marvel / be astonished')
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Qal (intransitive 'be astonished / marvel'); the chapter-singular impossible-knowledge-recognition scene
terms.literal: va-yitmehu ha-anashim ish el re'ehu — 'and the men marvelled, each unto his fellow' — the brothers' marvel at Yosef's impossible-knowledge seating-by-birthright
terms.standardEnglish: the men marvelled one with another (ASV/KJV); the men looked at one another in astonishment (NJPS); the men were astonished, every man to his fellow (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: the men marvelled one with another (ASV-baseline; the impossible-knowledge seating-by-birthright literary observation and the structural foreshadowing of the Gen 45 disclosure documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:33 stages one of the corpus's most striking impossible-knowledge moments: Yosef seats the brothers *ha-bekhor ki-vkhorato ve-ha-tza'ir ki-tze'irato* — 'the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth' — accurately ranking eleven brothers in birth-order, an act that is impossible knowledge for the disguised Egyptian official. The brothers respond by marveling (Qal *va-yitmehu*) one to another. The verse is mainstream-noted (Sarna, Alter, Sternberg, Fokkelman) as a deliberate identity-hint placed on the surface for the attentive reader — a structural foreshadowing of the Gen 45 disclosure-scene.** // **The lexeme.** *Tamah* (תָּמַהּ) is the corpus's standard 'be astonished / marvel / wonder' verb. The Qal-active is the basic stem; the cognate noun *timhon* ('astonishment') and the cognate adjective *tamuah* are related. The lexeme covers the cognitive-affective response of astonishment at something exceeding-expectation, often with a numinous or unsettling overtone. The semantic core is the 'response-to-the-extraordinary': the *tamah* names the cognitive-affective registration of something-impossible / something-exceeding-the-natural-order. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The verb recurs at: **Gen 43:33** (here); **Isa 13:8** (the prophetic Day-of-YHWH astonishment: *u-tamehu, panim lahavim peneihem* — 'and they shall be astonished one at another; their faces shall be as faces of flame'); **Isa 29:9** (*hitmahmehu u-temahu* — 'tarry ye and wonder', with the *tamah* paired with *hitmahmah*, governed by the sibling overlay entry [`hitmahmah-tarry-delay-hithpalpel-gen43`](#hitmahmah-tarry-delay-hithpalpel-gen43)); **Jer 4:9** (the Day-of-YHWH terror: *yashomu ha-kohanim ve-ha-nevi'im yitmahu* — 'the priests shall be astonished'); **Hab 1:5** (the famous: *re'u va-goyim ve-habbitu ve-hitamhu temahu, ki fo'al po'el bimeikhem lo ta'aminu ki yesappar* — 'behold ye among the nations, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I am working a work in your days which ye will not believe, though it be told you'; cited at Acts 13:41 in the NT); **Ps 48:6 [MT 48:5]** (the kings of the earth astonished at Zion: *hemmah ra'u ken tamahu, nivhalu nechpazu*); **Job 26:11** (Iyov's response to YHWH: *amudei shamayim yerofefu ve-yitmehu mi-ga'arato* — 'the pillars of heaven tremble and are astonished at his rebuke'); **Eccl 5:7 [MT 5:8]** (the wisdom-text's response to oppression). The lexeme's cross-corpus reach is moderate; its concentrated prophetic-Day-of-YHWH deployment (Isa, Jer, Hab) gives it an eschatological-numinous resonance. // **The Gen 43:33 deployment.** The brothers' marveling-at-the-seating is the narrative's structural identity-hint. Yosef has just seated them with miraculously-accurate knowledge of their birth-order (an act that would require knowing all eleven brothers personally and their relative ages — knowledge no Egyptian official could have). The brothers' marveling-one-to-another is the natural cognitive-affective response; the reader, who knows Yosef's identity, reads the marveling as the brothers' coming-into-proximity-with-the-truth without yet recognizing it. The literary device is widely cited (Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 247-248; Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 ch. 8; Fokkelman 1975). The Gen 45 disclosure-scene resolves what Gen 43:33 has foreshadowed: the brothers' marveling-at-impossible-knowledge will be answered by Yosef's *ani Yosef* self-disclosure. // **Overlay housing.** Cross-corpus reach (Isa, Jer, Hab, Ps, Job, Eccl) is moderate; the editorial point at Gen 43:33 is the chapter-specific literary-observation (the impossible-knowledge seating-and-marveling as identity-hint), not the general lexeme. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the verb is morphologically explicit, but (b) the recorded editorial substance is the literary-foreshadowing observation (the marveling as identity-hint), which is an interpretive reading widely noted but not grammatically required by the construction; (c) the rendering between 'marvelled' (ASV) and 'astonished' (NJPS / Alter) is a choice between attested registers. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *tamah*; BDB p. 1069; TDOT XV:649-654; NIDOTTE 4:309-310; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 125-126; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 547-548; on the literary-foreshadowing reading of Gen 43:33: R. Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 247-248; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 ch. 8; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on the Hab 1:5 prophetic-deployment: J. J. M. Roberts *Nahum, Habakkuk, and Zephaniah* OTL 1991.

terms.translit: mas'ot (Gen 43:34, the stately court-meal portion-lexeme from nasa 'to lift up'; cf. mas'at 'portion')
terms.strongs: H4864 (mas'eit, from nasa, 'to lift up'; the cognate noun for 'portion / lifted-up-thing')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun, feminine plural in construct (from the verbal root nasa, 'to lift up, to carry'); names the 'lifted-up-portion' of a feast
terms.literal: mas'ot — lifted-up-portions / things-borne-from-the-host's-table; the stately court-meal lexeme for portions sent from the host's place to the guests
terms.standardEnglish: messes (KJV/ASV — archaic); portions (NJPS / Alter / modern); servings (some moderns)
terms.wohChoice: messes (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:34; the stately court-meal portion-idiom and the broader cross-corpus mas'at-sense documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:34 describes Yosef's stately court-meal hospitality: *va-yissa mas'ot me-et panav aleihem* — 'and he took up portions from before his face [and sent them] unto them'. The noun *mas'ot* (the feminine-plural construct of *mas'eit*) is the stately court-meal lexeme for the portions lifted-up from the host's place at the head of the table and conveyed to the seated guests. The construction 'lift up X from before his face to them' is a court-ceremonial idiom marking the formal-hospitality protocol.** // **The lexeme.** *Mas'eit* (מַשְׂאֵת) derives from the verbal root *nasa* ('to lift up, to carry, to bear'). The *ma-* prefix forms a noun-of-result or noun-of-thing: *mas'eit* = 'that-which-is-lifted-up / that-which-is-borne'. The broader semantic range covers: (a) the stately court-meal portion (Gen 43:34, the present occurrence; 2 Sam 11:8 of David's *mas'at* to Uriyah; Esth 2:18 of Achashverosh's *mas'at* at the royal-feast for Esther); (b) the burnt-offering smoke ('lifted up' from the altar; Judg 20:38, 40 the *mas'eit* of smoke as a battle-signal); (c) the gift / tribute / portion (Jer 38:14; 40:5; Amos 5:11); (d) the lifted-up-hands of prayer (Ps 141:2 *minchat areb mas'at kappai*); (e) the lifting-up of the soul / heart (Lam 3:41); (f) the burden / charge (the responsibility-as-a-thing-borne). The Gen 43:34 deployment belongs to (a): the stately court-meal portion. // **The court-meal context.** The 2 Sam 11:8 parallel is the closest lexical match: David sends Uriyah from the palace to his own house with a *mas'at* — a stately portion from the royal table, intended to honor and disarm. The Esther 2:18 parallel is similar: Achashverosh distributes *mas'at* at the great banquet honoring Esther's elevation. The three deployments (Gen 43:34, 2 Sam 11:8, Esth 2:18) cluster as the stately-court-meal portion-idiom across three royal-court contexts (the Yosef Egyptian-palace; the Davidic monarchy; the Persian royal-court). // **The Gen 43:34 deployment.** Yosef sends portions to his brothers from the host's place at the head of the table; the gesture is the stately-hospitality marker. The narrative-immediately-following observation that Binyamin's portion is *chamesh yadot* (five-fold, governed by the sibling overlay [`chamesh-yadot-fivefold-portion-gen43`](#chamesh-yadot-fivefold-portion-gen43)) marks the differential-favor that the host is publicly displaying — the reader who knows Yosef's identity reads this as Yosef-favoring-the-Rachel-line-brother; the brothers (who do not know) register it as a foreign-court's mysterious-favor. // **The ASV-baseline 'messes'.** The KJV/ASV rendering 'messes' preserves the archaic English court-meal lexeme but is opaque to modern readers ('mess' as a court-portion is obsolete English). NJPS 'portions' and Alter 'portions' modernize. The WoH retains the ASV-baseline for register-consistency; the modernization 'portions' is noted as the natural-modern reading. // **Overlay housing.** The broader *mas'eit* lexeme has cross-corpus reach across the senses listed above; the editorial point at Gen 43:34 is the chapter-specific stately court-meal portion-idiom, with the 2 Sam 11:8 and Esth 2:18 cross-corpus parallels noted. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the lexeme is morphologically explicit, but (b) the specific 'court-meal-portion' sense at Gen 43:34 is one of several attested senses for *mas'eit*, and (c) the rendering between 'messes' (ASV-archaic) and 'portions' (modern) is between attested approaches. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *mas'eit*, *nasa*; BDB p. 673; TDOT X:24-40 (nasa); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 126; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 548; on the 2 Sam 11:8 parallel: P. K. McCarter *II Samuel* AB 1984 pp. 285-286; on the Esth 2:18 parallel: J. D. Levenson *Esther* OTL 1997.

terms.translit: chamesh yadot ('five hands / five portions / fivefold', Gen 43:34)
terms.strongs: H2568 (chamesh, 'five') + H3027 (yad, in the 'portion / share / part' sense)
terms.partOfSpeech: numeral-noun construction: cardinal-number + plural noun in the 'portion / share' sense (the corpus's first 'X yadot' fractional/multiplier construction)
terms.literal: chamesh yadot — five-hands / five-portions / five-shares — the multiplier construction naming a portion five-fold the size of the others
terms.standardEnglish: five times so much as any of theirs (ASV/KJV); five times as much as that of any of the others (NJPS); five times more than the portions of all the rest (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: five times so much as any of theirs (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:34; the chamesh-yadot multiplier construction and the distinct chimmesh fifth-part-fraction lexeme at Gen 41:34 documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:34 records the differential-favor in Yosef's stately court-meal: Binyamin's *mas'at* (the stately court-portion, governed by the sibling overlay [`masot-court-feast-portions-gen43`](#masot-court-feast-portions-gen43)) is *chamesh yadot* — 'five hands / five portions' — greater than that of any of the others. The construction *chamesh yadot* is the corpus's FIRST attested 'X yadot' fractional-multiplier construction; it uses the noun *yad* ('hand') in the specialized 'portion / share / part' sense, qualified by the cardinal-number to express the multiplier.** // **The lexeme *yad* in the 'portion' sense.** The noun *yad* (יָד, 'hand') has a specialized cross-corpus deployment as 'portion / share / part' in distributive-quantity constructions. The semantic transfer from anatomical-hand to 'portion' is metonymic: a 'hand' of grain or money is a unit-portion or a held-quantity. The cross-corpus attestations of the 'yadot' portion-construction are limited but pointed: **Gen 43:34** (here, the first attestation: *chamesh yadot* = five-portions); **2 Sam 19:43 [MT 19:44]** — the men of Israel argue with the men of Yehudah over David's restoration: *eser yadot li ba-melekh* ('I have ten portions / parts in the king'); **2 Kgs 11:7 = 2 Chr 23:8** — the *yadot* divisions of the Levitical guards (the priestly-administrative usage). The construction is the standard idiomatic 'X portions / X shares' form. // **Distinction from the Gen 41:34 chimmesh fifth-part-fraction.** The Gen 41:34 *chimmesh et eretz Mitzrayim* deploys the Piel of the verbal root *ch-m-sh* (the root from which 'five' derives) in a tax-or-administrative sense — 'take up the fifth-part' (ASV) or 'organize-in-fives / organize-in-divisions' (the administrative-reading; governed by sibling overlay [`chimmesh-fifth-part-or-fifth-division-gen41`](#chimmesh-fifth-part-or-fifth-division-gen41)). The Gen 41:34 *chimmesh* deploys the root in the FRACTION sense (one-fifth); the Gen 43:34 *chamesh yadot* deploys the cardinal 'five' in the MULTIPLIER sense (fivefold). The two are lexically distinct constructions sharing only the underlying numeric root. The distinction is important: the Gen 43:34 portion is not 'one-fifth' of someone's portion (which would be smaller) but 'five-times' someone's portion (which is larger). The reader who confuses the two constructions misreads the verse. // **The Gen 43:34 deployment.** The fivefold-portion to Binyamin is the public-honor marker that Yosef displays to the disguised brothers; the differential-favor is meant to be visible. The reader who knows Yosef's identity reads the gesture as Yosef-honoring-the-Rachel-line-brother (the only brother on the scene who shares Yosef's mother); the brothers may be tested by the differential-favor (will they resent Binyamin's favor as they once resented Yosef's *ketonet passim* favor?). The differential-favor's pedagogical function is widely noted (Sarna, Alter): Yosef tests whether the brothers' character has changed since they sold him over Ya'aqov's favoritism. The chapter ends with the brothers drinking and being merry with Yosef (*va-yishtu va-yishkeru immo*, governed by the sibling overlay [`yishkeru-merry-or-drunk-gen9-gen43`](#yishkeru-merry-or-drunk-gen9-gen43)) — apparently without resentment, but the cup-test of chapter 44 will be the definitive resolution. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular construction in the multiplier-sense; the 2 Sam 19:43 cross-corpus parallel governs the cross-corpus 'yadot' portion-construction when Samuel is translated. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the construction is grammatically explicit, but (b) the distinction between the multiplier (fivefold) and fraction (one-fifth) readings is interpretive (the numeric-root is shared with the Gen 41:34 *chimmesh* fraction-construction); (c) the literary-pedagogical reading of the differential-favor as test is interpretive. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *yad*, *chamesh*; BDB pp. 388-389 (yad), 332-333 (chamesh); TDOT V:393-426 (yad); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 126; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 548-549; on the Gen 41:34 / 43:34 numeric-root distinction: J. Skinner *Genesis* ICC 1910 p. 484; on the pedagogical-test reading: R. Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 248.

terms.translit: va-yishkeru ('and they drank / became drunk / were merry', Gen 43:34, Qal of shakhar)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Qal imperfect-with-vav-consecutive 3mp
terms.literal: shakhar — to be drunk / become drunk; the standard intoxication-verb of the HB
terms.standardEnglish: were merry (ASV/KJV — euphemistic); drank their fill (NJPS); got drunk (Alter — literal); were filled with drink (some moderns)
terms.wohChoice: were merry (ASV-baseline at Gen 43:34; the Gen 9:21 Noah-drunkenness echo and the rendering choice between 'merry' (euphemism) and 'became drunk' (literal) documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 43:34 closes the stewardship-feast scene with the brothers' response: *va-yishtu va-yishkeru immo* — 'and they drank, and were merry with him' (ASV) or 'they drank and became drunk with him' (literal). The verb *shakhar* (Qal *va-yishkeru*) is the standard 'become drunk' verb of the HB. The rendering choice between the euphemistic 'were merry' (ASV/KJV) and the literal 'became drunk' (NJPS/Alter) is a real interpretive decision; the deliberate lexical-echo of Gen 9:21 (Noah's *va-yishkar* — the corpus's first drunkenness, with negative outcome) is a literary observation worth flagging.** // **The lexeme.** *Shakhar* (שָׁכַר) is the corpus's standard intoxication-verb. The cognate noun *shekhar* (the 'strong drink' of the priestly drinking-prohibition Lev 10:9, etc.) names the intoxicating-beverage. The Qal-active means specifically 'to become drunk / be drunk'; the lexeme is NOT the casual-drinking lexeme (which would be *shatah*, the verb of generic drinking) but the intoxication-specific verb. The Gen 43:34 construction pairs *va-yishtu* (the casual-drinking verb, Qal of *shatah*) with *va-yishkeru* (the intoxication verb) — the sequence is 'they drank, and they got drunk'. The pairing makes the intoxication-reading lexically explicit. // **The Gen 9:21 echo.** The corpus's first drunkenness is at Gen 9:21: Noah after the flood plants a vineyard, drinks of the wine, *va-yishkar* ('and was drunk'), and uncovers himself within his tent — the scene leads to Cham's transgression and the cursing of Kena'an. The Gen 9:21 deployment is therefore the corpus's foundational drunkenness-scene, with overwhelmingly negative narrative consequences.
