The Gen 43:34 *va-yishkeru* is the next attestation of the verb-stem (the Lot-incestuous-drunkenness scene at Gen 19:32-35 uses different verbal constructions — the Hiphil *nashqenu* 'we made him drink' — though it deploys the *shakhar*-conceptual frame). The lexical-echo from Gen 9:21 to Gen 43:34 is striking: the Yosef-cycle's reunion-feast deploys the same intoxication-verb that the post-Flood scene deployed. // **The literary-interpretive question.** The brothers' drinking-to-merry / drinking-to-drunkenness with the disguised Yosef has been read in two registers: (a) **The benign reading** — the brothers' drinking-with-Yosef marks the reunion-festivity, the easing of the morning's terror, the surface-restoration of brotherly fellowship; the rendering 'were merry' (ASV) captures the celebratory tone; the drinking is appropriate to the stately court-meal. (b) **The darker reading** — the brothers' drunkenness (lexically explicit by the *yishkeru*-pairing) is a pre-test condition: the cup-test of chapter 44 will be more decisive in the morning-after. The drunkenness may also re-echo the Gen 9:21 → Gen 19:32-35 narrative-tradition of drunkenness-as-vulnerability (Noah uncovered; Lot's daughters' incest). The Gen 43:34 drunkenness may be the brothers' moment-of-letting-down-their-guard before the cup-test (Gen 44:1-13). The Alter rendering 'they got drunk with him' surfaces the darker reading. // **The rendering choice.** ASV/KJV 'were merry' (euphemistic) preserves the celebratory register without surfacing the intoxication-specificity. NJPS 'drank their fill' modernizes the euphemism. Alter 'they got drunk with him' is literal. The WoH retains the ASV-baseline 'were merry' for register-consistency; the literal-and-darker reading is documented in this entry. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular deployment in the Yosef-cycle; the Gen 9:21 cross-cycle anchor and the Gen 19:32-35 Lot-tradition documented as the literary cross-references; the broader *shakhar* lexeme is well-distributed across the corpus (the priestly Lev 10:9 prohibition; the prophetic indictments of drunkenness; the wisdom-warnings in Proverbs). → **OVERLAY** for the Gen 43:34 chapter-specific deployment with the Gen 9:21 literary-echo. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the verb is morphologically explicit, but (b) the rendering between 'were merry' (euphemism) and 'became drunk' (literal) is between attested approaches, and (c) the literary-echo to Gen 9:21 and the Lot-tradition is interpretive. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *shakhar*; BDB p. 1016; TDOT XIV:701-707; NIDOTTE 4:107-108; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 301; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 126; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 549; on the Gen 9:21 Noah-drunkenness as the corpus's foundational drunkenness-scene: D. M. Carr *Reading the Fractures of Genesis* 1996 pp. 102-104; on the pre-test reading of Gen 43:34: R. Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 248; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975.

terms.translit: mah-nitztaddaq (Hithpael imperfect 1cp of tzadaq, 'how shall we declare-ourselves-righteous / clear-ourselves / justify-ourselves', Gen 44:16)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Hithpael (reflexive-declarative) imperfect 1cp
terms.literal: nitztaddaq — to declare-oneself-righteous / clear-oneself / justify-oneself; the rare Hithpael (reflexive-declarative) of tzadaq, naming the speech-act of self-vindication
terms.standardEnglish: how shall we clear ourselves (ASV); how shall we justify ourselves (KJV / more literal); how shall we prove our innocence (NJPS); what can we plead (Alter, functional)
terms.wohChoice: how shall we clear ourselves (ASV-baseline at Gen 44:16; the Hithpael's reflexive-declarative force and the Yehudah-internal Gen 38:26 → Gen 44:16 tzadaq-arc documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:16 stages Yehudah's response to Yosef's silver-cup accusation with a rare verbal-form: *mah nomar la-adoni mah nedabber u-mah nitztaddaq* — 'what shall we say unto my lord? what shall we speak? or how shall we clear ourselves?' The verb *nitztaddaq* is the HITHPAEL of *tzadaq* — the reflexive-declarative stem, 'to declare-oneself-righteous / clear-oneself / justify-oneself'. The stem is rare in the HB and is here deployed as the speech-act of self-vindication — the action Yehudah declares the brothers cannot perform.** // **The Hithpael of *tzadaq*.** The verbal root *tz-d-q* generates several stems: the Qal ('to be righteous, be in the right' — the standard stative; the Gen 38:26 *tzadqah* of Tamar is Qal); the Piel ('to declare righteous' — used of human judicial verdicts); the Hiphil ('to declare righteous / vindicate / justify' — the dominant judicial stem, used of both human and divine justification-action); and the rare HITHPAEL ('to declare-oneself-righteous / clear-oneself / justify-oneself' — the reflexive-declarative). The Hithpael's force is precise: not the Qal-state-of-being-righteous but the active speech-act of declaring-oneself-righteous, the rhetorical-juridical attempt to prove-one's-own-innocence. The construction at Gen 44:16 is therefore not 'how can we BE righteous' (Qal) but 'how can we DECLARE OURSELVES righteous' (Hithpael) — the question concerns the rhetorical-juridical act, not the underlying moral state. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The Hithpael of *tzadaq* is rare: **Gen 44:16** (here, the corpus's first attestation) is the only Pentateuchal occurrence. Other principal attestations: the Qal and Hiphil dominate the cross-corpus distribution; the Hithpael is uncommon. The chapter-deployment is therefore distinctively-marked: Yehudah selects the rare stem to name the impossible-speech-act, the self-vindication that the brothers cannot perform. The lexical-choice signals that the issue is not WHETHER the brothers are righteous (a question of being) but WHETHER they can present themselves AS righteous (a question of speaking). // **The Yehudah-internal Gen 38:26 → Gen 44:16 *tzadaq*-arc.** The arc is one of the corpus's tightest Yehudah-character-development structures: // **(1) Gen 38:26 — Yehudah's first *tzadaq* moment.** After Tamar's *haker-na* exposes him, Yehudah declares *tzadqah mimmeni* — 'she is more righteous than I' (or, on the forensic reading, 'she is in the right; the fault is from me'). The Qal-stative declares the comparative-or-forensic verdict in which TAMAR is named righteous and YEHUDAH names himself the one at fault. The Qal-of-*tzadaq* at Gen 38:26 is governed by the existing overlay [`tzadqah-mimmeni-she-is-in-the-right`](#tzadqah-mimmeni-she-is-in-the-right). // **(2) Gen 44:16 — Yehudah's second *tzadaq* moment.** Six chapters later, in the same character's mouth, the Hithpael is deployed: *mah-nitztaddaq*. Yehudah — who once declared TAMAR's righteousness against his own — now declares his BROTHERS' inability to declare themselves righteous before Yosef. The character-arc is exact: the man who once acknowledged another's *tzadaq* now acknowledges the collective brotherhood's inability to perform *tzadaq* for themselves. The lexical-thread Gen 38:26 → Gen 44:16 (both Yehudah-speech-act *tzadaq*-occurrences) is the corpus's tightest Yehudah-internal lexical structure outside the Gen 43 / 44 *arav*-pledge arc. The bidirectional sibling-overlay link to [`tzadqah-mimmeni-she-is-in-the-right`](#tzadqah-mimmeni-she-is-in-the-right) is wired: the Gen 38 entry has been extended with a 'Cross-reference (the Gen 44:16 *nitztaddaq* sibling-overlay link)' paragraph that names this entry by id and documents the Yehudah-tzadaq-arc; this entry cross-references the Gen 38 entry by id. // **The project's third overlay-overlay sibling pair.** The Gen 38 ↔ Gen 44 *tzadaq*-arc joins the ratified Gen 37 ↔ Gen 38 *haker-na* sibling-pair ([`haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif`](#haker-na-nakar-recognition-motif) ↔ [`haker-na-tamar-recognition-gen38`](#haker-na-tamar-recognition-gen38)) and the Gen 38 ↔ Gen 43/44 *arav*-sibling-pair ([`eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff`](#eravon-pledge-triad-signet-cord-staff) ↔ [`arav-eravon-yehudah-surety-pledge-gen43-44`](#arav-eravon-yehudah-surety-pledge-gen43-44)) as the project's third overlay-overlay sibling-pair anchored at Gen 38. The three pairs trace the chapter-38 Yehudah-character-arc across three lexical-thematic registers: recognition (haker-na), surety (arav), and righteousness-declaration (tzadaq). Gen 38 is therefore the cycle's anchor-chapter for Yehudah's character-development, with three overlay-overlay sibling pairs marking the chapter's load-bearing function. // **The rhetorical-juridical impossibility.** Yehudah's *mah-nitztaddaq* concedes the collapse of legal-defense: in the face of the silver-cup found in Binyamin's sack, the brothers cannot rhetorically present themselves as righteous; the proof-of-innocence speech-act is unavailable. The concession opens onto the following clause *ha-Elohim matza et-avon avadekha* ('Elohim hath found out the iniquity of thy servants', governed by the new central [`avon-iniquity-cross-corpus-keyword`](#avon-iniquity-cross-corpus-keyword) entry) — the rhetorical-collapse leads to the comprehensive iniquity-confession. The two speech-acts together form the chapter's confession-pivot: the inability-to-clear-themselves leads to the iniquity-found-out. // **Overlay housing.** Genesis-internal Yehudah-character-arc sibling-doublet → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional cross-reference to the Gen 38 sibling. The cross-corpus reach of the broader *tzadaq* root is governed by other entries (the central anchors at Gen 15:6, etc.); the chapter-specific Hithpael deployment in Yehudah's mouth is here. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the Hithpael stem is morphologically explicit, but (b) the rendering between 'clear ourselves' (ASV), 'justify ourselves' (KJV), and 'prove our innocence' (NJPS) is a choice between attested registers; (c) the Yehudah-character-arc reading is interpretive (the Gen 38 → Gen 44 lexical-thread is direct, but the character-development claim is the editorial substance); (d) the deliberate-rhetorical-collapse reading is interpretive. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *tzadaq* (Hithpael); BDB pp. 842-843; TDOT XII:239-264; NIDOTTE 3:744-769; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 305; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 131; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 564; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 333; on the Hithpael of *tzadaq*: B. Johnson 'tzedek' in TDOT XII; on the Gen 38 ↔ Gen 44 Yehudah-character-arc: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1 and *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 211, 264-265; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975.

terms.translit: asher yimmatze ito me-avadekha va-met (Gen 44:9, the brothers' self-imprecatory oath: 'with whomsoever it be found, let him die')
terms.strongs: H4191 (mut, 'to die', here in the imperfect-with-vav-consecutive as an oath-imprecation)
terms.partOfSpeech: self-imprecatory oath-formula: relative clause + finding-verb (Niphal) + suffix + min-particle + collective subject + va-met (the death-imprecation)
terms.literal: asher yimmatze ito me-avadekha va-met — 'with whomsoever of thy servants it [the cup] be found, and [that man shall] die' — the over-broad self-imprecatory oath formula, with the collective enslavement coda ve-gam-anachnu nihyeh la-adoni la-avadim ('and we also will be my lord's bondmen')
terms.standardEnglish: with whomsoever of thy servants it be found, let him die, and we also will be my lord's bondmen (ASV/KJV); whichever of your servants is found in possession of it shall die, and the rest of us shall become slaves to my lord (NJPS)
terms.wohChoice: with whomsoever of thy servants it be found, let him die, and we also will be my lord's bondmen (ASV-baseline at Gen 44:9; the Genesis-internal echo to Gen 31:32 documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:9 records the brothers' over-broad self-imprecation in response to the silver-cup accusation: *asher yimmatze ito me-avadekha va-met ve-gam-anachnu nihyeh la-adoni la-avadim* ('with whomsoever of thy servants it be found, let him die, and we also will be my lord's bondmen'). The construction is a marked oath-form: a death-imprecation on the individual whose possession-of-the-object is discovered, plus a collective-enslavement self-imprecation on the rest. The over-breadth (the brothers stake the collective freedom on the supposed-innocence of all) marks the oath as confidently-rash; the literary parallel to Gen 31:32 (Ya'aqov's analogous oath about Lavan's terafim) is striking and documented.** // **The construction.** The oath-formula deploys: (i) the indefinite-relative *asher* introducing the conditional-finding; (ii) the Niphal of *matza* ('to be found') with the 3ms suffix referring to the cup; (iii) the partitive *min* + collective subject *me-avadekha* ('from among thy servants'); (iv) the death-imprecation *va-met* (Qal of *mut*, in the imperfect-with-vav-consecutive used as the oath-conclusion 'let him die / he shall die'); (v) the collective-enslavement coda *ve-gam-anachnu nihyeh la-adoni la-avadim*. The over-breadth is grammatically explicit: the brothers do not say 'whichever of us is found will be enslaved alongside death' but 'let him die AND we also be enslaved' — they stake their freedom on the supposed-innocence of the (singular) finder. The construction is over-confident: in the rare-but-real possibility that the cup is found with one of them, the cost is death plus collective enslavement. // **The Gen 31:32 parallel — Ya'aqov's analogous self-curse.** The literary parallel to Gen 31:32 is one of the corpus's most-noted documentary-internal echoes: when Lavan accuses Ya'aqov of stealing his *terafim* (household-gods), Ya'aqov declares: *im asher timtza et eloheikha lo yichyeh* — 'with whomsoever thou findest thy gods, he shall not live' (Gen 31:32). The parallels with Gen 44:9 are exact: (i) both involve a missing precious-object (Lavan's *terafim* / Yosef's silver-cup) hidden in the youngest-Rachel-line member's possessions (Rachel hides the *terafim*; Binyamin's sack contains the cup); (ii) both invoke a death-curse on the finder that the speaker does not realize will boomerang (Ya'aqov inadvertently curses Rachel; the brothers inadvertently curse Binyamin); (iii) both formulae are over-broad (Ya'aqov says *lo yichyeh*, the brothers say *va-met*); (iv) both contexts involve search-by-status (Lavan's *trial* searches the camp; Yosef's steward searches eldest-to-youngest). The Gen 31:32 → Gen 44:9 echo is widely-noted by named scholarship: the Rachel-line theme (Rachel/Binyamin), the Ya'aqov-and-his-sons-as-deceivers theme, the boomeranging-oath theme. Rachel's death at Gen 35:18 (in childbirth of Binyamin) is often connected to Ya'aqov's Gen 31:32 oath; whether Rachel's death is causally related to the oath is a midrashic-and-modern-interpretive debate (Sarna, Westermann, Alter discuss). The Gen 44:9 brothers' analogous oath might-or-might-not be similarly fatal for Binyamin (the chapter's climax depends on what happens next). // **The literary signature.** The Gen 31:32 → Gen 44:9 pattern is one of the cycle's documented intertextual structures: the same kind of rash-oath sworn by Ya'aqov in his youthful confrontation with Lavan is now sworn by his sons in their confrontation with the disguised Yosef. The pattern's literary force is character-genealogical: the sons inherit the father's rhetorical-rashness, and the cycle's drama depends on whether the inheritance is broken at Gen 44 (whether Yehudah's substitution-speech of Gen 44:18-34 can avert the boomeranging-oath). The literary observation is named-scholarship: Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative*, Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative*, Sarna *JPS Genesis*. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific oath-formula with a documented Genesis-internal echo (Gen 31:32 → Gen 44:9); the broader cross-corpus self-imprecatory oath-vocabulary (chai-X formulae, chalilah-disavowals, etc.) is governed elsewhere; this entry is anchored at the Gen 44:9 chapter-specific construction with the Gen 31:32 echo as literary cross-reference. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the construction is grammatically explicit, but (b) the over-broad / rash reading is interpretive; (c) the Gen 31:32 echo is a literary observation, not a lexical-identity claim; (d) the boomeranging-oath reading is interpretive-narratological. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *mut*; BDB pp. 559-561; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 304; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 130; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 562; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 332; on the Gen 31:32 → Gen 44:9 boomeranging-oath echo: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 and *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 264; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on Rachel's death and the Gen 31:32 oath: N. Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 220 (the Gen 31:32 commentary); for the midrashic and rabbinic readings of the boomeranging-oath: Genesis Rabbah on Gen 31 + Gen 44.

terms.translit: va-yiqre'u simlotam (Gen 44:13; cf. Gen 37:29 va-yiqra et-begadav of Re'uven, Gen 37:34 va-yiqra Ya'aqov simlotav)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Qal imperfect-with-vav-consecutive 3mp + plural noun (the garments)
terms.literal: qara begadim/simlot — to tear the garments / to rend the clothes; the standard HB grief-rending formula performed at the news-of-death / news-of-calamity / discovery-of-loss moment
terms.standardEnglish: they rent their clothes (ASV/KJV); they tore their clothes (NJPS / NRSV); they rent their garments (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: they rent their clothes (ASV-baseline at Gen 44:13; the Yosef-cycle grief-formula triplet Gen 37:29 → Gen 37:34 → Gen 44:13 documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:13 records the ten brothers' grief-response to the cup-discovery in Binyamin's sack: *va-yiqre'u simlotam va-ya'amos ish al chamoro va-yashuvu ha-irah* — 'then they rent their clothes, and laded every man his ass, and returned to the city'. The construction *qara + simlot/begadim* (the Qal of *qara* 'to tear, rend' paired with a garment-noun) is the standard HB grief-rending formula performed at the news-of-death / news-of-calamity / discovery-of-loss moment. The Gen 44:13 deployment is the third occurrence in the Yosef-cycle's grief-rending triplet: Gen 37:29 (Re'uven at the empty pit, the cycle's first occurrence — *va-yiqra et begadav*); Gen 37:34 (Ya'aqov on receiving the bloodied tunic — *va-yiqra Ya'aqov simlotav*); Gen 44:13 (the ten brothers at the cup-discovery — *va-yiqre'u simlotam*). The triplet is one of the corpus's tightest cross-chapter grief-formula structures.** // **The lexeme.** The Qal of *qara* ('to tear, rend') in combination with a garment-noun is the standard HB grief-rending formula. The action is performative: the speaker rends his own clothing to physically embody the rupture-of-circumstance, the breaking-of-the-ordinary. The formula's force is ritual: the rending is not casual-tearing but ceremonial-tearing, marking the moment of grief publicly and irreversibly. The verb itself appears in other registers (Hiphil 'tear away', etc.), but the *qara + garment* construction is the grief-formula specifically. // **The Yosef-cycle triplet.** The three occurrences form a deliberate-literary triplet: (i) **Gen 37:29** — Re'uven returns to the pit to retrieve Yosef and finds it empty: *va-yashav el echav va-yiqra et begadav* — 'and he returned unto his brothers and rent his garments'. Re'uven's rending is the cycle's first grief-formula deployment, performed in private discovery-of-loss. (ii) **Gen 37:34** — Ya'aqov receives the bloodied *ketonet passim* and concludes Yosef has been devoured: *va-yiqra Ya'aqov simlotav va-yasem saq be-motnav va-yit'abel al beno yamim rabbim* — 'and Ya'aqov rent his garments, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days'. Ya'aqov's rending is paired with the *saq* (sackcloth) and the *avel* (mourning) lexemes, the corpus's most concentrated grief-cluster. (iii) **Gen 44:13** — the ten brothers at the cup-discovery: *va-yiqre'u simlotam* — 'then they rent their clothes'. The collective-subject distinguishes this third occurrence from the two Gen 37 individual-subject occurrences. The triplet's structural-significance: the three grief-rending occurrences mark the three principal points of the cycle's grief-arc (Re'uven's individual-grief at the pit; Ya'aqov's paternal-grief at the tunic; the brothers' collective-grief at the cup). The brothers as collective-subject in Gen 44:13 is itself marked: the same brothers who once engineered Re'uven's and Ya'aqov's grief now grieve themselves at what they interpret as Elohim's discovery-of-their-iniquity (which Yehudah will articulate at v 16). // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The grief-rending formula recurs as a corpus-wide grief-marker, with the Pentateuchal anchor at Gen 37:29 (Re'uven). The principal attestations: **Num 14:6** (Yehoshua and Kalev rend their garments at the people's rebellion-response to the spies' report); **Josh 7:6** (Yehoshua at Ai's defeat); **Judg 11:35** (Yiftach at his daughter's appearance); **2 Sam 1:11** (David at the news of Sha'ul's death — *va-yachazek David bi-vgadav va-yiqra'em ve-gam kol ha-anashim asher itto*); **2 Sam 3:31** (David at Avner's death); **2 Sam 13:31** (David at Amnon's reported-death); **1 Kgs 21:27** (Ach'av at Eliyahu's curse); **2 Kgs 2:12** (Elisha at Eliyahu's ascent); **2 Kgs 5:7** (the king of Israel at Naaman's letter); **2 Kgs 6:30** (Yehoram at the famine in Shomron); **2 Kgs 11:14** (Athalyah at Yo'ash's coronation); **2 Kgs 18:37 = Isa 36:22** (Elyaqim and Shevna at Ravshakeh's blasphemy); **2 Kgs 19:1 = Isa 37:1** (Chizqiyahu at the same); **2 Kgs 22:11 + 19 = 2 Chr 34:19 + 27** (Yoshiyahu at the Torah-scroll discovery); **Esth 4:1** (Mordekhai at Haman's edict); **Job 1:20** (Iyov at the news of his children's death); **Job 2:12** (Iyov's friends at his appearance); **Jer 36:24** (the contrast — the king and his servants do NOT rend at Yirmiyahu's scroll); **Joel 2:13** (the prophet's reframing — *qiru levavkhem ve-al bigdeikhem*, 'rend your heart, and not your garments', the inward grief-rending). The lexeme is corpus-saturating in the grief-and-mourning register. // **Overlay housing.** The Yosef-cycle grief-formula triplet is Genesis-internal; the wider cross-corpus distribution is genuine and substantial (Num, Josh, Judg, Samuel × 4 occurrences, Kings × 10 occurrences, Chronicles, Esther, Iyov, Jeremiah, Joel) and noted as a promotion-path-seed; the chapter-specific deployment as the Yosef-cycle triplet's third occurrence is what is documented here. → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-seed noted for future Samuel-Kings translation activation. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit (Qal of *qara* + garment-noun); (b) the Yosef-cycle triplet (Gen 37:29 + 37:34 + 44:13) is textually verifiable; (c) the grief-formula function is documented across named scholarship; (d) the ASV-baseline 'they rent their clothes' is the direct rendering; (e) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *qara*; BDB p. 902; TDOT XIII:175-181; NIDOTTE 3:992-993; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 304; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 130; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 562; on the grief-rending formula's cross-corpus distribution: G. Stählin 'Das Bild der Witwe' JAC 17 (1974) 5-20; M. I. Gruber *Aspects of Nonverbal Communication in the Ancient Near East* Studia Pohl 12, 1980; on the Joel 2:13 prophetic-reframing: H. W. Wolff *Joel and Amos* Hermeneia 1977; on the Yosef-cycle triplet: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975.

terms.translit: tarof toraf (paronomastic infinitive-absolute Qal + Pual perfect 3ms of taraf, 'surely [he is] torn in pieces' / 'torn-torn'); Gen 37:33 (Ya'aqov on the bloodied tunic) and Gen 44:28 (Ya'aqov reported-by-Yehudah, the seven-chapter verbatim-echo)
terms.strongs: H2963 (taraf, 'to tear / tear in pieces / rend [by a wild beast]')
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, paronomastic infinitive-absolute + finite-verb construction (Qal infinitive-absolute tarof + Pual perfect 3ms toraf), with the intensifying-emphasis force
terms.literal: tarof toraf — 'tearing he-is-torn' / 'with-tearing he-was-torn' — the paronomastic intensifier construction with the Qal infinitive-absolute + Pual finite-verb
terms.standardEnglish: surely he is torn in pieces (ASV/KJV); he has surely been torn to pieces (NJPS); he has surely been torn by beasts (NRSV); yes, he has been torn to shreds (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: surely he is torn in pieces (ASV-baseline at Gen 37:33 and Gen 44:28; the chapter-pair verbatim echo locking Ya'aqov's continued belief in the Gen 37 false-evidence documented in commentary; the cross-corpus taraf distribution noted)
terms.rationale: **The paronomastic infinitive-absolute + finite-verb construction *tarof toraf* (literally 'tearing he-is-torn') appears twice in the Yosef cycle in Ya'aqov's mouth, seven chapters apart, in verbatim repetition: Gen 37:33 (Ya'aqov's immediate response to seeing the bloodied *ketonet passim*: *chayah ra'ah akhalathu, tarof toraf Yosef* — 'an evil beast hath devoured him; Yosef is without doubt torn in pieces') and Gen 44:28 (Ya'aqov reported-by-Yehudah, the patriarch's continuing-belief: *va-yetze ha-echad me'itti va-omar akh tarof toraf ve-lo re'itiv ad henah* — 'and the one went out from me, and I said, Surely he is torn in pieces; and I have not seen him since'). The verbatim-echo across seven chapters is one of the corpus's most concentrated lexical-cross-chapter structures, locking the patriarch's continued belief in the Gen 37 false-evidence and confirming that the deception has held across the entire intervening narrative time.** // **The construction.** The paronomastic infinitive-absolute + finite-verb construction is the standard HB intensifier (the formula *VERB-Inf + VERB-finite*, here *taraf-tarof + taraf-toraf*, names emphasis-by-cognate-repetition: 'surely / indeed / without-doubt / with-emphasis the action'). The verbal root *t-r-f* ('to tear / tear in pieces / rend [by a wild beast]') generates the Qal active (the wild-beast-as-subject tearing-action), the Niphal/Pual passive (the prey-as-subject being-torn), and several derived forms (the noun *terefah* 'torn-prey / carrion'). The Gen 37:33 + 44:28 construction uses the Pual passive: the prey (Yosef) IS-TORN (passive), not Yosef does-the-tearing. The intensifier paronomasia names the unambiguity of the supposed-tearing: 'surely / without doubt'. // **The Gen 37:33 → Gen 44:28 verbatim-echo.** The seven-chapter cross-chapter verbatim-repetition is the cycle's signature lock-in of Ya'aqov's continued misinformation. At Gen 37:33 the patriarch concludes from the bloodied tunic that Yosef has been killed by a wild beast (the *chayah ra'ah*, governed by the sibling overlay [`chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast`](#chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast)); at Gen 44:28, reported by Yehudah in his great surety-speech, the patriarch is shown to STILL hold the same conclusion — *akh tarof toraf*, 'surely he is torn in pieces'. The lexical-verbatim of the second occurrence (the same *tarof toraf* construction in the same patriarch's mouth) confirms that Ya'aqov has not revised his Gen 37 conclusion in the seven-chapter / twenty-two-year intervening narrative time. The deception has held; the bloodied-tunic-evidence has continued to determine the patriarch's understanding-of-the-past. Yehudah's deployment of the patriarch's words — quoting Ya'aqov's own *tarof toraf* — is part of his rhetorical-strategy: he makes the patriarch's grief audible to the *shallit* (who is in fact the supposedly-torn-in-pieces brother) by reproducing the patriarch's exact words. The reader who knows Yosef's identity hears the dramatic-irony with concentrated force: Yosef hears his father's belief about his death reported by the brother who knows the truth, in the patriarch's own words. // **The cross-corpus *taraf* distribution.** The verb is well-attested in the corpus: **Gen 37:33 + 44:28** (the Yosef-cycle pair); **Exod 22:12** (the law of the borrowed-animal-torn-by-a-beast: *im taroph yittareph yevi'ehu eid, ha-terefah lo yeshallem* — 'if it be torn in pieces, then let him bring it for witness, and he shall not make good that which was torn'); **Jer 5:6** (*aryeh mi-ya'ar hikkam ze'ev aravot yeshoddedem, namer shoqed al areihem kol ha-yotze mehennah yittareph* — 'a lion out of the forest shall slay them, a wolf of the evenings shall destroy them, a leopard shall watch against their cities: every one that goeth out thence shall be torn in pieces'); **Hos 5:14** (*ki anokhi kha-shachal le-Ephraim ve-kha-kefir le-veit Yehudah, ani ani etrof va-elekh* — 'for I will be unto Ephraim as a lion, and as a young lion to the house of Yehudah: I, even I, will tear and go away'); **Hos 6:1** (*ki hu taraf ve-yirpa'enu*, 'for he hath torn, and he will heal us'); **Hos 13:8** (*epgashem ke-dov shakkul ve-eqra segor libbam, ve-okhlem sham ka-lavi, chayyat ha-sadeh tebbaqe'em* — 'I will meet them as a bear bereaved of her whelps, and will rend the caul of their heart, and there will I devour them like a lion'); **Mic 5:7 [MT 5:8]**; **Nah 2:13 [MT 2:12]** (the lion's-den image); **Ps 7:3 [MT 7:2]** (David's plea against pursuing enemies *pen yitrof ke-aryeh*); **Ps 17:12** (*dimyono ke-aryeh yikhsof li-trof*); **Ps 22:14 [MT 22:13]** (the lion-imagery of the psalmist's suffering); **Ps 50:22** (the divine threat); **Job 16:9; 18:4** (the wild-beast-imagery of the divine-anger); **Ezek 19:3 + 6; 22:25 + 27** (the prophetic-leonine imagery of the prophet's people-and-leaders). The lexeme's predominant register is the lion-or-wild-beast-as-subject tearing-action, frequently in prophetic-or-poetic imagery. // **The bidirectional sibling-link to `chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast`.** The companion overlay entry [`chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast`](#chayah-raah-evil-or-wild-beast) governs the Gen 37 chapter-bracket *chayah ra'ah* construction (the cover-story 'an evil beast hath devoured him' deployed at the cycle's beginning at v 20 and v 33). The Gen 37:33 deployment uses BOTH constructions together: *chayah ra'ah akhalathu, tarof toraf Yosef*; the Gen 44:28 deployment uses only *tarof toraf* in Ya'aqov's retrospective lament. The two overlay entries thus jointly govern the wild-beast-devouring narrative-frame: the *chayah ra'ah* entry for the cover-story creature-naming chapter-bracket; this entry for the *tarof toraf* paronomastic chapter-pair (Gen 37:33 + Gen 44:28). The bidirectional cross-reference is wired: the Gen 37 entry has been extended with a 'Cross-reference (the Gen 44:28 *tarof toraf* sibling-overlay link)' paragraph that names this entry by id; this entry cross-references the Gen 37 entry by id. The two are deliberate companions per the ratified sibling-overlay-entries pattern. // **Overlay housing.** Genesis-internal chapter-pair verbatim-echo (Gen 37:33 + Gen 44:28); the cross-corpus *taraf* distribution is governed by other contexts when those texts are translated (the Jeremiah, Hosea, Psalms, Ezekiel deployments will activate when their books are translated); the chapter-specific Yosef-cycle echo is here. → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional sibling-link. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit (the paronomastic infinitive-absolute + Pual finite); (b) the chapter-pair verbatim-echo is textually verifiable; (c) the patriarchal-belief-continuity reading is documented across named scholarship; (d) the ASV-baseline 'surely he is torn in pieces' is the direct rendering; (e) the cross-corpus *taraf* distribution is verifiable. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *taraf*; BDB p. 382; TDOT V:350-357; NIDOTTE 2:343-345; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 305; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 131; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 569; on the Gen 37:33 → Gen 44:28 verbatim-echo: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 8 and *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 264; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on the paronomastic infinitive-absolute construction: J. Joüon and T. Muraoka *A Grammar of Biblical Hebrew* §123; on the wild-beast-tearing register: T. Mettinger 'The Lion of Yahweh' SEÅ 51 (1986) 148-157.

terms.translit: ba-gadol hechel u-va-qaton killah ('began at the eldest, and left off at the youngest', Gen 44:12)
terms.strongs: H1419 (gadol, 'great / eldest') + H6996 (qaton, 'little / youngest') + H2490 (chalal III, Hiphil hechel 'began') + H3615 (kalah, Piel killah 'finished / left off')
terms.partOfSpeech: literary-structural construction: prepositional phrase ba- + adjective-substantive + Hiphil verb (the beginning-action); paired with prepositional phrase ba- + adjective-substantive + Piel verb (the finishing-action)
terms.literal: ba-gadol hechel u-va-qaton killah — 'in / at the great / eldest he began, and in / at the little / youngest he finished' — the literary-structural birth-order-as-search-order construction
terms.standardEnglish: and began at the eldest, and left off at the youngest (ASV/KJV); starting with the oldest and ending with the youngest (modern paraphrase); he searched from oldest to youngest (NJPS); beginning with the eldest and ending with the youngest (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: and began at the eldest, and left off at the youngest (ASV-baseline; the literary-marker function as Binyamin-saved-for-last and the Yosef-cycle birth-order-as-structural-foregrounding documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:12 records the steward's silver-cup search in a striking literary-structural construction: *va-yechappes ba-gadol hechel u-va-qaton killah va-yimmatze ha-gavia be-amtachat Binyamin* — 'and he searched, and began at the eldest, and left off at the youngest: and the cup was found in Binyamin's sack'. The merism eldest→youngest (*ba-gadol hechel u-va-qaton killah*) names the search-order as proceeding from oldest brother to youngest, prolonging the brothers' suspense and Yosef's test by saving Binyamin's sack for last. The literary-construction is part of the cycle's persistent foregrounding of birth-order as a structural marker.** // **The construction.** The construction is a tight literary-structural merism: (i) *ba-gadol* (preposition + substantive: 'in / at the great-one' = 'at the eldest'); (ii) *hechel* (Hiphil of *chalal* III: 'he began'); (iii) the conjunction *u-* ('and'); (iv) *va-qaton* (preposition + substantive: 'and in / at the little-one' = 'at the youngest'); (v) *killah* (Piel of *kalah*: 'he finished / left off'). The merism eldest→youngest (paired with the begin→finish action-pair) names the temporal-spatial-progression: the steward's search proceeds from sack-to-sack in the order eldest-brother-first through youngest-brother-last. The construction's grammatical precision is the chapter's literary signature: the search is staged not as random-search but as ordered-search-by-birth-order. // **The literary-narratological function.** The ordered-search-by-birth-order has a precise narratological function: it prolongs the brothers' (false) relief and the reader's tension. As each older brother's sack is searched and found innocent, the brothers' confidence grows and the reader's awareness of the impending revelation sharpens. By the time the steward arrives at Binyamin's sack — the last in the search-order — the relief of the older brothers is at its peak (they have all been cleared), making the cup-discovery at the youngest brother's sack maximally surprising and devastating. The literary effect depends on the search-order: a random-search or a youngest-first search would not produce the same prolonged-suspense and devastating-reversal effects. The construction is therefore a piece of the cycle's narratological-architecture, not a casual description of the steward's method. // **The Yosef-cycle birth-order-as-structural-foregrounding.** The Gen 44:12 search-order joins a series of Yosef-cycle scenes where birth-order is structurally foregrounded: (i) **Gen 43:33** — the stewardship-feast seating-order: *va-yeshvu lefanav ha-bekhor ki-vkhorato ve-ha-tza'ir ki-tze'irato va-yitmehu ha-anashim ish el re'ehu* ('and they sat before him, the firstborn according to his birthright, and the youngest according to his youth: and the men marvelled one with another' — governed by the sibling overlay [`tamah-marvel-impossible-knowledge-seating-gen43`](#tamah-marvel-impossible-knowledge-seating-gen43)). The Gen 43:33 seating-order names the eleven brothers seated in birth-order-sequence by Yosef's steward; the brothers marvel at the impossible-knowledge of their birth-order by a stranger. (ii) **Gen 44:12** (here) — the search-order. (iii) **Gen 48:13-20** — Ya'aqov's crossed-hands blessing of Ephraim and Menasheh (the firstborn-and-second crossed): Ya'aqov inverts the birth-order in the blessing, placing his right-hand on the younger Ephraim against Yosef's protest. The Gen 48 scene is the cycle's most concentrated birth-order-inversion-as-blessing structure. The Yosef-cycle's persistent foregrounding of birth-order is therefore one of the cycle's structural-thematic threads: the cycle traces the displacement of older-brother-precedence by younger-brother-significance (Yosef the eleventh-born surpassing the ten elders; Ephraim the second-born receiving the elder-blessing). // **The Gen 43:33 → Gen 44:12 chapter-pair.** The Gen 43:33 seating-order and the Gen 44:12 search-order form a chapter-pair structural-deployment: both occur in Yosef's stewardship-household; both stage the brothers' birth-order as a literary marker; both involve Yosef's steward as the executing-agent of the staged-by-birth-order action. The chapter-pair confirms that the Gen 44:12 search-order is not an isolated detail but is part of the cycle's deliberate birth-order-as-structural-marker pattern. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific literary-structural construction; the broader cross-corpus birth-order-as-narrative-marker is a corpus-wide thematic structure (the younger-brother-displacement pattern across the patriarchal narratives — Avel/Qayin, Yitzchaq/Yishma'el, Ya'aqov/Esav, Yosef/eleven-elders, Ephraim/Menasheh — but the specific search-by-birth-order *ba-gadol hechel u-va-qaton killah* construction is chapter-specific. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is grammatically explicit; (b) the merism eldest→youngest is textually verifiable; (c) the narratological function as suspense-prolongation is documented across named scholarship; (d) the Yosef-cycle birth-order-as-structural-foregrounding pattern is established in literary-critical scholarship; (e) the Gen 43:33 → Gen 44:12 chapter-pair is textually verifiable. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *gadol*, *qaton*, *chalal* III (Hiphil), *kalah* (Piel); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 304; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 130; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 562; on the narratological-suspense function of the search-order: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 and *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 264; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; on the Yosef-cycle birth-order-as-structural-foregrounding: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; G. W. Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* CBQMS 4, 1976; on the younger-brother-displacement pattern across the patriarchal narratives: J. Goldin 'The Youngest Son or Where Does Genesis 38 Belong' JBL 96 (1977) 27-44; W. Brueggemann *Genesis* Interpretation 1982.

terms.translit: shenayim yaledah-li ishti (Ya'aqov reported by Yehudah, Gen 44:27)
terms.strongs: H8147 (shnayim, 'two') + H3205 (yalad, 'to bear / bring forth') + H802 (ishah, 'wife') + 1cs suffix
terms.partOfSpeech: literary-pragmatic construction: cardinal-number + Qal perfect 3fs verb (with dative-of-advantage) + noun-with-suffix
terms.literal: shenayim yaledah-li ishti — 'two-sons [she] bare-to-me my-wife' — the construction's marked exclusivity: only Rachel (the singular 'my wife') and only her two sons (Yosef and Binyamin) are in view
terms.standardEnglish: my wife bare me two sons (ASV/KJV literal); ye know that my wife bore me only two (NJPS, interpretive expansion making the exclusivity explicit); my wife bore me two (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: my wife bare me two sons (ASV-baseline literal at Gen 44:27; the construction's marked Rachel-exclusivity in Ya'aqov's reported-by-Yehudah retelling documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:27 records Yehudah's reporting-of-Ya'aqov's speech: *va-yomer avdekha avi eleinu attem yedatem ki shenayim yaledah-li ishti* — 'and thy servant my father said unto us, Ye know that my wife bare me two sons'. The construction is marked: Ya'aqov speaks as if only Rachel were 'wife' (Le'ah, Bilhah, and Zilpah are excluded from the *ishti* designation; the singular 'my wife' refers exclusively to Rachel), and as if only Yosef and Binyamin were his children (the ten elder brothers — sons of Le'ah, Bilhah, and Zilpah — are excluded from the *yaledah-li shenayim* count). The phrasing is a literary marker of Ya'aqov's enduring Rachel-centric grief and his lexical-rhetorical inability to count his Le'ah-and-handmaid sons in this moment. The literary observation is documented across the standard commentaries (Sarna, Westermann, Alter, Hamilton).** // **The construction.** The construction deploys: (i) the cardinal *shenayim* ('two'); (ii) the Qal perfect 3fs *yaledah* ('she bore'); (iii) the dative-of-advantage *-li* ('to me'); (iv) the singular *ishti* ('my wife'). The grammatical features are all explicit: *shenayim* is precisely 'two', not 'two-of-the-ones-she-bore-me'; *ishti* is grammatically the singular 'my wife', not 'my-wives' or 'one-of-my-wives'. The construction's marked-exclusivity is grammatically explicit: Ya'aqov speaks as if Rachel were his only wife and Yosef-and-Binyamin were his only children. The exclusion of Le'ah, Bilhah, and Zilpah, and of the ten elder brothers, is grammatically encoded — not a reader-inference but the construction's literal meaning. // **The literary signature of Ya'aqov's Rachel-centric grief.** The Genesis narratives are explicit about Ya'aqov's preference for Rachel over Le'ah (Gen 29:30-31), his elevated love for Rachel's son Yosef over the others (Gen 37:3 *ki ben zequnim hu lo*), and his elevated love for Binyamin after Yosef's apparent death (Gen 42:38 *u-ve-Binyamin sotheidekha*; Gen 43:14 *ka-asher shakholti shakhalti*; Gen 44:30 *ve-nafsho qeshurah ve-nafsho*). The Gen 44:27 *shenayim yaledah-li ishti* construction is therefore consistent with — indeed it concentrates — the patriarchal Rachel-centrism that the cycle has been documenting. The literary observation is that Ya'aqov's grief has so concentrated on the Rachel-line sons that he speaks, in this private-grief register, as if the ten Le'ah-and-handmaid sons were not his. The ten brothers — who are present-and-overhearing the patriarch's words as Yehudah reports them — are textually erased by the patriarch's own speech. The dramatic-irony is sharp: the same ten brothers whose erasure-from-the-count their father performs are the ones now standing before the disguised Yosef (one of the two 'my wife's sons') and offering themselves into slavery to save the other 'my wife's son'. The patriarchal-erasure that the patriarch performs is being inverted by the brothers' substitution-offer. // **The named-scholarship documentation.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 306 notes the marked exclusivity ('Jacob speaks as though only Rachel were truly his wife'). Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 131 documents the patriarchal Rachel-centrism as 'tragically narrow'. Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 264 reads the phrase as 'eloquent in its exclusiveness'. Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 565 treats the phrase as 'a poignant indication of the depth of Ya'aqov's love for Rachel and her children'. The literary observation is consensus modern-critical scholarship. // **The rendering choice.** The ASV-baseline 'my wife bare me two sons' is literal; the NJPS 'ye know that my wife bore me only two' adds the interpretive 'only' to surface the marked-exclusivity; Alter retains the literal. The WoH preserves the ASV-baseline literal; the interpretive-expansion 'only' is documented as an option but not adopted on the surface (the Hebrew does not literally contain 'only'; the exclusivity is grammatically encoded but lexically implicit). // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific Ya'aqov-character-marker (reported-speech in Yehudah's retelling); the patriarchal Rachel-centrism is a corpus-wide thematic structure but the *shenayim yaledah-li ishti* construction is chapter-specific. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the construction's grammatical features are explicit (direct), but (b) the marked-exclusivity reading is interpretive (the consensus reading is named-scholarship-documented but the absence-of-an-explicit-'only' allows the construction to be read as merely descriptive); (c) the literary-character-marker function is interpretive. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 306; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 131; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 565; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 264; on Ya'aqov's Rachel-centric character-development across the cycle: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; on the patriarchal-favoritism theme: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 8; G. W. Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* CBQMS 4, 1976.

terms.translit: ki khamokha ke-Par'oh ('for thou art even as Pharaoh', Gen 44:18)
terms.partOfSpeech: court-deference formula: causal particle + kha- comparative-particle + 2ms suffix + ke- comparative-particle + named monarch (Pharaoh)
terms.literal: ki khamokha ke-Par'oh — 'for [thou art] like-thee as-Pharaoh' — the unique court-deference formula equating the addressee with the monarch-of-Mitsrayim
terms.standardEnglish: for thou art even as Pharaoh (ASV/KJV literal); for thou art the like of Pharaoh (Alter); for you are the equal of Pharaoh (NJPS); for you are like Pharaoh himself (modern)
terms.wohChoice: for thou art even as Pharaoh (ASV-baseline at Gen 44:18; the chapter-singular court-deference formula and its structural counterpart to Gen 37:8 ha-malokh timlokh aleinu documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:18 opens Yehudah's great surety-speech with the most extreme acknowledgment of Yosef's authority in the cycle: *va-yiggash elav Yehudah va-yomer bi adoni yedabber-na avdekha davar be-aznei adoni ve-al yichar appekha be-avdekha ki khamokha ke-Par'oh* — 'then Yehudah came near unto him, and said, Oh my lord, let thy servant, I pray thee, speak a word in my lord's ears, and let not thine anger burn against thy servant; for thou art even as Pharaoh'. The construction *ki khamokha ke-Par'oh* is essentially unique in the HB: there is no exact parallel of the *kha-X ke-Y* deferential-equation-to-the-monarch construction. The construction names Yosef as Pharaoh's equal in Yehudah's eyes — the maximally-elevated court-deference Yehudah can perform.** // **The construction.** The construction deploys the comparative-construction *kamo* (cf. Lev 24:14 etc.; the longer form *kamokha* — 'like-thee' — uses the 2ms suffix) followed by *ke-Par'oh* ('as Pharaoh'). The deferential-equation is grammatically explicit: 'thou [art] like-thee as-Pharaoh' — i.e., 'thou art equivalent to Pharaoh', 'thou art as Pharaoh is'. The *ki* is causal: Yehudah explains his careful manner of address by noting that the addressee is the monarch's equal. The construction's emphatic-rhetorical force is the maximum-deference-acknowledgment: Yehudah names Yosef as not-merely-the-shallit but as-Pharaoh-himself in the deferential register. // **The structural counterpart to Gen 37:8.** The Gen 37:8 brothers' refusal-of-Yosef's-dominion deploys the construction *ha-malokh timlokh aleinu im-mashol timshol banu* ('shalt thou indeed reign over us, or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?'). The brothers — including (presumably) Yehudah — refuse the dominion-claim Yosef's dreams imply. The Gen 44:18 *ki khamokha ke-Par'oh* is therefore the structural-and-thematic counterpart of the Gen 37:8 refusal: Yehudah, who once participated in the brothers' refusal of Yosef's dominion-over-them, now performs the maximum-deference-acknowledgment of Yosef's dominion-equivalence-with-Pharaoh. The character-arc Gen 37:8 → Gen 44:18 traces Yehudah's complete reversal: from refusing-Yosef's-dominion to acknowledging-Yosef-as-monarch-equivalent. The reversal is one of the cycle's tightest character-arc structures. // **The chapter-singular construction.** No exact parallel of the *kha-X ke-Y* deferential-equation-to-the-monarch formula occurs elsewhere in the HB. The closest cross-corpus deferential-court constructions are: (i) the *chai Par'oh* / *chei nafshekha* oath-formulae (governed by the central [`chei-x-oath-by-the-life-formula`](#chei-x-oath-by-the-life-formula) entry); (ii) the *adoni ha-melekh* address-formula (the standard royal-address); (iii) the *ke-malakh ha-Elohim* construction (the king-as-divine-messenger formula, e.g. 2 Sam 14:17). The Gen 44:18 construction's specific *kha-X ke-Y* formula equating the addressee with a named monarch is essentially unique. The chapter-singular character of the construction makes it a literary-singular: a one-off deferential-formula deployed at the chapter's most pressured moment, before Yehudah's substitution-speech. // **The chapter-internal literary-rhetorical function.** The Gen 44:18 deference-formula's literary-rhetorical function is to set up the speech's risk: Yehudah is approaching the monarch-equivalent to ask for the impossible (Binyamin's release), and the deference-formula simultaneously (a) acknowledges Yosef's authority to refuse and (b) appeals to Yosef's monarchic-honor to consider the request. The construction is rhetorically-strategic: by naming the addressee as monarch-equivalent, Yehudah binds Yosef to monarchic-honor obligations (the duty to hear the petitioner, the duty to consider the supplication). The chapter's speech-act-architecture depends on the construction: without the deference-formula opening, the substitution-speech would lack the rhetorical-pressure that the Yehudah-as-suppliant-to-monarch construction generates. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular court-deference construction; the broader court-deference vocabulary is governed by other entries (the *chai Par'oh* oath-formula, the standard royal-address); the chapter-specific *ki khamokha ke-Par'oh* construction is here. → **OVERLAY**. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the construction's grammatical features are explicit, but (b) the unique-construction reading depends on the absence-of-cross-corpus-parallels analysis (which is interpretive); (c) the structural-counterpart-to-Gen-37:8 reading is interpretive (the lexical-connection is not direct, but the thematic-reversal is named-scholarship-documented); (d) the rhetorical-strategic function is interpretive-narratological. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *kamo* / *kamokha*; BDB pp. 455-456; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 306; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 132; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 565; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 334; on the Gen 37:8 → Gen 44:18 Yehudah-character-reversal: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 8 and *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 264-265; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; on the Yehudah-speech's rhetorical-architecture: J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; W. Brueggemann *Genesis* Interpretation 1982 pp. 327-340.

terms.translit: shillamtem ra'ah tachat tovah ('ye have rewarded evil for good', Gen 44:4)
terms.strongs: H7999 (shalem, Piel: 'to repay, recompense, reward') + H7451 (ra'ah, 'evil / bad') + H8478 (tachat, 'instead of / in return for') + H2896 (tovah, 'good')
terms.partOfSpeech: moral-reversal idiom: Piel of shalem (recompense-verb) + abstract-noun (evil) + tachat-preposition (in-return-for) + abstract-noun (good)
terms.literal: shillamtem ra'ah tachat tovah — 'ye have repaid / recompensed evil in-the-place-of good' — the moral-reversal idiom naming the inversion of just-recompense (good-for-good, evil-for-evil) by repaying-evil-for-good
terms.standardEnglish: wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good (ASV/KJV); why have you repaid good with evil (NJPS); why do you repay good with evil (Alter); why have you returned evil for good (modern)
terms.wohChoice: wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good (ASV-baseline at Gen 44:4; the cross-corpus 'evil for good' moral-reversal formula documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 44:4 stages the steward's accusation against the brothers (on Yosef's instruction): *lammah shillamtem ra'ah tachat tovah* — 'wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good?'. The construction is the standard HB 'evil-for-good' moral-reversal idiom — the inversion of just-recompense (good-for-good, evil-for-evil) by repaying-evil-for-good. The idiom recurs across the corpus's wisdom-and-Psalmic literature as a marked indictment-of-injustice-formula.** // **The construction.** The construction deploys: (i) the Piel of *shalem* — the recompense / repayment / reward verb in its causative-active register (the Qal of *shalem* is 'to be complete / whole / at peace'; the Piel 'to make-complete / make-whole / repay / recompense'; the recompense-sense is the dominant Piel register); (ii) the abstract-noun *ra'ah* ('evil / bad / harm'); (iii) the substitution-preposition *tachat* (governed by the new central [`tachat-substitution-formula`](#tachat-substitution-formula) entry — here in the 'in-return-for / in-the-place-of' register, distinct from the substitution-of-persons register at Gen 44:33); (iv) the abstract-noun *tovah* ('good / benefit / favor'). The grammatical-rhetorical force is the inversion-of-just-recompense: instead of repaying good-for-good (which would be the just response), the addressed-party has repaid evil-for-good (the moral inversion). The idiom names the action as morally-reversed: the good-received has been answered by evil-returned. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** The 'evil-for-good' moral-reversal formula is one of the corpus's standard indictment-of-injustice idioms, especially in the wisdom-and-Psalmic literature: // **(1) Wisdom literature.** **Prov 17:13** — *meshiv ra'ah tachat tovah lo tamish ra'ah mi-beito* — 'whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house'. The wisdom-tradition's locus-classicus of the moral-reversal indictment, with the consequential-warning attached. // **(2) Psalter (the lament-psalms).** **Ps 35:12** — *yeshallemuni ra'ah tachat tovah shekhol le-nafshi* — 'they reward me evil for good, to the bereaving of my soul' (the persecuted-righteous's complaint); **Ps 38:21 [MT 38:20]** — *u-meshallemei ra'ah tachat tovah yistinuni tachat radoffi tov* — 'they that render evil for good are mine adversaries; because I follow the thing that is good'; **Ps 109:5** — *va-yasimu alai ra'ah tachat tovah ve-sin'ah tachat ahavati* — 'and they have rewarded me evil for good, and hatred for my love' (the imprecatory-psalm); **Ps 7:5 [MT 7:4]** (a related construction: *im gamalti sholmi ra* — 'if I have rewarded evil unto him that was at peace with me'). // **(3) Prophets.** **Jer 18:20** — *ha-yeshullam tachat tovah ra'ah, ki karu shuchah le-nafshi, zekhor amdi lefaneikha le-dabber aleihem tovah le-hashiv et chamatekha mehem* — 'shall evil be recompensed for good? for they have digged a pit for my soul. Remember how I stood before thee to speak good for them, and to turn away thy wrath from them' (Yirmiyahu's lament-prayer). The Yirmiyahu deployment is one of the corpus's most concentrated moral-reversal complaints. // **(4) Historical narratives.** **1 Sam 25:21** (David's reflection on Naval's response to his sheep-shearing-request: *akh la-sheqer shamarti et kol asher la-zeh ba-midbar... va-yashev-li ra'ah tachat tovah* — 'surely in vain have I kept all that this man hath in the wilderness... and he hath returned me evil for good'). The David-Naval scene is the historical-narrative anchor of the moral-reversal formula. // **The Gen 44:4 deployment force.** The construction at Gen 44:4 is the steward's accusation-on-Yosef's-behalf: the brothers have ALLEGEDLY received good (the silver replaced in their sacks, the noon-feast, the safe-return-promise) and have ALLEGEDLY repaid it with evil (the silver-cup theft). The allegation is of course false on its face — the brothers have not stolen the cup — but the irony cuts deeper: the brothers HAVE in fact repaid evil-for-good in the underlying Gen 37 transaction (Yosef was the dream-favored beloved-son who was sold into slavery by his brothers, a literal repayment-of-evil-for-good). The Gen 44:4 accusation, false on the immediate-occasion, is true on the deeper-history. The literary irony is sharp: the accusation that the brothers innocently deny (the cup-theft) is the metaphorical-replay of the brothers' actual-guilt that they have hidden for twenty-two years (the Gen 37 sale). Yehudah's eventual confession at v 16 (*ha-Elohim matza et-avon avadekha*, governed by the new central [`avon-iniquity-cross-corpus-keyword`](#avon-iniquity-cross-corpus-keyword) entry) implicitly acknowledges the deeper truth even while the surface-allegation is being responded to. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular formula in the Yosef-cycle; the cross-corpus 'evil-for-good' wisdom-and-Psalmic moral-reversal formula has substantial cross-corpus reach (Proverbs, Psalms, Jeremiah, 1 Samuel) and is noted as a promotion-path-seed for future Psalter / Proverbs / 1 Samuel translation activation. → **OVERLAY** for now, with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the cross-corpus 'evil-for-good' moral-reversal formula is verifiable; (c) the ASV-baseline 'wherefore have ye rewarded evil for good' is the direct rendering; (d) the *shalem* Piel-of-recompense + *tachat*-in-return-for + abstract-nouns construction is grammatically transparent. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *shalem* (Piel), *ra'ah*, *tachat*, *tovah*; BDB pp. 1022-1023 (shalem), 949 (ra'ah), 1066 (tachat), 373 (tovah); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 304; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 130; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 561; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 332; on the 'evil-for-good' moral-reversal formula in wisdom-literature: M. V. Fox *Proverbs 10-31* AB 2009 pp. 631-633 (on Prov 17:13); on the Psalter's moral-reversal complaints: H.-J. Kraus *Psalms 1-59* CC, 1988; on Jer 18:20: J. Bright *Jeremiah* AB 1965; on the 1 Sam 25 David-Naval scene: P. K. McCarter *1 Samuel* AB 1980 pp. 393-398.

terms.translit: be-hitvadda Yosef el-echav (the Hithpael infinitive of yada 'to know', here in the 'make oneself known / self-disclose' register; Gen 45:1)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Hithpael (reflexive-causative: to-cause-oneself-to-be-known, to-make-oneself-known); marked rare-form within the Yosef cycle
terms.literal: be-hitvadda — at the making-oneself-known / when [Yosef] made-himself-known [to his brothers]; the Hithpael of yada in the self-disclosure register
terms.standardEnglish: made himself known (ASV/KJV/NRSV); revealed himself (modern); disclosed himself (functional)
terms.wohChoice: made himself known (ASV-baseline preserved; the marked Hithpael's recognition-arc-inversion role with the Gen 42:7 hitnakker documented in commentary; sibling-link to `nakar-hitnakker-recognition-feigning-gen42`)
terms.rationale: **Gen 45:1 deploys the marked Hithpael of *yada* — *be-hitvadda Yosef el-echav* ('while Yosef made himself known unto his brethren') — as the chapter's disclosure-scene signature verb. The Hithpael of *yada* is rare across the HB and chapter-singular within the Yosef cycle: the construction is the explicit literary inverse of Gen 42:7's *va-yitnakker aleihem* ('made himself strange to them', the Hithpael of *nakar*, governed by the SIBLING overlay [`nakar-hitnakker-recognition-feigning-gen42`](#nakar-hitnakker-recognition-feigning-gen42)). The disclosure-scene's signature verb is therefore part of the cycle's recognition-and-feigning Hithpael-pair: *hitnakker* (recognition-withheld at Gen 42:7) → *hitvadda* (recognition-disclosed at Gen 45:1).** // **The lexeme.** The Hithpael of *yada* (יד״ע) is morphologically the reflexive-causative of the standard cognition-verb 'to know'. The Hithpael's force is precise: 'to cause oneself to be known', 'to make oneself known', 'to self-disclose'. The construction is grammatically transparent (the standard Hithpael reflexive-causative) but is rare in the HB: the only other close cross-corpus parallel in this specific sense is **Num 12:6** — the divine speech to Aharon and Miryam about the Mosheh-prophecy distinction: *im yihyeh nevi'akhem YHWH ba-mar'ah elav etvadda ba-chalom adabber bo* ('if there be a prophet among you, I YHWH will make myself known unto him in a vision, I will speak unto him in a dream'). The Num 12:6 deployment is the divine-self-disclosure to the prophet; the Hithpael names YHWH's own self-disclosure-through-vision as the medium of prophetic knowledge. The Gen 45:1 deployment is therefore in a register otherwise reserved (within this lexical-form) for divine-self-disclosure — Yosef's self-disclosure to the brothers is lexically marked by a construction the corpus typically uses for divine-self-revelation. The literary force is named scholarship observation (Sarna, Westermann, Sternberg): the verb's marked-rare-register lends the disclosure-scene a charge that resonates with the cycle's broader providential-reframing theology (at vv 5-8). // **The recognition-arc Hithpael-pair.** The cycle's recognition-arc deploys two Hithpael-stems at structurally-opposed moments. (a) **At Gen 42:7**, *va-yitnakker aleihem* (Hithpael of *nakar*, governed by the SIBLING overlay entry) marks Yosef's deliberate-concealment from the brothers: the recognition-withheld stem. The Hithpael of *nakar* is itself rare (only one other HB occurrence in this sense, at 1 Kgs 14:5-6, Achiyah and Yarov'am's wife). (b) **At Gen 45:1**, *be-hitvadda Yosef el-echav* (Hithpael of *yada*) marks Yosef's deliberate-self-disclosure to the brothers: the recognition-disclosed stem. The Hithpael of *yada* is similarly rare (only Num 12:6 in this register). The Hithpael-pair maps the recognition-arc's full reflexive-causative range — the deliberate-concealing at Gen 42 and the deliberate-disclosing at Gen 45 — at the cycle's two most-structurally-load-bearing moments. The Gen 42:7 / Gen 45:1 chapter-pair is one of the cycle's neatest lexical-architectures: at the moment the brothers first arrive in Mitsrayim, Yosef-the-shallit performs *hitnakker* (the active-concealing); at the moment the brothers' Yehudah-speech has finally collapsed Yosef's restraint, Yosef performs *hitvadda* (the active-disclosing). The two chapter-singular Hithpaels stand at the cycle's recognition-and-disclosure arc's structural extremes. // **Bidirectional sibling-link to `nakar-hitnakker-recognition-feigning-gen42`.** The two entries are deliberate companions per the sibling-overlay-entries pattern with bidirectional cross-reference. This entry names the Gen 42 sibling by id; the sibling entry's rationale has been extended to name this entry by id. The pair governs the cycle's recognition-arc Hithpael-stem structure (Gen 42 → 45). Both Hithpaels are chapter-singular within Genesis in their respective scenes; both are rare across the HB; both stand at structurally-load-bearing moments of the cycle's recognition-and-disclosure architecture. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular Hithpael-of-*yada* construction within Genesis (the only other HB occurrence of the Hithpael in this register is Num 12:6); the chapter-specific disclosure-scene deployment is here; the broader cross-corpus distribution of the lexeme *yada* is corpus-wide and governed by other contexts. → **OVERLAY** with bidirectional sibling-link to the companion entry. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the verb is morphologically explicit (Hithpael of *yada*); (b) the marked-rare-form status is verifiable (only Num 12:6 in this register); (c) the Gen 42:7 / Gen 45:1 chapter-pair is grammatically and structurally explicit; (d) the ASV-baseline 'made himself known' is the direct rendering. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *yada* (Hithpael); BDB p. 394; TDOT V:448-481; NIDOTTE 2:409-414; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 307; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 142; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 574; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 338; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 263-264; Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 8 (the recognition-arc reading); Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on Num 12:6's divine-self-disclosure register: B. A. Levine *Numbers 1-20* AB 1993 pp. 327-330.

terms.translit: nivhalu mi-panav (Niphal of bahal 'be terrified, dismayed, in confusion'; Gen 45:3 ve-lo yakhlu echav la-anot oto ki nivhalu mi-panav)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Niphal 3mp perfective (the standard Niphal-of-bahal register: be-dismayed, be-terrified, be-paralyzed-by-confusion, be-in-sudden-fear)
terms.literal: nivhalu mi-panav — they were dismayed / terrified / paralyzed from-his-presence; the brothers' speechlessness in the face of the disclosure
terms.standardEnglish: they were troubled at his presence (KJV); they were dismayed at his presence (ASV/NRSV); they were dumbfounded (NJPS); they were stunned (modern)
terms.wohChoice: they were dismayed at his presence (ASV-baseline preserved; the Niphal-of-bahal as the corpus's principal sudden-terror / paralyzing-dismay lexeme and the chapter's structural-inverse of Yehudah's just-completed surety-speech documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 45:3 stages the brothers' paralyzed response to Yosef's disclosure: *ve-lo yakhlu echav la-anot oto ki nivhalu mi-panav* — 'and his brethren could not answer him; for they were dismayed at his presence'. The Niphal of *bahal* (בהל) in the *nivhalu* construction is the standard HB lexeme for sudden-terror / paralyzing-dismay / inability-to-speak-or-act-from-shock. Chapter-singular within Genesis (the lexeme's only Genesis occurrence); corpus-wide elsewhere. The chapter's literary force is the structural-inverse of Yehudah's just-completed Gen 44:18-34 surety-speech: the speaker (Yehudah) of one of the corpus's most extended speeches has become the speechless-with-the-brothers in the disclosure-scene.** // **The lexeme.** *Bahal* (בהל) in the Niphal is the corpus's principal sudden-terror / paralyzing-dismay / sudden-confusion lexeme. The Niphal's semantic-core is the *passive-experiencing-of-being-dismayed* — the dismay is something that happens-to-the-experiencer, not something they consciously do. The lexeme's range covers the affective ('terror, dismay, alarm'), the cognitive ('confusion, bewilderment'), and the behavioral-result ('paralysis, inability to act or speak'). The construction *nivhal mi-pnei* + (someone) is the standard formula for being-dismayed-from-the-presence-of: the dismay is provoked-and-located-in-relation-to the dismay-causing-party. The construction's force at Gen 45:3 is the brothers' speechlessness *originating* in Yosef's *panim* ('face / presence'): not just generic-shock but the specific paralysis-from-encountering-Yosef-himself. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** *Bahal* (Niphal) is extensively distributed: **Exod 15:15** (the nations' dismay at the Exodus); **Judg 20:41**; **1 Sam 28:21**; **2 Sam 4:1** (Ish-boshet's dismay); **Ps 6:3, 11** (the lament's *bahal*-formula); **Ps 30:8**; **Ps 48:6**; **Ps 83:18 [MT 83:17]**; **Ps 90:7**; **Ps 104:29**; **Isa 13:8** (the Bavel-judgment's *u-tziryim ve-chavalim yochezun ka-yoledah yachilun, ish el re'ehu yitmahu, penei lehavim peneihem*); **Ezek 7:27**; **Job 4:5, 21:6, 23:15-16**; **Dan 11:44**. The lexeme is one of the principal Niphal-stem terror-verbs across the corpus. // **The chapter's literary force.** The narrative-architecture of the Gen 42-45 cycle deploys speech-and-silence as a structural pattern. The Gen 44:18-34 Yehudah-speech is one of the corpus's most extended sustained-speeches (seventeen verses of continuous direct-speech from Yehudah). At the disclosure-moment in Gen 45:1-3, the role-reversal is structural: Yosef speaks the disclosure (vv 3-4); the brothers, who had Yehudah-as-speaker just verses earlier, are now collectively speechless (*lo yakhlu... la-anot*). The lexeme *nivhalu* carries the specific affective load of the speechlessness-from-shock: the brothers do not answer because they cannot answer. The literary point (Alter, Sternberg, Sarna): the speech-arc of the cycle inverts at the disclosure — the brothers move from Yehudah's extended speech-act to collective speechlessness; Yosef moves from the steward-mediated test-speech to the direct disclosure-speech. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular within the active corpus (the lexeme's only Genesis occurrence); the cross-corpus distribution is extensive and would justify central housing when the broader corpus is in view (Psalter, Job, Isaiah, Ezekiel). The chapter's specific disclosure-scene paralysis-deployment is here; the broader cross-corpus *bahal*-vocabulary is noted as a strong promotion-seed for the eventual Psalter / Job / prophetic translations. → **OVERLAY** with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the verb is morphologically explicit (Niphal of *bahal*); (b) the *nivhal mi-pnei* + (person) construction is grammatically transparent; (c) the cross-corpus distribution is verifiable; (d) the ASV-baseline 'dismayed at his presence' is the consensus rendering; (e) the structural-inverse with Yehudah's Gen 44 speech is documented across the named scholarship. Named scholarship only. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *bahal*; BDB p. 96; TDOT II:3-5; NIDOTTE 1:609-610; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 308; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 142; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 574; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 264; on the speech-arc / speechlessness-arc of the disclosure-scene: M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 8; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975.

terms.translit: mekhartem oti (Qal 2mp perfective of makhar 'to sell'; Gen 45:4 asher-mekhartem oti Mitzraymah; Gen 45:5 ki-mekhartem oti hennah)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb, Qal perfective; the transactional-sale lexeme deployed in Yosef's own verbal-naming of the Gen 37 sale at the disclosure-scene
terms.literal: mekhartem oti — ye sold me; the brothers' Gen 37 transaction-of-the-brother as Yosef now names it at the disclosure
terms.standardEnglish: ye sold (ASV/KJV/NRSV); you sold (NJPS); sold (modern)
terms.wohChoice: ye sold (ASV-baseline preserved; the Yosef-cycle's makhar-arc Gen 37:27 + 28 + 36 → Gen 45:4-5 as the cycle's transactional-moral-keyword documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 45:4 and 45:5 deploy the Qal of *makhar* ('to sell') in Yosef's own verbal-naming of the Gen 37 sale: at v 4 *ani Yosef achikhem asher-mekhartem oti Mitzraymah* ('I am Yosef your brother, whom ye sold into Mitsrayim'); at v 5 *al-tea'tzevu ve-al-yichar be-eineikhem ki-mekhartem oti hennah* ('be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither'). The lexeme is one of the Yosef-cycle's central transactional-keywords. The cycle's *makhar*-arc traces: Gen 37:27 (Yehudah's proposal: *lekhu ve-nimkerennu la-Yishme'elim*); Gen 37:28 (the brothers' execution: *va-yimkeru et Yosef la-Yishme'elim*); Gen 37:36 (Potifar's purchase: *u-Medanim makheru oto el-Mitzrayim*); now at Gen 45:4-5 Yosef explicitly names the action with the same verb. The cycle's moral-keyword arc — sale-of-the-brother (Gen 37) → providential-reframing-without-erasure (Gen 45) — is anchored at the cycle's lexical-repetition of *makhar*.** // **The lexeme.** *Makhar* (מכר) is one of the corpus's principal transactional / commercial / sale lexemes. The Qal-stem covers the standard sale-of-property / sale-of-person register; the Niphal is the passive 'to be sold'. The lexeme's distribution is extensive: the slave-law texts (Exod 21:7-8; 21:16; 22:1-2; the Deuteronomic slave-laws); the H-Code's land-law and Jubilee-system (Lev 25:14-15; 25:23-50); the prophets' indictments (1 Sam 12:9, Judg 2:14, Joel 4:3, Amos 2:6 — the famous indictment *al-mikhram ba-kesef tzaddiq*, 'because they sold the righteous for silver'); the post-exilic literature (Neh 5:8 — the redemption-from-sale formula); the Esther 7:4 famous 'we are sold' formula. The lexeme's cycle-wide reach makes the Yosef-cycle's deployment one of its earliest patriarchal-narrative anchor-occurrences. // **The cycle's makhar-arc.** The cycle's lexical-architecture of the sale is precise. At Gen 37:27 Yehudah proposes the sale-not-killing as the merciful-alternative: *lekhu ve-nimkerennu la-Yishme'elim... ki-achinu vesarenu hu* ('come, and let us sell him to the Yishme'elim... for he is our brother and our flesh'). The proposal frames the sale as preserving-the-brother-from-fratricide. At Gen 37:28 the execution of the proposal is recorded: *va-yimkeru et Yosef la-Yishme'elim be-esrim kasef* ('and they sold Yosef to the Yishme'elim for twenty pieces of silver') — the twenty-shekel slave-price governed by the overlay [`twenty-kesef-slave-price-yosef-sale`](#twenty-kesef-slave-price-yosef-sale). At Gen 37:36 the cycle's first phase closes with the Mitsrayim-resale: *u-Medanim makheru oto el-Mitzrayim le-Potifar* ('and the Medanim sold him into Mitsrayim unto Potifar'). The literary point is that Yosef's providential-reframing does not erase the action's moral-weight: he names the sale (twice) before he names the providential-purpose. The construction is the chapter's affective-pivot: the brothers' guilt-response is named and addressed before the providential-reframing-formula is articulated.** // **The *atzav* root and its Gen cross-cycle echoes.** The Niphal of *atzav* names the experience of being-grieved / pained / pained-with-regret. The root *atzav* / *itzavon* recurs at structurally-significant Gen-cycle moments: **Gen 3:16** (the woman's labor *itzavon* — the post-Eden pain of childbirth: *ha-rbah arbeh itzvonekh ve-heronekh, be-etzev teldi vanim*); **Gen 3:17** (the ground's *itzavon* — the post-Eden pain of agricultural labor: *be-itzavon tochalennah kol yemei chayyekha*); **Gen 5:29** (Lemekh's etymology of Noach: *zeh yenachamenu mi-ma'aseinu u-me-itzvon yadeinu min-ha-adamah asher er'rah YHWH*, 'this one shall comfort us concerning our work and the toil of our hands, because of the ground which YHWH hath cursed'); **Gen 6:6** (the climactic anthropopathism: *va-yinnachem YHWH ki-asah et ha-adam ba-aretz va-yit'atzev el libbo*, 'and it repented YHWH that he had made the human in the earth, and it grieved him at his heart'). The semantic-effect at Gen 45:5: Yosef tells the brothers not to be angry-with-themselves / not to let-anger-burn-against-themselves in their own self-assessment. The combination *al-tea'tzevu* + *al-yichar be-eineikhem* covers the full self-assessment range: do not grieve (the emotional pain), do not be angry-with-yourselves (the moral self-condemnation). The emotional-discharge is comprehensive. // **The literary force.** The construction's placement is structurally precise: Yosef names the sale (*ki-mekhartem oti hennah*) at v 5a, deploys the emotional-discharge-instruction (*al-tea'tzevu ve-al-yichar be-eineikhem*) at v 5b, and articulates the providential-purpose (*ki le-michyah shelachani Elohim lifneikhem*) at v 5c.
