terms.translit: va-yomer Yisra'el (Gen 45:28; the chapter's name-pivot from Ya'aqov vv 25, 27, 27 to Yisra'el v 28)
terms.partOfSpeech: narrative-internal name-shift; the chapter-internal pivot from the patriarchal-aetiology name Ya'aqov to the covenantal-name Yisra'el at the moment of acceptance-and-determination
terms.literal: va-yomer Yisra'el — and Yisra'el said; the chapter-closing speech-attribution under the covenantal-name, distinct from the v 25 / v 27 chapter-narration under Ya'aqov
terms.standardEnglish: Israel said (ASV/KJV/NRSV/NJPS — preserving the source's name)
terms.wohChoice: Yisra'el said (the source's name preserved per the WoH proper-name convention; the chapter-internal Ya'aqov/Yisra'el name-shift literary observation and the source-critical reading documented in commentary)
terms.rationale:
**Gen 45:28 marks the chapter's narrative-pivot from the Ya'aqov-name (vv 25 *el-Ya'aqov avihem*, v 27 *ruach Ya'aqov avihem* twice) to the Yisra'el-name (v 28 *va-yomer Yisra'el*): 'and Yisra'el said, It is enough; Yosef my son is yet alive: I will go and see him before I die'. The name-shift is a marked literary observation: the patriarch's acceptance-of-the-news and his determination-to-go is voiced under the Yisra'el-name (the covenantal-name granted at Gen 32:29 [MT 32:29] + 35:10), not the Ya'aqov-name (the patriarchal-aetiology name from Gen 25:26). The Yisra'el-name resumes the patriarchal-resolve register. The chapter's narrative-pivot at v 28 — from grief-stricken-Ya'aqov to determined-Yisra'el — is one of the cycle's principal Ya'aqov/Yisra'el-alternation moments and is documented as a classic literary observation across mainstream commentaries (von Rad, Sarna, Alter, Brueggemann, Westermann).** // **The Ya'aqov / Yisra'el name-alternation pattern.** The corpus's Ya'aqov / Yisra'el name-alternation is one of its most-studied source-critical and literary observations. The patriarch carries two names: (i) **Ya'aqov** (יַעֲקֹב) — the birth-name, from the aetiology *aqev* (Gen 25:26, 27:36) — the heel-grabber / supplanter; (ii) **Yisra'el** (יִשְׂרָאֵל) — the covenantal-name, granted at Penuel (Gen 32:29 [MT 32:29], the J / E aetiology *sarita im-Elohim ve-im-anashim*, governed by the existing overlay [`yisrael-name-aetiology-sarah-im-elohim`](#yisrael-name-aetiology-sarah-im-elohim)) and re-granted at Beit-El (Gen 35:10, the P doublet-aetiology, governed by the existing overlay [`yisrael-second-renaming-beit-el-p-doublet`](#yisrael-second-renaming-beit-el-p-doublet)). The two names persist in alternating use across the rest of the cycle (Gen 32-50) without either supplanting the other definitively. The pattern's interpretive readings: (a) the **source-critical** reading treats the alternation as evidence of the cycle's composite-composition — J / E preferring different names at different points, P / R-editorial layers harmonizing only partially. (b) The **literary** reading treats the alternation as deliberate-modulation: the patriarch is named Ya'aqov in scenes foregrounding his patriarchal-vulnerability / grief / supplanting-cunning, and Yisra'el in scenes foregrounding his covenantal-determination / divine-encounter / patriarchal-authority. The two readings are not mutually-exclusive: the cycle's compositional-history may have produced an alternation that the final-form editor has shaped into a literary-meaningful pattern. // **The chapter's name-shift.** The chapter-internal narrative uses Ya'aqov consistently through vv 25, 27, 27 — *el-Ya'aqov avihem* (v 25, the brothers' return-to-the-father); *ruach Ya'aqov avihem* (v 27, the spirit-revival). At v 28 the name shifts: *va-yomer Yisra'el* (the speech-attribution under the covenantal-name). The shift coincides with the patriarch's acceptance-of-the-impossible-news and his determination-to-act (the *elkha ve-er'enu be-terem amut* speech, 'I will go and see him before I die'). The shift's literary force is named (Sarna, Alter, von Rad, Westermann, Brueggemann): the grief-stricken-and-disbelieving patriarch of vv 25-27 is named Ya'aqov; the determined-and-acting patriarch of v 28 is named Yisra'el. The covenantal-name resumes at the moment of patriarchal-resolve. The pattern is consistent with the cycle's broader alternation: scenes of patriarchal-acceptance and resolve tend to use Yisra'el (Gen 46:1-2, 47:27-31, 48:2, 49:1-2); scenes of patriarchal-grief or familial-relationship tend to use Ya'aqov. // **The cross-cycle parallel name-shifts.** The pattern recurs at structurally-significant moments after Gen 45:28: **Gen 46:1-2** — the descent-prologue: *va-yissa Yisra'el ve-khol asher-lo... va-yomer Elohim le-Yisra'el be-mar'ot ha-laylah va-yomer Ya'aqov Ya'aqov va-yomer hineni* — the Yisra'el-name in the action-of-departure verses, the Ya'aqov-name in the divine-address (the deity calls the patriarch by the older name); **Gen 47:27-31** — the post-settlement section: *va-yeshev Yisra'el be-eretz Mitzrayim be-eretz Goshen va-ye'achzu vah va-yifru va-yirbu me'od* — Yisra'el in the settlement-context; **Gen 48:2** — the blessing-of-Yosef's-sons: *va-yaggeid le-Ya'aqov va-yomer hinneh binkha Yosef ba elekha va-yitchazzeq Yisra'el va-yeshev al ha-mittah* — the Ya'aqov / Yisra'el alternation within a single verse (Ya'aqov-the-patient, Yisra'el-the-strengthened-and-blessing); **Gen 49:1-2** — the deathbed-blessings: *va-yiqra Ya'aqov el-banav... shim'u el-Yisra'el avikhem* — the Ya'aqov-as-caller, Yisra'el-as-prophetic-blessor distinction within a single passage. The alternation-pattern is a load-bearing structural feature of the cycle. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific name-shift literary observation; the broader cycle-wide Ya'aqov/Yisra'el alternation is a load-bearing source-critical / literary observation across the cycle and is potentially a central-candidate for cycle-wide treatment. The chapter-anchored Gen 45:28 acceptance-pivot is here. → **OVERLAY** as the chapter-specific deployment with the cycle-wide pattern documented. The broader pattern flagged as a potential future cycle-wide central entry. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the name-shift is a literary-and-source-critical observation rather than a lexical-decision (the names themselves are uncontested; the shift's literary-significance is interpretive); (b) the cycle's broader alternation-pattern admits both source-critical and literary readings; (c) the v 28 acceptance-pivot reading is documented across modern critical scholarship as the consensus literary-observation; (d) the source's name is preserved on the surface per the WoH proper-name convention; the interpretive observation is documented in the rationale. Named scholarship only; no project synthesis. // **Scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 311; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 147; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 583; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 265; on the cycle's Ya'aqov/Yisra'el alternation: G. von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972; W. Brueggemann *Genesis* Interpretation 1982 pp. 348-350; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on the source-critical readings of the alternation: J. Wellhausen *Prolegomena* 1883; S. R. Driver *Introduction to the Literature of the OT* 1913; R. E. Friedman *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003; on the literary readings: M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 8.

**Cross-reference (the Gen 46:1-2-5 name-shift sibling-overlay link).** The chapter-46 continuation of the Ya'aqov/Yisra'el name-shift pattern is governed by the sibling overlay-entry [`yaaqov-yisrael-name-shift-cycle-wide-pattern-gen46`](#yaaqov-yisrael-name-shift-cycle-wide-pattern-gen46). The chapter-46 distribution: v 1 *va-yissa Yisra'el ve-khol asher-lo va-yavo Be'erah Shava*; v 2 *va-yomer Elohim le-Yisra'el be-mar'ot ha-laylah va-yomer Ya'aqov Ya'aqov*; v 5 *va-yaqom Ya'aqov mi-Be'er Shava... va-yisu vnei-Yisra'el et-Ya'aqov avihem*; v 8 *ve-eleh shmot bnei-Yisra'el ha-ba'im Mitzraymah Ya'aqov u-vanav*. The chapter-46 distribution is the cycle's densest single-chapter alternation-cluster: the patriarch is Yisra'el in the action-of-departure and the people-named-collective registers, and Ya'aqov in the divine-address (the doubled-call) and in the genealogy-of-his-own-line. The bidirectional cross-reference jointly tracks the cycle-wide alternation pattern across Gen 45-46; the future Gen 47-50 chapters will continue the pattern and may justify promotion to a cycle-wide central entry.

terms.translit: Be'erah Shava (Gen 46:1 va-yavo Be'erah Shava; v 5 va-yaqom Ya'aqov mi-Be'er Shava)
terms.partOfSpeech: toponym (locative); the cross-patriarchal stopping-point Be'er-Sheva at the chapter's departure-narrative
terms.literal: Be'erah Shava — to Be'er-Sheva; the toponym of the patriarchal node at the southern Negev where the patriarchs stop, build altars, encounter the deity, and depart
terms.standardEnglish: to Beersheba (ASV/KJV/NJPS/NRSV); to Beer-sheba (alternative)
terms.wohChoice: to Be'er-Sheva (WoH proper-name transliteration with hyphen; the cross-patriarchal-stopping-point literary observation documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:1 and 46:5 deploy the toponym Be'er-Sheva at the chapter's pivotal opening: Ya'aqov journeys to Be'er-Sheva, offers sacrifices to the Elohim of his father Yitzchaq, receives the night-vision theophany authorizing the descent, and rises from Be'er-Sheva for the journey to Mitsrayim. The Be'er-Sheva deployment is editorially-deliberate: the same site has functioned as a cross-patriarchal stopping-point across the cycle, with Avraham, Yitzchaq, and Ya'aqov all making major departure-and-encounter moves from / at the site. The Gen 46:1 stopping-and-sacrifice immediately before leaving the land closes the patriarchal-Be'er-Sheva node deliberately.** // **The cross-patriarchal Be'er-Sheva cluster.** **(a) Gen 21:33** — Avraham plants the *eshel* (tamarisk) at Be'er-Sheva and calls on YHWH El Olam (*va-yiqra sham be-shem YHWH El Olam*); the site is named at v 31 from the *shvua*-oath between Avraham and Avimelekh (with the *sheva*-seven-lambs / *shvua*-oath wordplay). **(b) Gen 26:23-25** — Yitzchaq goes up from Gerar to Be'er-Sheva (*va-ya'al mi-sham Be'er Shava*); YHWH appears to him *ba-laylah ha-hu* (in that night) with the *anokhi Elohei Avraham avikha al-tira ki-itkha anokhi* compound formula (governed by `anokhi-elohei-X-avikha-ancestral-god-formula` and `al-tira-fear-not-divine-encouragement-formula`); Yitzchaq builds an altar and calls on the name of YHWH; the well-digging-tradition continues. **(c) Gen 28:10** — Ya'aqov leaves Be'er-Sheva for Charan: *va-yetze Ya'aqov mi-Be'er Shava va-yelekh Charanah*; the chapter's opening before the Beit-El stairway-vision; the departure-from-Be'er-Sheva inaugurates Ya'aqov's twenty-year Aram-exile. **(d) Gen 46:1 (here)** — Ya'aqov returns to Be'er-Sheva for the final departure: *va-yissa Yisra'el ve-khol asher-lo va-yavo Be'erah Shava va-yizbach zvachim le-Elohei aviv Yitzchaq* ('and Yisra'el took his journey with all that he had, and came to Be'er-Sheva, and offered sacrifices unto the Elohim of his father Yitzchaq'). The deployment closes the Be'er-Sheva node: Avraham planted there; Yitzchaq encountered the deity there; Ya'aqov departed from there at the start of the Aram-period and now stops there at the end of his life-in-Kena'an. The chapter's literary architecture is therefore a deliberate-closure of the cross-patriarchal-Be'er-Sheva node. // **The wider HB Be'er-Sheva tradition.** The Be'er-Sheva toponym recurs across the corpus: **Josh 15:28; 19:2** (the tribal-allocation); **Judg 20:1; 1 Sam 3:20; 2 Sam 3:10; 17:11; 24:2, 7, 15; 1 Kgs 4:25; 2 Kgs 12:1** (the *mi-Dan ve-ad Be'er Shava* / 'from Dan to Be'er-Sheva' formula naming the territorial-extent of Israel); **1 Sam 8:2** (Shemu'el's sons judging at Be'er-Sheva); **1 Kgs 19:3** (Eliyahu fleeing to Be'er-Sheva). The prophetic-tradition's Be'er-Sheva-pilgrimage-shrine indictments: **Amos 5:5** (*ve-Be'er Shava lo ta'avoru*, 'do not pass through to Be'er-Sheva' — the prophet's indictment of pilgrimage-to-shrines); **Amos 8:14** (*chei derekh Be'er Shava*, the swearing-by-the-way-of-Be'er-Sheva). The post-exilic redeployment at **Neh 11:27, 30**. The Be'er-Sheva toponym is therefore one of the corpus's most-deployed patriarchal-and-monarchical southern-border toponyms. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific cross-patriarchal-node observation; the Gen 21:33 / 26:23-25 / 28:10 / 46:1 cluster is the patriarchal-Be'er-Sheva node; the wider 1 Sam / Amos / Neh reception is documented as cross-corpus reach; the Amos 5:5 / 8:14 prophetic-pilgrimage-shrine indictments flagged as promotion-seed for the Amos translation. → **OVERLAY** with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the toponym is morphologically explicit; (b) the cross-patriarchal cluster is HB-internal-explicit (the four chapters' deployments are documentary); (c) the wider HB Be'er-Sheva distribution is exhaustively verifiable; (d) the cross-cycle literary-architecture observation is documented across mainstream scholarship (Cassuto, Sarna, Westermann, Sternberg, Wenham). // **Scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 311-312; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 153-154; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 587-589; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 pp. 440-441; on the Be'er-Sheva archaeology: Z. Herzog 'Tel Beersheba' *NEAEHL* 1993 vol. 1 pp. 167-173; on the Amos 5:5 / 8:14 prophetic-indictments: J. L. Mays *Amos* OTL 1969; on the cross-patriarchal-Be'er-Sheva cluster as a deliberate literary-architecture: U. Cassuto *Commentary on the Book of Genesis* II 1964 / ET 1974; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308.

terms.translit: be-mar'ot ha-laylah (Gen 46:2)
terms.partOfSpeech: construct-chain (preposition-bet + plural construct noun mar'ot + definite-article + noun ha-laylah); the night-vision technical-term
terms.literal: be-mar'ot ha-laylah — in the visions of the night; the night-vision technical-term for the apocalyptic / theophanic / divinatory vision-experience
terms.standardEnglish: in the visions of the night (ASV/KJV/NJPS/NRSV — uncontested as the construction is grammatically transparent)
terms.wohChoice: in the visions of the night (ASV-baseline; the construction's cross-corpus distribution as the fixed night-vision technical-term documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:2 deploys the construction *be-mar'ot ha-laylah* ('in the visions of the night') as the introduction to the deity's address to Ya'aqov at Be'er-Sheva. The plural-construct *mar'ot* (from *mar'ah*, 'vision') with the definite-articled *ha-laylah* names a marked night-vision experience: the construction is a fixed technical-term for the apocalyptic / theophanic / divinatory vision-experience, recurring across the corpus in similar contexts. The Gen 46:2 deployment is the only Genesis occurrence of the specific *mar'ot ha-laylah* construction; the cross-corpus distribution concentrates in the apocalyptic and wisdom literature (Daniel, Job).** // **The lexeme.** The noun *mar'ah* (מַרְאָה) covers (a) the vision-experience (the seeing-event), (b) the appearance / look (of a thing or person), (c) the prophetic-vision (in the technical-prophetic register). The construction *mar'ot ha-laylah* names the night-vision specifically — the deity's speaking-to-the-prophet-in-a-night-vision technical-context. The plural-construct *mar'ot* (rather than singular *mar'eh*) is editorially-marked: the multiple-visions-of-the-night construction names the vision-experience as belonging to a larger class of night-visions. // **The cross-corpus distribution.** // **(a) Genesis** — only Gen 46:2 (the chapter's deployment, the only Genesis occurrence of the specific *mar'ot ha-laylah* construction). // **(b) Daniel — the apocalyptic concentration.** **Dan 2:19** — Dan 2 closes the king's-dream-and-its-interpretation arc with Daniel's reception: *be-chezvah di leiliya* (the Aramaic equivalent: *in a vision of the night*). The Aramaic *chezvei leiliya* is the direct parallel to the Hebrew *mar'ot ha-laylah*. **Dan 7:7** — *chazeh havayt be-chezvei leiliya* ('I saw in the night visions'); Dan 7's apocalyptic-beast-vision opens with the formula. **Dan 7:13** — *chazeh havayt be-chezvei leiliya va-aru im-anenei shemaya ke-bar-enash atah hava*; Dan 7's son-of-man vision deploys the formula again. The Daniel-cluster's three deployments make the apocalyptic night-vision construction the book's signature divine-disclosure marker. // **(c) Job — the wisdom-and-suffering tradition.** **Job 4:13** — *bi-se'ifim me-chezyonot laylah bi-nfol tardemah al-anashim* ('in thoughts from the visions of the night, when deep sleep falleth on men'). Eliphaz's first-speech opens with the night-vision experience of seeing the spectral-figure. **Job 33:15** — *ba-chalom chezyon laylah bi-nfol tardemah al-anashim bi-tnumot alei mishkav* ('in a dream, in a vision of the night, when deep sleep falleth upon men, in slumberings upon the bed'). Elihu's night-vision teaching, paralleling Eliphaz's Job 4 formulation. // **(d) Isaiah** — **Isa 29:7** — *ve-hayah ka-chalom chezon laylah hamon kol-ha-goyim* ('it shall be as a dream of a night vision, the multitude of all the nations'). The eschatological-judgment passage's analogue. // **The pattern's literary force.** The night-vision technical-term marks the deity's-disclosure as belonging to a specific genre of nocturnal-divine-experience: the deity-speaking-to-the-prophet-at-night via vision. The genre is distinct from (a) the dream-narrative-revelation (the *chalom* genre — Yosef's dreams Gen 37, 40, 41; Avimelekh's dream Gen 20; the Mesopotamian-court-divination-tradition), (b) the daytime-theophany (the *va-yera el* type-scene), (c) the prophetic-trance-vision (the *machazeh* genre — Avram's Gen 15 vision-by-day). The night-vision genre is editorially-distinct: the deity speaks in night-visions to communicate decisions of major covenantal / apocalyptic / eschatological weight. The Gen 46:2 deployment fits the genre: the deity's authorization of the descent to Mitsrayim is communicated in a night-vision, marking the moment as belonging to the high-formality theophanic-disclosure register. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific Genesis-deployment of the night-vision formula; the cross-corpus reach into Daniel, Job, Isaiah is documentary but the Genesis-internal singularity makes this the chapter-anchored entry. Promotion-seed for the eventual Daniel / Job translations: the construction's apocalyptic-concentration makes it a natural cross-corpus central candidate when those texts are translated. → **OVERLAY** with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the cross-corpus distribution (Dan 2, 7; Job 4, 33; Isa 29) is exhaustively verifiable; (c) the night-vision genre-distinction is documented across the standard scholarship (Cassuto, Sarna, Westermann, Westermann's Genre-criticism). // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *mar'ah*; BDB pp. 909-910; TDOT IX:208-226 (on the cluster of seeing-and-vision lexemes); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 312; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 154-155; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 587-588; Cassuto *Commentary on the Book of Genesis* II 1964 / ET 1974; on the Daniel night-vision cluster: J. J. Collins *Daniel* Hermeneia 1993; on Job 4 + 33: D. J. A. Clines *Job 1-20* WBC 1989, *Job 21-37* WBC 2006; on the broader night-vision / dream-genre distinction: M. Lichtenstein 'Dream-Theophany and the E Document' JANES 1969; F. Husser *Dreams and Dream Narratives in the Biblical World* 1999.

terms.translit: ha-El (Gen 46:3 anokhi ha-El Elohei avikha, 'I am the El, the Elohim of thy father')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun (proper noun / divine name El) with definite article; the definite-articled form of El, marked relative to the standard anarthrous El and the standard Elohim
terms.literal: ha-El — the El; the definite-articled divine-name form, syntactically marked
terms.standardEnglish: I am God (ASV/KJV — flattening the ha-El definite-article); I am El (NJPS — preserving the El divine-name); the God (NRSV — capitalizing the definite-article)
terms.wohChoice: I am the El (WoH preserves *El* in transliteration per the divine-name convention with the definite article rendered as 'the El'; the *ha-El* form's editorial-markedness documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:3 deploys the construction *anokhi ha-El Elohei avikha* ('I am the El, the Elohim of thy father') with the definite-articled form *ha-El*. The form is editorially-marked: the standard anarthrous *El* (as in *El Shaddai*, *El Elyon*, *El Roi*, *El Olam* — the patriarchal compound-divine-names) and the standard *Elohim* (the most-common divine-designation) both lack the definite article; the *ha-El* form is restricted to a specific cluster of HB occurrences in the patriarchal-narratives and the Psalter and represents a marked-form syntactically. The construction here is paired with the *Elohei avikha* ancestral-god-formula (governed by the central [`anokhi-elohei-X-avikha-ancestral-god-formula`](#anokhi-elohei-X-avikha-ancestral-god-formula)), creating a doubled-divine-name-formula at the chapter's covenantal-foundational verse.** // **The *ha-El* cluster.** The definite-articled *ha-El* form has a tightly-restricted cross-corpus distribution: // **(a) Genesis** — **Gen 31:13** (the dream-of-Ya'aqov in Paddan-Aram: *anokhi ha-El Beit-El asher mashachta sham matzevah*, 'I am the El of Beit-El, where thou anointedst a pillar'); **Gen 35:1** (the deity to Ya'aqov: *kum aleh Beit-El... ve-aseh sham mizbeach la-El ha-nireh elekha be-vorchakha mi-pnei Esav achikha*, 'arise, go up to Beit-El... and make there an altar unto the El who appeared unto thee when thou fleddest from the face of Esav thy brother'); **Gen 35:3** (Ya'aqov's report: *la-El ha-oneh oti be-yom tzarati*, 'unto the El who answered me in the day of my distress'); **Gen 46:3 (here)**. The four Genesis-internal occurrences cluster in the Ya'aqov-cycle (Gen 31-46), making the form the cycle's distinctive marked-divine-name register. // **(b) Psalter — the densest concentration.** **Ps 18:31, 33** (and parallel **2 Sam 22:31, 33** — the David-thanksgiving): *ha-El tamim darko* (v 31) and *ha-El ha-me'azzereni chayil* (v 33), 'the El whose way is perfect' / 'the El who girdeth me with strength'. The double-deployment in a single Psalm marks the *ha-El* form as the Psalter's high-formality divine-designation in the thanksgiving-psalm register. **Ps 68:20-21** (the divine-victory psalm: *ha-El lanu El le-moshaot u-le-YHWH Adonai la-mavet totza'ot*, 'the El is to us an El of deliverances; and unto YHWH the Lord belong the issues from death'). **Ps 77:14** (the lament of Asaph: *Elohim ba-qodesh darkekha mi El gadol ke-Elohim*). The Psalter deployment establishes the *ha-El* form as a recognized high-register divine-designation. // **(c) Job — the wisdom-and-suffering tradition.** **Job 8:3** (Bildad's first speech: *ha-El ye'avet mishpat ve-im-Shaddai ye'avet tzedek*, 'doth the El pervert judgment? or doth Shaddai pervert justice?'); **Job 22:13** (Eliphaz's third speech: *ve-amarta mah-yada El ha-va'ad arafel yishpot*, 'and thou sayest, how doth the El know? can he judge through the dark cloud?'). The Job deployment recurs in the friends' speeches, in the contested-divine-justice register. // **(d) Isaiah** — **Isa 42:5** (the deutero-Isaian foundational divine-self-naming: *koh-amar ha-El YHWH bore ha-shamayim ve-noteihem rokah ha-aretz ve-tze'etza'eha*, 'thus saith the El YHWH, who created the heavens, and stretched them out; he that spread forth the earth, and that which cometh out of it'). The Isa 42:5 deployment is one of the deutero-Isaian's most-load-bearing divine-self-naming verses and combines the *ha-El* form with the YHWH-name and the cosmological-creator predication. // **The Gen 46:3 deployment's compound-formula force.** The verse combines: (a) the *anokhi* emphatic-pronoun (the canonical divine-self-disclosure opener; cf. Exod 20:2 Decalogue's *anokhi YHWH*); (b) the *ha-El* definite-articled El-form; (c) the *Elohei avikha* ancestral-god-formula (governed by `anokhi-elohei-X-avikha-ancestral-god-formula`). The verse is therefore a triple-compound divine-self-disclosure: the deity is named (i) by the emphatic pronoun, (ii) by the *ha-El* form, (iii) by the ancestral-genealogical formula. The construction is structurally one of the densest divine-self-disclosure verses in the patriarchal-narratives, paralleling Gen 26:24's four-formula compound (the entry's existing rationale documents the four-formula compound there). // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific deployment in the Ya'aqov-cycle's marked-divine-name cluster (Gen 31:13 + 35:1, 3 + 46:3); the cross-corpus reach into the Psalter / Job / Isaiah is documented but the cluster is overlay-anchored. Promotion-seed for the eventual Psalter / Job / Isaiah translations: the *ha-El* form is a recognized cross-corpus marked-form that could justify central treatment when those texts are translated. → **OVERLAY** with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the form is morphologically explicit (definite-article + El); (b) the cross-corpus *ha-El* cluster is exhaustively verifiable; (c) the form's syntactic-markedness is documented across the standard lexica (HALOT, BDB, TDOT s.v. El) and grammars; (d) the four Genesis-internal Ya'aqov-cycle occurrences are documentary; (e) the named scholarship documents the form's register (Cross, Sarna, Westermann, Cassuto). // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *El*; BDB pp. 41-44; TDOT I:242-261; NIDOTTE 1:400-401; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 313; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 155; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 588; Cassuto *Commentary on the Book of Genesis* II 1964 / ET 1974; on the *ha-El* form as the patriarchal-El-cult marker: F. M. Cross *Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic* 1973 ch. 1 (the Ugaritic-El-cult identification); A. Alt *Der Gott der Väter* 1929 (the ancestral-god reconstruction); M. S. Smith *The Early History of God* 1990/2002; on the Psalter deployment: H.-J. Kraus *Psalms 1-59* + *Psalms 60-150* CC 1988-89; on the Job deployment: D. J. A. Clines *Job 1-20* WBC 1989; on the Isa 42:5 deployment: J. L. Koole *Isaiah III* HCOT 1997-2001.

terms.translit: yashit yado al-eineikha (Gen 46:4)
terms.strongs: H7896 (shit, 'to put, place') + H3027 (yad, 'hand') + H5869 (ayin, dual eineikha, 'eyes')
terms.partOfSpeech: verb (qal impf 3ms) + noun-with-3ms-suffix + preposition + noun-dual-construct-with-2ms-suffix; the close-the-eyes-at-death formula
terms.literal: yashit yado al-eineikha — he will put his hand upon thine eyes; the close-the-eyes-at-death formula naming Yosef's gesture at Ya'aqov's death-bed
terms.standardEnglish: shall put his hand upon thine eyes (ASV/KJV); shall close your eyes (NJPS — modernized); will close your eyes (NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: shall put his hand upon thine eyes (ASV-baseline; the close-the-eyes-at-death formula and its chapter-singular HB occurrence documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:4 closes the deity's address to Ya'aqov at Be'er-Sheva with a tender personal-promise: *ve-Yosef yashit yado al-eineikha* ('and Yosef shall put his hand upon thine eyes'). The construction names the close-the-eyes-at-death gesture: the elder, on dying, has the closest family-member close his eyes at the moment of death — a ritual gesture marking the death-and-burial transition. The Gen 46:4 occurrence is the only HB instance of this specific construction; the broader patriarchal-death-rite preview is documented in the wider context (Gen 50:1 *va-yippol Yosef al-pnei aviv va-yevk alav va-yishshaq lo*, 'Yosef fell upon his father's face, and wept upon him, and kissed him'). The promise functions as a tender-personal-detail in the deity's covenantal-address: not only will the deity descend with Ya'aqov and bring him back up, but Yosef — the lost-and-found son — will be the one to close his father's eyes at death.** // **The lexeme.** The verb *shit* (Qal: 'to put, place, set') is the standard HB verb for placing-an-object-on-or-against-a-surface. The construction *shit yad al* + (object) names the placing-of-the-hand on/upon the object; here the object is *eineikha* (thine eyes, dual-construct). The phrase deploys the standard HB construction for the close-the-eyes-at-death gesture. The verb's deployment elsewhere covers (a) placing-the-hand-in-blessing (Gen 48:14 *va-yishlach Yisra'el et-yemino va-yashit al-rosh Ephraim*, the blessing-gesture by hand-placement); (b) placing-the-foot-on-the-conquered (Josh 10:24); (c) general object-placement. The Gen 46:4 construction is therefore a specific-application of the general placing-verb in the death-bed-ritual register. // **The cross-cultural ANE close-the-eyes-at-death gesture.** The close-the-eyes-at-death gesture is well-attested across the ancient Near East. The Egyptian-tradition's *opening-of-the-mouth* ritual at burial includes a related eye-related gesture (the *opening* counterpart of the *closing*); the Mesopotamian-and-Levantine death-rituals attest to the close-the-eyes gesture as the eldest-son's-duty. The HB deployment at Gen 46:4 fits the ANE-cultural context. The verse's literary point is that Yosef — though geographically distant in Mitsrayim and absent from the family for twenty-two years — will be present at the death and perform the eldest-son-ritual (Yosef being the firstborn of Rachel, the favored-wife, and now the elevated-vizier). The promise resolves the chapter-internal tension: Ya'aqov can descend to Mitsrayim because Yosef will be there to perform the death-ritual when the time comes. // **The Gen 50:1 fulfilment.** The Gen 46:4 promise is fulfilled at Gen 50:1: *va-yippol Yosef al-pnei aviv va-yevk alav va-yishshaq lo* ('and Yosef fell upon his father's face, and wept upon him, and kissed him'). The fulfilment-verse does not specifically name the eye-closing gesture but documents Yosef's presence at the death and his enacting of the close-family-rituals: falling upon the face, weeping, kissing. The cycle's deathbed-arc is therefore foreshadowed at Gen 46:4 and fulfilled at Gen 50:1; the editorial-architecture is precise. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-singular construction within the HB; the broader patriarchal-death-rite preview is documented at Gen 50:1 (the fulfilment-scene). → **OVERLAY** as a chapter-singular construction with the cross-corpus fulfilment documented. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the verb *shit* + *yad* + *al* + *eineikha* construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the chapter-singular HB-occurrence status is verifiable; (c) the Gen 50:1 fulfilment is HB-internal-explicit; (d) the ANE cross-cultural close-the-eyes-at-death gesture is documented in the comparative-ritual scholarship. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *shit*, *yad*, *ayin*; BDB pp. 1011, 388-389, 744-747; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 313; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 156; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 589-590; on the ANE close-the-eyes-at-death gesture: J. Tropper *Nekromantie* AOAT 223, 1989; on the Gen 50:1 fulfilment: G. von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972; on the Egyptian opening-of-the-mouth ritual: J. Assmann *Death and Salvation in Ancient Egypt* 2005.

terms.translit: taph (Gen 46:5 ve-et-tappam ve-et-nesheihem)
terms.partOfSpeech: collective noun, masculine singular; the dependents-class noun ('little ones'), conventionally including children and possibly women in the social-class sense
terms.literal: taph — little ones, dependents, the dependents-class; the social-class noun naming the non-able-bodied non-warrior members of a household / group / community
terms.standardEnglish: little ones (ASV/KJV); children (NJPS — modernized); children (NRSV); little ones (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: little ones (ASV-baseline; the dependents-class noun's broader social-class sense and corpus-saturating cross-corpus distribution documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:5 deploys the noun *taph* ('little ones') in the family-transport scene: *va-yisu vnei-Yisra'el et-Ya'aqov avihem ve-et-tappam ve-et-nesheihem ba-agalot asher-shalach Par'oh la-set oto* ('and the sons of Yisra'el carried Ya'aqov their father, and their little ones, and their wives, in the wagons which Pharaoh had sent to carry him'). The lexeme *taph* is the corpus's standard dependents-class noun, naming the non-able-bodied non-warrior members of a household / group / community. The construction is editorially-significant: the chapter's transport-narrative organizes the family by class — the wagons carry (a) Ya'aqov (the patriarch), (b) the *taph* (the dependents), (c) the wives. The able-bodied sons walk; the dependents ride. The lexeme has corpus-saturating cross-corpus distribution especially across the Exodus / Numbers / Deuteronomy / Joshua / Judges narratives.** // **The lexeme's semantic-range.** The noun *taph* covers a semantic-range that has been debated in the scholarship: (a) the *children-specifically* sense (the narrow reading: *taph* = young children); (b) the *dependents-class* sense (the wider reading: *taph* = non-able-bodied non-warrior members, including children, possibly women, possibly elderly); (c) the *those-who-take-small-steps* etymological-derivation (from *t-p-p* / *t-p-h* 'to walk with short steps, mince along'). The corpus's deployments are mixed: some contexts narrow to children specifically (Gen 47:24 the seed-and-family-food provision); others broaden to dependents (Exod 10:10, 24 the Pharaoh-Mosheh negotiation on whether the *taph* may leave). The HB itself does not consistently distinguish the senses; the lexeme is used flexibly across contexts. // **The cross-corpus distribution — the corpus-saturating cluster.** // **(a) Genesis** — **Gen 34:29** (the Shimon-and-Levi-at-Shechem aftermath: *ve-et-kol-cheilam ve-et-kol-tappam ve-et-nesheihem shavu*, the women-and-dependents taken captive); **Gen 43:8** (Yehudah's plea: *ve-naqumah ve-nelekhah... ve-gam tappenu*, 'and we will arise and go... also our little ones'); **Gen 45:19** (Pharaoh's grant: *qechu lakhem me-eretz Mitzrayim agalot le-tappkhem ve-li-nsheikhem*, 'take you wagons out of the land of Mitsrayim for your little ones, and for your wives'); **Gen 46:5 (here)**; **Gen 47:12** (Yosef's provisioning: *va-yekhalkel Yosef et-aviv ve-et-echav ve-et kol-beit aviv lechem le-fi ha-taph*, 'and Yosef nourished his father, and his brethren, and all his father's household, with bread, according to their families' — note: literally 'to the mouth of the dependents'); **Gen 50:8, 21** (the Ya'aqov-burial transport and the post-Ya'aqov-death sustenance-promise). // **(b) Exodus — the negotiation-cluster.** **Exod 10:10** (Pharaoh: *re'u ki ra'ah neged peneikhem*, the rejection of taking the *taph*); **Exod 10:24** (Pharaoh's later modified-offer: *gam tappkhem yelekh imkhem*, 'let your little ones also go with you'); **Exod 12:37** (the Exodus-departure count: *ke-shesh-me'ot eleph ragli ha-gevarim levad mi-taph*, 'about six hundred thousand on foot that were men, beside little ones' — distinguishing the warrior-count from the dependents-count). // **(c) Numbers — the wilderness narratives.** **Num 14:3, 31** (the spies-rebellion: the people fear for the *taph*); **Num 16:27** (the Qorach-rebellion: the *taph* at the rebels' tents); **Num 31:9, 17, 18** (the Midyan-war captives); **Num 32:16, 17, 24, 26** (the Reubenite-and-Gadite request: the *taph* stay in the cattle-cities). // **(d) Deuteronomy — the law-and-ceremonial recital.** **Deut 1:39** (the wilderness-generation: 'your *taph* who today have no knowledge of good and evil'); **Deut 2:34; 3:6** (the conquest-ban formulae); **Deut 20:14** (the war-rules); **Deut 29:10** (the covenant-renewal assembly); **Deut 31:12** (the seventh-year Torah-reading assembly includes the *taph*). // **(e) Joshua-Judges** — **Josh 1:14; 8:35** (the Joshua-narrative); **Judg 21:10, 11** (the Yavesh-Gilad incident). // The cross-corpus distribution makes *taph* one of the corpus's most-distributed social-class nouns. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific Yosef-cycle deployment (Gen 43:8; 45:19; 46:5 here; 47:12; 50:8, 21); the cross-corpus reach into Exodus / Numbers / Deuteronomy / Joshua / Judges is documentary but the cycle-internal cluster is the chapter-anchored entry. Promotion-seed for the eventual Exodus / Numbers / Deuteronomy translations: the lexeme's saturating cross-corpus distribution makes it a natural cross-corpus central candidate. → **OVERLAY** with promotion-seed noted. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the noun is morphologically explicit; (b) the corpus-saturating cross-corpus distribution is exhaustively verifiable; (c) the semantic-range debate is documented across the standard lexica (HALOT, BDB, TDOT); (d) the Yosef-cycle cluster (Gen 43:8 + 45:19 + 46:5 + 47:12 + 50:8, 21) is HB-internal-explicit. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *taph*; BDB pp. 381-382; TDOT V:331-336; NIDOTTE 2:336-337; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 314; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 156; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 590; on the lexeme's semantic-range debate: M. Locher 'Tap' BN 1981; on the Exod 10:10, 24 negotiation-deployment: B. S. Childs *The Book of Exodus* OTL 1974; on the corpus-wide cross-corpus distribution: G. von Rad *Theologie des Alten Testaments* 1957 / ET *Old Testament Theology* 1962-65.

terms.translit: miqneihem ve-et-rekhusham (Gen 46:6 va-yiqchu et-miqneihem ve-et-rekhusham asher rakhshu be-eretz Kena'an)
terms.strongs: H4735 (miqneh, 'cattle, livestock') + H7399 (rekhush, 'goods, property, movable possessions')
terms.partOfSpeech: noun-pair (miqneh 'cattle' + rekhush 'goods'); the patriarchal-mobile-wealth formula
terms.literal: miqneh + rekhush — cattle + goods; the patriarchal-mobile-wealth pair-formula naming the totality of movable patriarchal-possessions
terms.standardEnglish: their cattle, and their goods (ASV/KJV); their livestock and their goods (NJPS); their livestock and the goods (NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: their cattle, and their goods (ASV-baseline; the patriarchal-mobile-wealth-formula's cross-corpus distribution documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:6 deploys the noun-pair *miqneh* + *rekhush* in the descent-narrative's transition-to-departure scene: *va-yiqchu et-miqneihem ve-et-rekhusham asher rakhshu be-eretz Kena'an va-yavo'u Mitzraymah* ('and they took their cattle, and their goods, which they had gotten in the land of Kena'an, and came into Mitsrayim'). The pair-formula is the corpus's standard inventory-formula for the patriarchal-mobile-wealth, recurring across the patriarchal narratives as the fixed-pair for the totality of movable patriarchal possessions: livestock and accumulated goods. The formula appears at the cycle's principal patriarchal-movement scenes: Avraham's departure from Charan (Gen 12:5); Avraham-and-Lot's separation (Gen 13:6); Ya'aqov's flight from Lavan (Gen 31:18); Esav's departure to Se'ir (Gen 36:6, 7). The chapter-46 deployment closes the patriarchal-movement-cluster: the descent-to-Mitsrayim is structurally-paralleled to all prior patriarchal-movements through the same wealth-inventory-formula.** // **The two lexemes.** **(a) *Miqneh*** (מִקְנֶה) — the noun derived from the verbal root *qanah* ('to acquire, possess'). The semantic-core is *acquired-livestock*: the noun names the totality of acquired animals (sheep, goats, cattle, donkeys, camels). The lexeme is used in the patriarchal-narratives as the principal wealth-marker: the patriarchs are *anshei miqneh* ('men of cattle', Gen 46:32, 34) — i.e., pastoral herders whose principal wealth is livestock. The construction recurs as the wealth-marker across Gen 13:2 (Avraham); Gen 26:14 (Yitzchaq); Gen 30:43 (Ya'aqov); Gen 36:7 (Esav). The lexeme's deployment is therefore one of the patriarchal-narrative's most-distributed wealth-and-class markers. **(b) *Rekhush*** (רְכוּשׁ) — the noun derived from the verbal root *rakhash* ('to gather, acquire'). The semantic-core is *accumulated-movable-property*: the noun names the totality of movable possessions other than livestock (vessels, tents, clothing, gold/silver, agricultural-equipment). The lexeme is distinguished from (a) *miqneh* (livestock specifically), (b) *rechush* (a variant-spelling), (c) *segullah* (a treasured-possession in a more-honorific register). The construction *miqneh* + *rekhush* therefore covers the patriarchal-mobile-wealth comprehensively: livestock-plus-everything-else-movable. // **The cross-corpus distribution — the patriarchal-mobile-wealth cluster.** // **(a) Avraham-and-Sarai (Gen 12:5)** — *va-yiqach Avram et-Sarai ishto ve-et-Lot ben-achiv ve-et-kol-rekhusham asher rakhashu ve-et-ha-nefesh asher-asu be-Charan*, 'Avram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their possessions which they had gathered, and the souls whom they had gotten in Charan'. The first patriarchal-departure deployment; the construction is *rekhush* only (without *miqneh*) but uses the same *rakhash* root-and-derived-noun, marking the first appearance of the inventory-formula. **(b) Avraham-and-Lot separation (Gen 13:6)** — *ve-lo-nasa otam ha-aretz lashevet yachdav ki-hayah rekhusham rav*, 'and the land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together: for their substance was great'. The construction uses *rekhush* alone here, but the context names the cattle-conflict (vv 7-8). **(c) Ya'aqov's flight from Lavan (Gen 31:18)** — *va-yinhag et-kol-miqnehu ve-et-kol-rekhusho asher rakhash miqneh qinyano asher rakhash be-Paddan-Aram*, 'and he carried away all his cattle, and all his substance which he had gathered, the cattle of his getting, which he had gathered in Paddan-Aram'. The construction here is the explicit *miqneh* + *rekhush* pair, exactly parallel to Gen 46:6. The Gen 31:18 deployment is the cycle's most-closely-parallel deployment to Gen 46:6: both are patriarchal-major-movement-scenes (Ya'aqov leaving Paddan-Aram for Kena'an at Gen 31:18; Ya'aqov leaving Kena'an for Mitsrayim at Gen 46:6); both use the inventory-formula to mark the totality of mobile-wealth. **(d) Esav's departure to Se'ir (Gen 36:6, 7)** — *va-yiqach Esav et-nashav ve-et-banav ve-et-bnotav ve-et-kol-nafshot beito ve-et-miqnehu ve-et-kol-behemto ve-et kol-qinyano asher rakhash be-eretz Kena'an*; the construction here uses *miqneh* + *behemah* + *qinyan* — a slightly-expanded variant of the inventory-formula. **(e) Gen 46:6 (here)** — the chapter's deployment closing the patriarchal-movement-cluster with the explicit *miqneh* + *rekhush* pair, lexically-parallel to Gen 31:18. The lexical-link Gen 31:18 / Gen 46:6 marks the chapter's structural-parallel to the earlier Paddan-Aram-departure: just as Ya'aqov-twenty-years-earlier-departed-from-Paddan-Aram with all his cattle and goods, so Ya'aqov-now-departs-from-Kena'an with all his cattle and goods. The cycle-internal symmetry is editorially-deliberate. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific patriarchal-mobile-wealth-formula deployment; the cross-corpus distribution (Gen 12:5; 13:6; 31:18; 36:6, 7; 46:6) is the patriarchal-movement-cluster. The pair-formula's cross-corpus reach beyond Genesis is limited; the formula is therefore overlay-anchored. → **OVERLAY** as the patriarchal-movement-cluster's documented inventory-formula. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the two-lexeme pair is morphologically explicit; (b) the patriarchal-movement-cluster distribution is exhaustively verifiable; (c) the Gen 31:18 / 46:6 explicit-pair lexical-link is documentary; (d) the semantic-distinction between *miqneh* (livestock) and *rekhush* (movable-possessions-other-than-livestock) is documented across the standard lexica. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *miqneh*, *rekhush*; BDB pp. 889-890 (miqneh), 940 (rekhush); TDOT XIII:43-54 (qanah / miqneh); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 314; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 156; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 590; on the patriarchal-mobile-wealth inventory-formula and the patriarchal-pastoralism-anthropology: K. van der Toorn *Family Religion in Babylonia, Syria and Israel* 1996; M. Liverani *Israel's History and the History of Israel* 2005; on the Gen 31:18 / 46:6 lexical-link: U. Cassuto *Commentary on the Book of Genesis* II 1964 / ET 1974.

terms.translit: ben ha-Kena'anit (Gen 46:10)
terms.partOfSpeech: construct-chain (ben 'son' + definite-articled feminine-singular gentilic adjective); the mother-ethnicity-qualifier
terms.literal: ben ha-Kena'anit — son of the Kena'anite woman; the mother-ethnicity-qualifier identifying Sha'ul's mother as Kena'anite
terms.standardEnglish: the son of a Canaanitish woman (ASV/KJV); the son of a Canaanite woman (NJPS/NRSV); the son of a Canaanite woman (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: the son of a Kena'anite woman (WoH transliteration of Kena'an; the mother-ethnicity-qualifier as the genealogy's only such marker documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:10 closes Shim'on's six-son list with a unique mother-ethnicity-qualifier: *u-vnei Shim'on Yemu'el ve-Yamin ve-Ohad ve-Yakhin ve-Tzochar ve-Sha'ul ben ha-Kena'anit* ('and the sons of Shim'on: Yemu'el, and Yamin, and Ohad, and Yakhin, and Tzochar, and Sha'ul the son of a Kena'anite woman'). The qualifier *ben ha-Kena'anit* — 'son of the Kena'anite woman' — is the only mother-ethnicity-qualifier in the entire seventy-souls genealogy; among the four matriarchal-lines and their descendants, only Sha'ul is given an explicit mother-ethnicity-marker. The notice is editorially-marked: the qualifier-clause names the mother's-non-Israelite-ethnic identification specifically, with no surrounding-context.** // **The cross-corpus parallel.** The same qualifier recurs at **Exod 6:15** in the parallel-Shim'on-list: *u-vnei Shim'on Yemu'el ve-Yamin ve-Ohad ve-Yakhin ve-Tzochar ve-Sha'ul ben ha-Kena'anit, eleh mishpechot Shim'on* ('and the sons of Shim'on: Yemu'el, and Yamin, and Ohad, and Yakhin, and Tzochar, and Sha'ul the son of a Kena'anite woman: these are the families of Shim'on'). The Exod 6:15 verbatim-repetition confirms the qualifier as a fixed-tradition element of the Shim'on-line tradition, not a Gen-46-specific narrative gloss. The Num 26:13 wilderness-census Shim'on-list does NOT include the qualifier: *li-Nemu'el mishpachat ha-Nemu'eli, le-Yamin mishpachat ha-Yemini, le-Yakhin mishpachat ha-Yekhini, le-Zerach mishpachat ha-Zerachi, le-Sha'ul mishpachat ha-Sha'uli*. The Num 26:13 omission marks the qualifier as belonging to the older Gen 46 / Exod 6 tradition rather than to the Num 26 census-tradition. // **The interpretive readings.** Modern critical scholarship reads the qualifier through several frames: **(a) Documentary-historical reading.** The qualifier preserves an older tradition that Shim'on (or his line through Sha'ul) intermarried with the Kena'anite population. The notice is editorially-significant: it acknowledges an inter-ethnic marriage within the patriarchal-period and preserves the historical-memory of such marriages. Sarna and Wenham document this reading. **(b) Source-critical reading.** The qualifier is a documentary-fossilization in the older Gen 46 tradition that was either omitted or harmonized in the later Num 26 census-tradition. Friedman and Carr treat the variant as a source-critical-marker. **(c) Literary-narrative reading.** The qualifier may foreshadow the later tribal-fate of Shim'on as the smallest and most-dispersed tribe (cf. the Shim'on omission from the Mosheh-blessing at Deut 33; the Shim'on enclave within Yehudah at Josh 19:1-9). Cassuto and Sarna note this reading. **(d) Cross-cultural ANE reading.** The notice fits the cross-cultural ANE pattern of recording inter-ethnic marriages within tribal-genealogical-traditions: the Mari-Texts, the Ugaritic-prosopography, and the Egyptian-execration-texts attest to similar mother-ethnicity-qualifiers in genealogical-records. The Gen 46:10 qualifier participates in this broader ANE genealogical-tradition. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific genealogy-internal observation; the Exod 6:15 verbatim-parallel and the Num 26:13 contrast-omission are documentary. The qualifier as the genealogy's only mother-ethnicity-marker is the chapter-anchored literary observation. → **OVERLAY** as the chapter-internal singular-marker. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the qualifier is morphologically explicit; (b) the Exod 6:15 parallel and Num 26:13 contrast-omission are HB-internal-verifiable; (c) the genealogy's uniqueness of the mother-ethnicity-marker is exhaustively verifiable across vv 8-27; (d) the cross-cultural ANE pattern is documented in comparative-scholarship. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *ben*, *Kena'ani*; BDB pp. 119-122 (ben), 489 (Kena'ani); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 314; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 158; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 594; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 p. 443; Cassuto *Commentary on the Book of Genesis* II 1964 / ET 1974; on the source-critical reading: R. E. Friedman *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003; D. M. Carr *Reading the Fractures of Genesis* 1996; on the Shim'on-tribal-fate readings: J. A. Soggin *Joshua* OTL 1972; on the cross-cultural ANE genealogical-tradition: D. E. Fleming *The Legacy of Israel in Judah's Bible* 2012.

terms.translit: va-yamot Er ve-Onan be-eretz Kena'an (Gen 46:12)
terms.partOfSpeech: narrative-historical aside in the archival-document context; the genealogy's only such cross-reference
terms.literal: va-yamot Er ve-Onan be-eretz Kena'an — and Er and Onan died in the land of Kena'an; the genealogy's narrative-historical aside cross-referencing the Gen 38 Yehudah-Tamar narrative
terms.standardEnglish: and Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan (ASV/KJV/NJPS/NRSV — uncontested)
terms.wohChoice: and Er and Onan died in the land of Kena'an (WoH transliteration; the genealogy's only narrative-historical aside as cross-reference to Gen 38:7-10 documented in commentary; sibling-link to the existing overlay `ve-shichet-artzah-onan-euphemism`)
terms.rationale: **The Yehudah-line in the seventy-souls genealogy at Gen 46:12 includes a unique narrative-historical aside: *u-vnei Yehudah Er ve-Onan ve-Shelah va-Feretz va-Zarach va-yamot Er ve-Onan be-eretz Kena'an va-yihyu vnei-Feretz Chetzron ve-Chamul* ('and the sons of Yehudah: Er, and Onan, and Shelah, and Peretz, and Zerach; but Er and Onan died in the land of Kena'an. And the sons of Peretz were Chetzron and Chamul'). The aside is the genealogy's ONLY narrative-historical cross-reference: among the seventy-souls list's 19 verses (vv 8-27), only the Yehudah-line includes this kind of explanatory-narrative note about prior-deaths in the patriarchal-land. The cross-reference is to Gen 38:7-10, where Er was put-to-death by YHWH for being *ra* in YHWH's eyes (v 7) and Onan was put-to-death by YHWH for the *shichet artzah* act (v 9; governed by the existing overlay [`ve-shichet-artzah-onan-euphemism`](#ve-shichet-artzah-onan-euphemism)). The Gen 46:12 aside lexically-explicitly references Gen 38 by naming both Er and Onan and naming their death-location.** // **The structural-significance of the cross-reference.** The Gen 38 Yehudah-Tamar interlude is one of the Yosef-cycle's most-discussed narrative-units; the chapter-38 narrative is editorially-bracketed within the larger Gen 37 → 39 Yosef-narrative arc, interrupting the Yosef-narrative with a complete Yehudah-line genealogical-narrative. The Gen 46:12 aside in the seventy-souls genealogy is the cycle's editorial-acknowledgment of the Gen 38 narrative as belonging to the line's official-history: the genealogy could have simply listed Er, Onan, Shelah, Peretz, Zerach as Yehudah's five sons; instead, the genealogy notes that Er and Onan died, signaling the audience to remember the Gen 38 narrative. The architectural-link Gen 38 ↔ Gen 46:12 is therefore one of the cycle's most-editorially-deliberate cross-references. // **The genealogy's continuation of the Yehudah-line.** The aside continues with the Peretz-grandsons (Chetzron and Chamul), making the Yehudah-line the only line in the genealogy with explicit-grandson-naming (the Asher-line at v 17 also names grandsons through Beriah). The two grandson-naming branches (Yehudah-through-Peretz; Asher-through-Beriah) mark the two lines as editorially-foregrounded for the seventy-souls count. The Yehudah-Peretz-grandson tradition is the Davidic-line's foundation: Peretz is David's tenth-generation ancestor (Ruth 4:18-22, the *toledot Peretz* closing the Ruth-narrative; 1 Chr 2:4-15 the post-exilic genealogy). The Gen 46:12 deployment therefore not only cross-references the Gen 38 deaths but also foregrounds the Peretz-line that will become the Davidic-line. // **Bidirectional sibling-link to the existing overlay `ve-shichet-artzah-onan-euphemism`.** The chapter-46 aside is paired with the existing chapter-38 overlay entry that governs Onan's act. The two entries jointly cover the Yehudah-line's Gen 38 narrative-historical fork: the chapter-38 entry documents the *shichet artzah* euphemism for Onan's act; the chapter-46 entry documents the seventy-souls-list's editorial-acknowledgment of Er-and-Onan's deaths. Both rationales cross-reference the other by id. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific genealogy-internal cross-reference; the Gen 38 reach is documented; the sibling-link to the existing overlay is bidirectional. → **OVERLAY** with sibling-link wired. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the cross-reference is grammatically and textually explicit; (b) the genealogy's uniqueness of this kind of cross-reference is verifiable; (c) the Gen 38:7-10 narrative-historical referent is HB-internal-explicit; (d) the Peretz-line / Davidic-line continuation is documented across mainstream scholarship (Sarna, Westermann, Wenham, Alter). // **Scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 315; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 158; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 595; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 p. 443; on the Gen 38 narrative-architecture and the Yehudah-Tamar Davidic-line foundation: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on the Peretz-line / Davidic-line continuation: K. Spronk *The Book of Ruth* HCOT 2010.

terms.translit: ve-Yov / ve-Yashuv (Gen 46:13)
terms.partOfSpeech: proper-name textual-critical variant; the Yissakhar-son's name in the MT (Yov) vs the Samaritan, LXX, Num 26:24, and 1 Chr 7:1 traditions (Yashuv)
terms.literal: Yov (MT) / Yashuv (Sam, LXX, Num 26:24, 1 Chr 7:1) — the variant readings of the third Yissakhar-son's name; the MT preserves an isolated reading against the broader textual-traditions
terms.standardEnglish: Job (ASV/KJV — using the Anglicization of MT Yov); Iob (some) / Jashub (NRSV margin, following Num 26:24 + Sam + LXX); Iob / Jashub (NJPS)
terms.wohChoice: Yov (MT preserved per the MT-fidelity baseline established at Gen 22:13; the Sam / LXX / Num 26:24 / 1 Chr 7:1 *Yashuv* variant documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:13 lists the four Yissakhar-sons in the MT: *u-vnei Yissakhar Tola u-Puvvah ve-Yov ve-Shimron* ('and the sons of Yissakhar: Tola, and Puvvah, and Yov, and Shimron'). The third son's name *Yov* (יוֹב) is preserved as an isolated MT reading against a substantial textual-tradition that reads *Yashuv* (יָשׁוּב). The reading-history: the Samaritan Pentateuch reads *ve-Yashuv*; the Septuagint (LXX) reads *Iasoub* (= Yashuv); the parallel Num 26:24 reads *Yashuv* (*mishpachat ha-Yashuvi*); the post-exilic 1 Chr 7:1 reads *Yashuv*. The MT-tradition therefore stands alone in preserving *Yov*; all major early-tradition witnesses preserve *Yashuv*. The variant is one of the genealogy's documented textual-critical loci.** // **The textual-critical analysis.** The variant is widely understood as a scribal-error in the MT: the original reading was almost certainly *Yashuv* (with the cross-corpus textual-tradition confirming this), and the MT *Yov* reflects a graphical-corruption (the *waw* and *shin* / *waw* and *shin-shewa* visual similarity in some scripts; the omission of the *shin* in transcription). Tov treats the variant as a transmission-error in the MT-tradition that did not affect the broader textual-traditions (Tov *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible* 3rd ed. 2012). The harmonizing-translation tradition: KJV/ASV preserve the MT reading and Anglicize as 'Job' (which is unrelated to the famously-suffering Iyov of the wisdom-tradition; the names are distinct in Hebrew, with the Yissakhar-son being *Yov* יוֹב and the suffering-figure being *Iyov* אִיּוֹב, a different orthography). Modern critical translations vary: NRSV and NJPS follow the cross-corpus *Yashuv* reading; some include a footnote on the MT variant. // **The Num 26:24 parallel.** The Num 26:24 wilderness-census Yissakhar-list reads: *le-Tola mishpachat ha-Tola'i, le-Fuvah mishpachat ha-Funi, le-Yashuv mishpachat ha-Yashuvi, le-Shimron mishpachat ha-Shimroni* ('of Tola, the family of the Tolaites: of Puvah, the family of the Punites: of Yashuv, the family of the Yashuvites: of Shimron, the family of the Shimronites'). The Num 26:24 *Yashuv* (mishpachat ha-Yashuvi) is the wilderness-census tradition's reading; the *mishpachat ha-Yashuvi* (the family of the Yashuvites) is the tribal-clan-name based on the eponymous Yashuv. The Gen 46:13 / Num 26:24 textual-tradition agreement (against the MT *Yov*) is documentary. // **The 1 Chr 7:1 parallel.** The 1 Chr 7:1 post-exilic Yissakhar-list reads: *ve-li-vnei Yissakhar Tola u-Fuvah Yashuv ve-Shimron arba'ah* ('and the sons of Yissakhar were Tola, and Puvvah, Yashuv, and Shimron, four'). The Chronicler's reading confirms the *Yashuv* tradition into the post-exilic period. // **The Samaritan and LXX traditions.** The Samaritan Pentateuch at Gen 46:13 reads *ve-Yashuv*; the LXX reads *Iasoub*. Both textual-traditions confirm the broader *Yashuv* reading against the MT *Yov*. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific textual-critical variant; the cross-corpus textual-traditions (Sam, LXX, Num 26:24, 1 Chr 7:1) are documentary. The MT-fidelity-baseline established at the Gen 22:13 *ayil* central-glossary entry (the MT principal reading translated; variants flagged in commentary) is followed: MT *Yov* preserved with WoH transliteration. → **OVERLAY** as the chapter-specific textual-critical variant. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the variant is textually explicit; (b) the cross-corpus distribution of the *Yashuv* reading is exhaustively verifiable (Sam, LXX, Num 26:24, 1 Chr 7:1); (c) the textual-critical-analysis is documented across the standard textual-critical scholarship (Tov, Wevers, Skinner, Hamilton). // **Scholarly literature.** Tov *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible* 3rd ed. 2012 pp. 132-133; J. W. Wevers *Notes on the Greek Text of Genesis* SCS 35, 1993 p. 781; Skinner *ICC Genesis* 1910 p. 493; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 315; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 158; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 596; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 344; on the Num 26:24 / 1 Chr 7:1 parallel: B. A. Levine *Numbers 21-36* AB 2000; S. Japhet *I & II Chronicles* OTL 1993; on the Samaritan Pentateuch: A. Tal *The Samaritan Pentateuch* 1994; on the LXX Genesis: J. W. Wevers *LXX Genesis* SCS 35, 1993.
