terms.translit: u-vnei Binyamin Bela va-Vekher ve-Ashbel Gera ve-Na'aman Echi va-Rosh Muppim ve-Chuppim va-Ard (Gen 46:21)
terms.partOfSpeech: list of ten sons; the chapter's deployment of the Binyamin-sons list, with substantial variation against the parallel lists at Num 26:38-40 and 1 Chr 7:6 / 8:1-2
terms.literal: the ten sons of Binyamin listed at Gen 46:21, with substantial textual-critical variation against the Num 26:38-40 (five sons) and 1 Chr 7:6 / 8:1-2 parallel lists
terms.standardEnglish: Bela, and Becher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Naaman, Ehi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Huppim, and Ard (ASV/KJV — uncontested at the name-form level)
terms.wohChoice: Bela, and Bekher, and Ashbel, Gera, and Na'aman, Echi, and Rosh, Muppim, and Chuppim, and Ard (WoH transliteration; the textual-critical variants against Num 26:38-40 + 1 Chr 7:6 / 8:1-2 documented in commentary)
terms.rationale:
**Gen 46:21 lists ten sons of Binyamin: Bela, Bekher, Ashbel, Gera, Na'aman, Echi, Rosh, Muppim, Chuppim, Ard. The list differs substantially from the three principal parallel-lists across the corpus and is one of the most-cited HB genealogical-textual-critical cruxes. The variants are extensively-documented across the textual-critical and form-critical scholarship.** // **The parallel-list cluster.** // **(a) Num 26:38-39** — the wilderness-census Binyamin-list (5 sons): *bnei Binyamin le-mishpechotam: le-Bela mishpachat ha-Bal'i, le-Ashbel mishpachat ha-Ashbeli, la-Achiram mishpachat ha-Achirami, li-Shfufam mishpachat ha-Shufami, le-Chufam mishpachat ha-Chufami*. The five sons are Bela, Ashbel, Achiram, Shfufam, Chufam. The further verses Num 26:40 then list two Bela-sons: *va-yihyu vnei-Bela Ard va-Na'aman* — the names Ard and Na'aman appear here as Bela's sons (i.e., Binyamin's grandsons), not as Binyamin's sons directly. // **(b) 1 Chr 7:6** — the post-exilic Chronicler's Binyamin-list (3 sons): *Binyamin Bela va-Vekher vi-Ydi'a'el sheloshah* ('the sons of Binyamin: Bela, and Bekher, and Yedi'a'el, three'). // **(c) 1 Chr 8:1-2** — the alternate Chronicler's Binyamin-list (5 sons): *u-Vinyamin holid et-Bela bekhoro Ashbel ha-sheni ve-Achrach ha-shelishi, Nochah ha-revi'i ve-Rafa ha-chamishi* ('and Binyamin begat Bela his firstborn, Ashbel the second, and Achrach the third, Nochah the fourth, and Rafa the fifth'). // **The variations.** Several distinct kinds of variation:

*(i) The total count.* Gen 46:21 = 10; Num 26:38-39 = 5; 1 Chr 7:6 = 3; 1 Chr 8:1-2 = 5. The counts are irreconcilable at the surface.

*(ii) The name-form variants.* (a) Echi (Gen 46:21) / Achiram (Num 26:38) — possibly the same name in different forms (or different individuals). (b) Muppim (Gen 46:21) / Shfufam (Num 26:39) — possibly a metathesis-variant of the same name. (c) Chuppim (Gen 46:21) / Chufam (Num 26:39) — possibly the same name. (d) Achrach (1 Chr 8:1) has no clear parallel in Gen 46:21 or Num 26.

*(iii) The generation-confusion.* Ard and Na'aman appear as Binyamin's sons in Gen 46:21 but as Bela's sons (Binyamin's grandsons) in Num 26:40. The Gera in Gen 46:21 has no parallel in Num 26 or 1 Chr 7 / 8; the Bekher in Gen 46:21 appears in 1 Chr 7:6 but not in Num 26 or 1 Chr 8.

*(iv) The *Rosh* singular-attestation.* The name *Rosh* in Gen 46:21 has no parallel in any other list. Some scholars have proposed that *Rosh* is a scribal-corruption (the word *rosh* in Hebrew also means 'head' and may have been a stray-noun later misread as a name); others (Rashi, traditional Jewish commentary) preserve it as a genuine eleventh-name. // **The two main interpretive readings.** // **(a) Documentary-critical reading.** The variations reflect different source-traditions: the Gen 46:21 list represents an older / P-source ten-son tradition; the Num 26:38-40 represents a later wilderness-period tradition that recounted some names as Bela's-sons rather than Binyamin's-sons; the 1 Chr 7:6 and 1 Chr 8:1-2 represent two distinct post-exilic Chronistic-traditions. The variations therefore document the historical-tradition's flux. **Wellhausen** *Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels* (1883) treats the variations as documentary-source-evidence; **Skinner** *ICC Genesis* (1910) names the variations as 'one of the most striking instances of conflict between parallel-lists in the HB'; **Friedman** *The Bible with Sources Revealed* (2003) assigns Gen 46:21 to P and traces the source-history. // **(b) Harmonizing reading.** The variations can be reconciled through generation-shifting: names that appear as Binyamin's sons in Gen 46:21 are reclassified as grandsons in Num 26:40 (where Ard and Na'aman become Bela's sons). The 1 Chr 7 and 8 lists are then read as Davidic-Solomonic-period census-revisions reflecting tribal-development across generations. **Cassuto** *Commentary on the Book of Genesis* II (1964) develops this reading; **Hamilton** *NICOT Genesis 18-50* (1995) preserves the harmonizing reading; **Sarna** *JPS Genesis* (1989) notes both readings without adjudicating. // **The two readings documented even-handedly.** The Editor presents both readings without adjudication. The documentary-critical reading is widely-mainstream in modern critical scholarship; the harmonizing reading is preserved in traditional Jewish and conservative-Christian commentary. The Gen 46:21 list is one of the corpus's most-cited HB genealogical-textual-critical-cruxes, and both readings are documented as named-positions. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific textual-crux; the cross-corpus parallel-list cluster (Num 26:38-40, 1 Chr 7:6, 1 Chr 8:1-2) is documentary. The Gen 46:21 list translated with WoH proper-name transliteration; the textual-critical variants documented WITHOUT adjudication. → **OVERLAY** as the chapter-specific textual-critical-crux. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the parallel-list distribution is exhaustively verifiable; (b) the variations are textually-explicit; (c) the documentary-critical and harmonizing readings are documented as named-positions across mainstream scholarship; (d) the Editor's even-handed presentation of both readings without adjudication is the standard textual-critical apparatus practice. // **Scholarly literature.** Skinner *ICC Genesis* 1910 pp. 493-494; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 596-597; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 315-316; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 158-159; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 pp. 443-444; Speiser *AB Genesis* 1964 p. 344; Tov *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible* 3rd ed. 2012; Cassuto *Commentary on the Book of Genesis* II 1964 / ET 1974; Wellhausen *Prolegomena zur Geschichte Israels* 1883; Friedman *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003; on the Num 26 wilderness-census Binyamin-list: B. A. Levine *Numbers 21-36* AB 2000; on the 1 Chr 7 + 8 Binyamin-lists: S. Japhet *I & II Chronicles* OTL 1993; on the Binyamin tribal-history: P. K. McCarter *II Samuel* AB 1984; D. Edelman 'Saulide-Davidic Rivalry' in *Tribes and Politics in the Hebrew Bible* 1991.

terms.translit: u-vnei-Dan Chushim (Gen 46:23)
terms.partOfSpeech: noun-plural-form deployed as a single-eponym-name; the chapter-singular construction *bnei Dan* + plural-name
terms.literal: Chushim — the plural-form name; the Dan-sons-list naming a single plural-form-name
terms.standardEnglish: Hushim (ASV/KJV); Hushim (NJPS/NRSV) — uncontested transliteration of the MT plural-form-name
terms.wohChoice: Chushim (WoH transliteration with 'Ch' for chet; the plural-form's editorially-marked construction and the Num 26:42 *Shucham* metathesis-variant documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:23 lists Dan's son(s) in an editorially-marked construction: *u-vnei-Dan Chushim* ('and the sons of Dan: Chushim'). The construction *bnei Dan* (plural construct 'sons of Dan') + *Chushim* (a name in plural-form) is unusual: the verse has a plural-subject *bnei* but only one named entity, which itself has a plural-form ending (*-im*). The construction admits three principal readings: (a) the clan-name plural reading: *Chushim* is a single eponymous-son whose name happens to have a plural-form (some HB names have the plural-form ending without indicating plurality); (b) the multiple-sons-collective reading: *Chushim* names multiple sons collectively under one tribal-eponym; (c) the textual-corruption reading: the construction reflects a scribal-error or text-tradition-variant. The Num 26:42 wilderness-census Dan-list reads: *eleh vnei Dan le-mishpechotam le-Shucham mishpachat ha-Shuchami* ('these are the sons of Dan after their families: of Shucham, the family of the Shuchamites') — using *Shucham* (a metathesis of *Chusham/Chushim*) instead of *Chushim*.** // **The lexeme analysis.** The name *Chushim* (חֻשִׁים) has the *-im* ending that in Hebrew typically marks the masculine-plural. However, several HB names have the *-im* ending without indicating plurality (e.g., *Mitsrayim* — 'Mitsrayim, Egypt' — is technically a dual-form but names a single entity; *Yerushalayim* — 'Yerushalayim, Jerusalem' — is technically a dual-form but names a single city). The clan-name plural reading is therefore lexically-defensible: *Chushim* could be a single-eponym whose name has a plural-form ending. The Num 26:42 *Shucham* form lacks the *-im* ending and could represent either (a) the original-singular form that was later expanded to a plural-form in Gen 46:23, or (b) a metathesis-variant of the same root (the consonants *ch-sh-m* in different orderings: *chushim* / *shucham*). The textual-history is unresolved; both readings are documented in the textual-critical scholarship. // **The construction analysis.** The construction *u-vnei-Dan Chushim* with a plural-subject *bnei* but a single-name follows a recognized pattern in the HB genealogies: when a tribal-line has only one named-son, the verse can use the plural *bnei* construct + the single-name (cf. Gen 36:18 *u-vnei Aholivamah eishet Esav Y'ush ve-Ya'lam ve-Korach*, where *bnei* is plural-construct introducing multiple sons; the variation in number with the actual count is editorially-flexible). The Gen 46:23 deployment is therefore not necessarily editorially-problematic at the construction-level; the unusualness lies in the plural-form name with the plural-construct subject. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific lexical-form observation; the Num 26:42 *Shucham* parallel-list is documentary. The MT-plural-form preserved as the proper-name; the cross-corpus *Shucham* variant flagged in commentary. → **OVERLAY** as a chapter-specific lexical-form observation. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the Num 26:42 *Shucham* variant is HB-internal-verifiable; (c) the clan-name-plural reading is documented in the standard lexica (HALOT, BDB); (d) the textual-history options are documented in the textual-critical scholarship (Tov, Skinner, Hamilton). // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *Chushim*; BDB p. 302; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 316; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 159; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 597; Skinner *ICC Genesis* 1910 p. 494; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 p. 444; Tov *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible* 3rd ed. 2012; on the Num 26:42 Shucham/Chushim parallel: B. A. Levine *Numbers 21-36* AB 2000; on the Dan-tribal-history: J. A. Soggin *Judges* OTL 1981.

terms.translit: ve-Serach achotam (Gen 46:17)
terms.partOfSpeech: proper-name + noun-with-3mp-suffix; the seventy-souls list's only named-female-grandchild
terms.literal: ve-Serach achotam — and Serach their sister; the chapter-internal singular-attestation of a named-female-grandchild in the seventy-souls genealogy
terms.standardEnglish: and Serah their sister (ASV/KJV/NJPS/NRSV — uncontested as the name is straightforward)
terms.wohChoice: and Serach their sister (WoH transliteration with 'ch' for chet; the seventy-souls list's only named-female-grandchild and the rabbinic-aggadic Serach-tradition documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:17 lists the Asher-line: *u-vnei Asher Yimnah ve-Yishvah ve-Yishvi u-Veriah ve-Serach achotam, u-vnei Veriah Chever u-Malki'el* ('and the sons of Asher: Yimnah, and Yishvah, and Yishvi, and Beriah, and Serach their sister. And the sons of Beriah: Chever, and Malki'el'). Serach is one of only two women named in the entire seventy-souls genealogy (the other is Dinah at v 15); both are explicit grand-daughters in the genealogical-architecture. The Asher-line's inclusion of Serach is editorially-marked: the other matriarchal-lines do not name granddaughters explicitly. Serach's deployment at Gen 46:17 establishes her as a named-figure in the patriarchal-tradition and provides the foundation for an extensive rabbinic-aggadic Serach-tradition.** // **The cross-corpus Serach attestations.** // **(a) Gen 46:17 (here)** — the naming-deployment in the seventy-souls list. // **(b) Num 26:46** — the wilderness-census Asher-list: *ve-shem bat-Asher Serach* ('and the name of the daughter of Asher was Serach'). The Num 26:46 deployment explicitly names Serach as the daughter of Asher, again as the only named-female in the Asher-line. The Num 26:46 deployment is editorially-significant: it confirms Serach's belonging-to-the-tribal-tradition across the patriarchal and wilderness periods. // **(c) 1 Chr 7:30** — the post-exilic Chronistic Asher-genealogy: *bnei Asher Yimnah ve-Yishvah ve-Yishvi u-Veriah ve-Serach achotam* — verbatim-identical to Gen 46:17. The Chronicler preserves the tradition into the post-exilic period. // **The rabbinic-aggadic Serach-tradition.** Serach receives extensive treatment in the rabbinic-and-aggadic tradition, primarily focused on the question of why she alone is named (and why she persists across the Gen 46 / Num 26 / 1 Chr 7 tradition as the only named-female-grandchild in the Asher-line). The principal aggadic traditions: // **(a) The long-lived-Serach tradition.** Targum Pseudo-Jonathan at Gen 46:17 develops the tradition that Serach lived an exceptionally long life, surviving from the seventy-souls-descent to Mitsrayim through to the Exodus and even beyond. The tradition is developed in **Genesis Rabbah 94:9** and **b. Sotah 13a**, which records that Serach was the one who informed Mosheh of the location of Yosef's bones (cf. Exod 13:19 the Yosef-bones-extraction tradition; Serach as the only living-link to the patriarchal-period who knew the burial-location). // **(b) The information-transmitter tradition.** Several aggadic traditions name Serach as the information-transmitter across generations: she announces to Ya'aqov that Yosef is alive in Mitsrayim (Sefer Ha-Yashar, in a tradition possibly influenced by the gentle-and-musical Serach-figure of medieval kabbalistic literature); she counsels the Levites on Mosheh's true identity; she recognizes the redemption-formula at the wilderness. // **(c) The piska b-emtza pasuq and the rare-naming significance.** Some aggadic traditions read Serach's naming as a sign of the deity's recognition of women in genealogical-tradition; the rabbinic tradition develops the theme that Serach was 'taken alive into the Garden of Eden' (alongside Eliyahu and a small group of immortal-figures). // **The named-female-in-genealogy observation.** Serach is editorially-marked as one of only two women named in the seventy-souls genealogy; the other is Dinah at v 15 (*ve-et Dinah vito*). Both are named as daughters of Le'ah (Dinah) and Asher (Serach) respectively. The pattern suggests that the genealogy preserves the names of women only when there is a specific narrative or tribal-significance to remember; Dinah's naming is tied to the Gen 34 narrative-block; Serach's naming is tied to a different tribal-tradition (the long-lived-Serach tradition or the named-female-grandchild Asher-tradition). The Asher-line's inclusion of a named-female-grandchild marks the line as editorially-distinctive within the genealogy. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific genealogy-internal observation; the cross-corpus Serach-attestations (Num 26:46, 1 Chr 7:30) and the rabbinic-aggadic Serach-tradition documented. → **OVERLAY** with promotion-seed flagged for the eventual Numbers / Chronicles / aggadic-tradition translation activations. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the name is morphologically explicit; (b) the cross-corpus Serach-attestations are HB-internal-verifiable; (c) the genealogy's unique-naming of females (Dinah + Serach only) is exhaustively verifiable; (d) the rabbinic-aggadic Serach-tradition is documented in the standard aggadic-tradition scholarship (Ginzberg, Heinemann). // **Scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 315; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 159; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 596; Wenham *WBC Genesis 16-50* 1994 p. 444; on the rabbinic-aggadic Serach-tradition: L. Ginzberg *Legends of the Jews* 1909-1938 vol. II pp. 39-40, 117; J. Heinemann *Aggadot ve-toldoteihen* 1974; on the long-lived-Serach tradition: J. Bronner 'Serah Bat Asher: The Long-Lived' *Stories of Heroines* 1994; on the Targum Pseudo-Jonathan Serach tradition: D. Shinan *Targum and Aggadah* 1992; on Num 26:46 the wilderness-census-deployment: B. A. Levine *Numbers 21-36* AB 2000; on 1 Chr 7:30: S. Japhet *I & II Chronicles* OTL 1993.

terms.translit: yotz'ei yerekho (Gen 46:26)
terms.partOfSpeech: participle (qal active masculine plural construct 'goers-out of') + noun-with-3ms-suffix (yerekho, 'his thigh'); the standard HB construction for direct biological descent through the male line
terms.literal: yotz'ei yerekho — those who came out of his thigh / loins; the procession-from-the-male-line euphemism for direct biological descent
terms.standardEnglish: that came out of his loins (ASV/KJV — preserving the ASV's modesty-flattening of 'thigh' to 'loins'); his direct descendants (NJPS — modernized); his direct descendants (NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: that came out of his loins (ASV-baseline; the literal *yerekh* 'thigh' force and the wider *yerekh*-as-euphemism construction documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:26 deploys the construction *yotz'ei yerekho* ('those who came out of his thigh / loins') in the seventy-souls genealogy's summary-verse: *kol-ha-nefesh ha-ba'ah le-Ya'aqov Mitzraymah yotz'ei yerekho mi-le-vad neshei vnei-Ya'aqov, kol-nefesh shishim va-shesh* ('all the souls that came with Ya'aqov into Mitsrayim, that came out of his loins, besides Ya'aqov's sons' wives, all the souls were threescore and six'). The construction is the standard HB euphemism for direct biological descent through the male line; the *yerekh* 'thigh' is the standard ANE-cultural euphemism for the male-reproductive organs, and the *yotz'ei yerekh* 'goers-out of the thigh' construction names those who proceed-from-the-male-line. The construction is one of the corpus's most-distributed direct-male-line-descent formulae, recurring across the patriarchal narratives, the Exodus-narrative, and the Judges and Kings traditions.** // **The lexeme.** The noun *yerekh* (יָרֵךְ) names (a) the literal thigh (the upper-leg body-part); (b) the side (of objects or geographical features — e.g., *yarketei Tzafon*, 'the recesses of the north'); (c) by extension and euphemistically, the male-reproductive-organs (the body-part adjacent to the genitalia). The euphemistic use is well-attested across the corpus and the broader ANE. The construction *yotz'ei yerekh + (person)* names the people-who-proceed-from-the-person's-male-reproductive-organs — i.e., the direct-biological-descendants through the male-line. The construction is therefore the standard HB formula for direct-male-line-descent, distinguishing from (a) general-descendants (using *zera* 'seed'), (b) genealogical-tradition (using *toledot*), (c) people-community (using *am*), (d) the wider household (using *beit*). // **The cross-corpus distribution.** // **(a) Gen 35:11** — the El-Shaddai promise to Ya'aqov at Beit-El: *peruh u-revuh goy u-qhal goyim yihyeh mimkha u-melakhim me-chalatzeikha yetze'u* ('be fruitful and multiply; a nation and a company of nations shall be of thee, and kings shall come out of thy loins'). The Gen 35:11 deployment uses *chalatzeikha* ('thy loins') rather than *yerekheikha*; the broader euphemism-class is the same. // **(b) Gen 46:26 (here)** — the chapter's deployment in the seventy-souls summary. // **(c) Exod 1:5** — the Exodus-narrative's opening reprise: *va-yehi kol-nefesh yotz'ei yerekh-Ya'aqov shiv'im nafesh* ('and all the souls that came out of the loins of Ya'aqov were seventy souls'). The Exod 1:5 deployment uses the verbatim-construction *yotz'ei yerekh-Ya'aqov*, directly cross-referencing the Gen 46:26 deployment. The Gen 46:26 / Exod 1:5 lexical-link is one of the corpus's most-cited inner-biblical genealogical-cross-references. // **(d) Judg 8:30** — Gid'on's descendants: *u-le-Gid'on hayah shiv'im banim yotz'ei yerekho* ('and Gid'on had threescore and ten sons of his body begotten'). The Gid'on-seventy-sons deployment uses the same construction; the seventy-number is editorially-parallel to the Gen 46:26-27 seventy-souls (see central `shivim-nefesh-seventy-souls-foundational-number-LXX-variant`). // **(e) 1 Kgs 8:19** — the Davidic-covenant fulfilment: *raq attah lo tivneh ha-bayit ki im-binkha ha-yotze me-chalatzekha hu yivneh ha-bayit li-shmi* ('nevertheless thou shalt not build the house; but thy son that shall come forth out of thy loins, he shall build the house unto my name'). The Solomon-as-Davidic-line successor formulation. // **(f) 2 Chr 6:9** — the parallel-Solomon-temple-narrative; verbatim-reprise of 1 Kgs 8:19. // **The *yerekh* / *chalatzayim* doublet.** The corpus uses two principal euphemistic-lexemes for the male-reproductive-organs: *yerekh* ('thigh') and *chalatzayim* ('loins'). The two are largely-interchangeable in the descent-formula register; the variation across the cluster (Gen 35:11 *chalatzeikha*; Gen 46:26 / Exod 1:5 *yerekh-Ya'aqov*; Judg 8:30 *yerekho*; 1 Kgs 8:19 *chalatzekha*) suggests the corpus's tolerance of both forms. The two euphemisms therefore constitute a single semantic-class. // **The *yerekh* / oath-formula deployment.** The *yerekh* lexeme also appears in the oath-gesture-formula: the deity-or-master places-the-hand-under-the-thigh of the addressee as an oath-binding gesture (governed by the existing central [`yad-tachat-yarekh-oath-gesture`](#yad-tachat-yarekh-oath-gesture)). The cross-corpus instances: Gen 24:2, 9 (Avraham's servant); Gen 47:29 (Ya'aqov's deathbed oath to Yosef). The oath-gesture-deployment confirms the *yerekh* as the locus of male-line-continuity and as the body-part that binds inter-generational oaths. The Gen 46:26 *yotz'ei yerekho* descent-formula deployment is part of the same broader *yerekh*-as-euphemism semantic-cluster. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific descent-formula deployment; the cross-corpus distribution (Gen 35:11, Exod 1:5, Judg 8:30, 1 Kgs 8:19, 2 Chr 6:9) is documentary. The Gen 46:26 / Exod 1:5 lexical-link is the foundational inner-biblical genealogical-cross-reference. → **OVERLAY** with promotion-seed flagged for the eventual Exodus / Judges / Kings translations. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the cross-corpus distribution is exhaustively verifiable; (c) the *yerekh* / *chalatzayim* lexical-equivalence is documented across the standard lexica (HALOT, BDB, TDOT); (d) the ASV-baseline 'loins' (modesty-flattening of *yerekh* 'thigh') is the standard rendering. // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *yerekh*, *chalatzayim*; BDB pp. 437-438 (yerekh), 323 (chalatzayim); TDOT VI:351-353 (yerekh); NIDOTTE 2:543-545; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 316; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 159; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 599; on the *yerekh*-as-euphemism: J. M. Sasson 'The Worship of the Golden Calf' in *Orient and Occident* 1973; on the Gen 46:26 / Exod 1:5 lexical-link: U. Cassuto *Commentary on the Book of Genesis* II 1964 / ET 1974; B. S. Childs *The Book of Exodus* OTL 1974; on the Judg 8:30 Gid'on-seventy-sons parallel: J. A. Soggin *Judges* OTL 1981; on the 1 Kgs 8:19 Davidic-line formulation: J. Gray *I & II Kings* OTL 1970.

terms.translit: et-Menasheh ve-et-Ephraim (MT Gen 46:20); LXX adds Makhir, Galaad, Sutalaam, Taam, Edom
terms.strongs: list-form construction; the LXX/MT seventy-five-vs-seventy variant at the Yosef-line
terms.partOfSpeech: textual-critical variant; the LXX-tradition adds five Yosef-line descendants at v 20, expanding the genealogy and producing the seventy-five cumulative count at v 27
terms.literal: the Gen 46:20 MT lists only Menasheh and Ephraim as Yosef's sons born in Mitsrayim; the LXX adds five additional descendants (Menasheh's son Makhir and grandson Galaad; Ephraim's sons Sutalaam and Taam and Sutalaam's son Edom), producing the LXX cumulative seventy-five count at v 27 vs the MT seventy
terms.standardEnglish: Manasseh and Ephraim (ASV/KJV — MT-tradition); Manasseh and Ephraim, with footnote on LXX expansion (NJPS/NRSV — modernized with textual-note)
terms.wohChoice: Menasheh and Ephraim (MT-tradition with WoH transliteration; the LXX five-additional-descendants expansion documented in commentary; central sibling-link to `shivim-nefesh-seventy-souls-foundational-number-LXX-variant`)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:20 names Yosef's two sons born in Mitsrayim: *va-yivvaled le-Yosef be-eretz Mitzrayim asher yaldah-lo Asnat bat-Poti Fera kohen On et-Menasheh ve-et-Ephraim* ('and unto Yosef in the land of Mitsrayim were born Menasheh and Ephraim, whom Asnat the daughter of Poti-Phera priest of On bare unto him'). The MT-tradition lists only the two sons; the LXX-tradition expands the verse with five additional descendants: Menasheh's son Makhir and grandson Galaad; Ephraim's sons Sutalaam and Taam; Sutalaam's son Edom. The LXX expansion produces the cumulative seventy-five count at v 27 (vs the MT seventy), which is the basis of the Acts 7:14 NT-tradition reading (Stephen's speech: *en psychais hebdomekonta pente*).** // **The LXX expansion in detail.** The LXX at Gen 46:20 reads (in retroverted Hebrew approximation): *va-yivvaled le-Yosef be-eretz Mitzrayim et-Menasheh ve-et-Ephraim. ve-tilvad-Makhir le-Menasheh u-Makhir holid et-Galaad. u-vnei Ephraim Sutalaam u-Taam. u-vnei Sutalaam Edom.* The expansion incorporates five additional descendants (Makhir, Galaad, Sutalaam, Taam, Edom). The additions are NOT inventions of the LXX-translator; they are drawn from the Num 26 wilderness-census parallel-tradition: **Num 26:29** *u-vnei Menasheh le-Makhir mishpachat ha-Makhiri u-Makhir holid et-Gilad* ('and of the sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the family of the Machirites; and Machir begat Gilead'); **Num 26:35** the Ephraim-list includes Shutelach, Bekher, Tachan. The LXX-translator (or the Vorlage) reads the Gen 46 list against the Num 26 list and incorporates the Num 26 grandsons into the Gen 46 count. The LXX therefore represents an internally-consistent expansion-tradition. // **The Dead Sea Scrolls evidence.** The 4QExoda fragment reads seventy-five at Exod 1:5, agreeing with the LXX-tradition. The Qumran-evidence establishes the seventy-five count as having Hebrew-Vorlage attestation, not as a LXX-only innovation. Tov treats the variant as one of the major Vorlage-difference cases between the MT and the LXX-Hebrew-Vorlage (Tov *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible* 3rd ed. 2012 pp. 132-133). // **The Acts 7:14 NT-tradition.** Acts 7:14 reads *en psychais hebdomekonta pente* — 'threescore and fifteen souls'. Stephen's speech follows the LXX-tradition's seventy-five count. The textual-critical implication: Stephen (or the Lukan author) was working from the LXX-tradition rather than from the MT-tradition; the seventy-five count was the count operative in the Hellenistic-Jewish tradition that Stephen represents. The Acts 7:14 reading is one of the NT's most-cited HB textual-critical cases. // **The interpretive implications.** The Editor's approach: translate the MT-tradition as the surface-baseline; flag the LXX-tradition expansion in commentary; do NOT adjudicate the textual-tradition. The Gen 46:20 surface-translation lists Menasheh and Ephraim only (MT); the v 27 cumulative count is seventy (MT); the LXX variant is documented as named-scholarship apparatus. The Acts 7:14 NT-tradition reading is documented WITHOUT theological adjudication. // **Central sibling-link to `shivim-nefesh-seventy-souls-foundational-number-LXX-variant`.** The Gen 46:20 LXX expansion is the source of the cumulative LXX seventy-five count at v 27. The two entries are central-overlay sibling-pair: the central [`shivim-nefesh-seventy-souls-foundational-number-LXX-variant`](#shivim-nefesh-seventy-souls-foundational-number-LXX-variant) governs the cumulative count at v 27; this overlay entry governs the LXX-tradition expansion-mechanism at v 20. Both entries cross-reference the other. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific Yosef-line expansion-mechanism; the central sibling-link is bidirectional. → **OVERLAY** with the central sibling-link wired. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the LXX expansion is textually-documentary; (b) the Num 26 source-tradition for the LXX additions is HB-internal-verifiable; (c) the cumulative count's relation to the v 27 LXX-vs-MT variant is grammatically and arithmetically transparent; (d) the Acts 7:14 NT-tradition reading is documentary; (e) the Editor's even-handed presentation of both textual-traditions is standard textual-critical practice. // **Scholarly literature.** Tov *Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible* 3rd ed. 2012 pp. 132-133; J. W. Wevers *Notes on the Greek Text of Genesis* SCS 35, 1993 pp. 779-783; on the Acts 7:14 reading: J. A. Fitzmyer *The Acts of the Apostles* AB 1998; on the LXX expansion-mechanism: A. Aejmelaeus *Trust and Distrust* 2007; on the 4QExoda evidence: E. Tov *Scribal Practices and Approaches Reflected in the Texts Found in the Judean Desert* 2004; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 315-316; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 596, 599-600; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 158, 161; on the Num 26 source-tradition: B. A. Levine *Numbers 21-36* AB 2000.

terms.translit: ve-et-Yehudah shalach le-fanav (Gen 46:28)
terms.partOfSpeech: narrative construction (Ya'aqov-as-subject sends Yehudah-as-object before-him-as-locative); the chapter's continuation of the Yehudah-as-leader emergence pattern across the Yosef-cycle
terms.literal: ve-et-Yehudah shalach le-fanav — and he sent Yehudah before him; the chapter's deployment of the Yehudah-as-leader pattern, with Yehudah chosen by Ya'aqov to go ahead to Yosef
terms.standardEnglish: and he sent Judah before him (ASV/KJV); he sent Judah ahead (NJPS modernized); he sent Judah ahead of him (NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: and he sent Yehudah before him (ASV-baseline; the Yehudah-as-leader emergence pattern across the Yosef-cycle documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:28 stages the chapter's narrative-pivot toward the Goshen-arrival: *ve-et-Yehudah shalach le-fanav el-Yosef le-horot le-fanav Goshnah va-yavo'u artzah Goshen* ('and he sent Yehudah before him unto Yosef, to show the way before him unto Goshen; and they came into the land of Goshen'). The choice of Yehudah — not Re'uven (the firstborn), not Yosef-already-in-Mitsrayim, not any other brother — is editorially-marked. The verse continues the cycle-wide Yehudah-as-leader emergence pattern, observable from Gen 37:26-27 (the sale-speech), through Gen 38 (the Yehudah-Tamar narrative as a complete tribal-line foundation), Gen 43:3-10 (the surety-pledge negotiation), Gen 44:14-34 (the great substitution-speech), to Gen 46:28 (here, the sent-before-Ya'aqov mission). The pattern reaches forward to Gen 49:8-12 (the lion-of-Yehudah patriarchal blessing) and beyond to the Davidic-monarchic and Messianic traditions.** // **The cycle-wide pattern.** The Yehudah-as-leader emergence is one of the cycle's principal character-arcs, documented in mainstream scholarship as a deliberate literary-architecture. The arc: // **(a) Gen 37:26-27** — the sale-speech: *ma-betza ki naharog et-achinu ve-khisinu et-damo? lekhu ve-nimkerennu la-Yishma'elim ve-yadenu al-tehi-vo ki-achinu vsareinu hu* ('what profit is it if we slay our brother and conceal his blood? come, and let us sell him to the Yishma'elites, and let not our hand be upon him; for he is our brother, our flesh'). Yehudah's first-recorded leadership moment within the brothers' group; he proposes the sale-instead-of-murder. Yehudah's voice prevails over Re'uven's failed-rescue-attempt (vv 21-22). // **(b) Gen 38** — the Yehudah-Tamar narrative as a complete tribal-line foundation. Yehudah's character-development through the chapter — the loss of two sons, the failed levirate-arrangement, the recognition at Petach Einayim, the *tzadqah mimmeni* admission, the eventual birth of Peretz (the Davidic-line ancestor). The chapter's editorial-bracketing within the Yosef-narrative (interrupting Gen 37 → 39) marks the Yehudah-line as the cycle's parallel-tribal-foundation alongside the Yosef-line. // **(c) Gen 43:3-10** — the surety-pledge negotiation: Yehudah's argument convinces Ya'aqov to send Binyamin. The chapter's principal moral-fulcrum (the Yehudah-as-replacement-Reuven moment; Re'uven's earlier offer at Gen 42:37 was rejected, but Yehudah's at Gen 43:9 is accepted). The surety-pledge (*arav-eravon*, governed by the existing overlay) is the cycle's verbal-pledge counterpart to the Gen 38 *eravon* (signet, cord, staff). // **(d) Gen 44:14-34** — the great substitution-speech: the cycle's longest-and-most-affective single-speech, Yehudah's offer-to-be-enslaved-in-Binyamin's-place. The speech is the cycle's moral-climax and the immediate-cause of Yosef's break-down-and-disclosure at Gen 45:1-3. // **(e) Gen 46:28 (here)** — the sent-before-Ya'aqov mission: Yehudah is chosen by Ya'aqov to go ahead to Yosef in Goshen. The choice reflects Yehudah's emergent role as the brothers' principal leader; Yehudah is the brother who has demonstrated the leadership-capacity through the Gen 43-44 negotiations. The verse's narrative-function: Yehudah acts as the verbal-mediator-and-pathfinder, the structural-counterpart to his earlier role as verbal-pledge-bearer. // **(f) Gen 49:8-12** — the lion-of-Yehudah patriarchal blessing: *Yehudah attah yodukha echeikha yadkha be-oref oyveikha yishtachavu lekha vnei avikha. gur Aryeh Yehudah mi-teref beni alita* etc. The deathbed-blessing names Yehudah as the line that will-prevail-among-the-brothers; the lion-of-Yehudah image becomes the foundation for the Davidic-Messianic tradition. // **The named scholarship.** **Nahum Sarna** *JPS Genesis* (1989) documents the cycle's Yehudah-as-leader emergence pattern as one of its principal character-arcs. **Robert Alter** *The Art of Biblical Narrative* (1981) and *The Five Books of Moses* (2004) reads the Yehudah-arc as one of the cycle's most-sophisticated character-developments. **Meir Sternberg** *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* (1985) names the arc as one of the cycle's two-major character-developments (the Yosef-arc and the Yehudah-arc, interwoven across the chapters). **Jan P. Fokkelman** *Narrative Art in Genesis* (1975) traces the verbal-pattern of Yehudah's speeches across the cycle. **Walter Brueggemann** *Genesis* Interpretation (1982) names the Yehudah-as-leader emergence as the cycle's moral-theological signature. The pattern is therefore one of the most-discussed cycle-internal character-arcs in mainstream modern scholarship. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific narrative-deployment; the cross-cycle Yehudah-leadership pattern is the wider context. → **OVERLAY** as a chapter-specific deployment with the wider cycle-pattern documented. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the narrative-construction is morphologically explicit (Yehudah sent-before-Ya'aqov); (b) but the cycle-wide leadership-emergence pattern is an interpretive observation, not a single-verse grammatical-fact; (c) the pattern's documentation across mainstream named scholarship is consistent; (d) the Davidic-Messianic forward-reach into Gen 49:8-12 and beyond is HB-internal-explicit but the literary-architectural reading is interpretive. // **Scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 316-317; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 160-161; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 600-601; Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1 + *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 266-267; M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; W. Brueggemann *Genesis* Interpretation 1982 pp. 354-355; G. von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972 pp. 401-405; G. W. Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* CBQMS 4, 1976; on Gen 49:8-12 the lion-of-Yehudah blessing: H.-J. Zobel *Stammesspruch und Geschichte* BZAW 95, 1965.

terms.translit: va-yera elav (Gen 46:29)
terms.partOfSpeech: verb (niphal impf 3ms vav-consec) + preposition-with-3ms-suffix; the Niphal of ra'ah in the reunion-context where elsewhere it is the standard theophanic verb
terms.literal: va-yera elav — and he showed/appeared himself unto him; the standard HB Niphal-of-ra'ah theophanic-verb here applied to the Yosef-Ya'aqov reunion
terms.standardEnglish: and he presented himself unto him (ASV/KJV — preserving the reunion-register reading); appeared to him (literal Niphal of ra'ah, the theophanic-register reading); and he appeared before him (NJPS); he presented himself to him (NRSV)
terms.wohChoice: and he presented himself unto him (ASV-baseline preserved for the reunion-register reading; the Niphal-of-ra'ah verbatim-coincidence with the theophany-formula documented in commentary)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:29 stages the chapter's reunion-climax: *va-ye'esor Yosef merkavto va-ya'al li-qra't Yisra'el aviv Goshnah va-yera elav va-yippol al-tzavarav va-yevk al-tzavarav od* ('and Yosef made ready his chariot, and went up to meet Yisra'el his father, to Goshen; and he presented himself unto him, and fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a good while'). The Niphal *va-yera elav* (literally 'and he showed/appeared himself unto him') is the corpus's standard theophanic-verb: the verbatim-construction *va-yera el-X* opens many of the patriarchal-and-Mosaic theophany-scenes, where the deity is the implied-subject. The Gen 46:29 deployment applies the same Niphal-of-*ra'ah* construction to the Yosef-Ya'aqov reunion, creating a verbatim-coincidence with the theophany-formula. The literary observation is well-documented across the named scholarship: the son-father reunion is described in the same lexical register as divine-self-disclosure.** // **The Niphal-of-*ra'ah* theophanic-formula.** The construction *va-yera + (preposition al / el) + X* with the deity as implied-subject is the corpus's most-distributed theophanic-formula. The principal patriarchal-and-Mosaic deployments: **(a) Gen 12:7** — *va-yera YHWH el-Avram va-yomer le-zar'akha etten et-ha-aretz ha-zot* ('and YHWH appeared unto Avram, and said, Unto thy seed will I give this land'). The Avraham-at-Shekhem theophany; the formula's foundational-deployment. **(b) Gen 17:1** — *va-yera YHWH el-Avram va-yomer elav ani El Shaddai* ('and YHWH appeared to Avram, and said unto him, I am El Shaddai'). The El-Shaddai self-disclosure. **(c) Gen 18:1** — *va-yera elav YHWH be-Elonei Mamre ve-hu yoshev petach ha-ohel* ('and YHWH appeared unto him by the oaks of Mamre, as he sat in the tent door'). The three-visitors theophany. **(d) Gen 26:2** — *va-yera elav YHWH va-yomer al-tered Mitzraymah* ('and YHWH appeared unto him, and said, Go not down into Egypt'). The Yitzchaq-at-Gerar theophany. **(e) Gen 26:24** — *va-yera elav YHWH ba-laylah ha-hu va-yomer anokhi Elohei Avraham avikha* ('and YHWH appeared unto him the same night, and said, I am the Elohim of Avraham thy father'). The Yitzchaq-at-Be'er-Sheva theophany (governed by `anokhi-elohei-X-avikha-ancestral-god-formula` and `al-tira-fear-not-divine-encouragement-formula`). **(f) Gen 35:1** — *va-yera Elohim el-Ya'aqov od be-vo'o mi-Paddan Aram* (the Beit-El-return theophany). **(g) Gen 35:9** — *va-yera Elohim el-Ya'aqov od* (the second Beit-El theophany; the P-source doublet, governed by `yisrael-second-renaming-beit-el-p-doublet`). **(h) Exod 6:3** — *va-era el-Avraham el-Yitzchaq ve-el-Ya'aqov be-El Shaddai* ('I appeared unto Avraham, unto Yitzchaq, and unto Ya'aqov, as El Shaddai'). The P-source's foundational verse for the divine-name distinction; the Niphal is here in 1cs form. The construction is therefore one of the corpus's most-distributed theophany-formulae. // **The Gen 46:29 deployment.** The Niphal-of-*ra'ah* at Gen 46:29 deploys the verbatim-construction in the human-to-human reunion-context: Yosef (the subject) shows himself to Ya'aqov (the object). The construction is grammatically-identical to the theophanic deployment, but the subject is a human son. The literary point: the Yosef-Ya'aqov reunion is being described in the same lexical-register as a theophany. The verbatim-coincidence is editorially-deliberate, marking the reunion-scene as belonging to the high-formality divine-encounter genre. The chapter has prepared the parallel structurally: the chapter's opening at vv 1-4 is a literal-theophany at Be'er-Sheva (the deity's authorization-of-the-descent); the chapter's reunion-climax at v 29 uses the same lexical-register to mark the son-father reunion as the human-theophanic correlative of the divine-theophanic-opening. The chapter is therefore structurally-bracketed: divine-theophany at the start (vv 1-4); human-reunion-as-theophany at the close (v 29). The literary observation is named across mainstream scholarship (Sarna, Alter, Cassuto). // **The reunion-register reading.** The ASV preserves the construction with the reunion-register reading 'he presented himself unto him', which preserves the Niphal's reflexive force without surfacing the theophanic-lexical-echo. The literal-rendering 'appeared to him' would surface the theophanic register at the cost of the reunion-narrative naturalness. The ASV's choice is therefore appropriate to the reunion-context; the theophanic-lexical-echo is documented in commentary. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific literary-lexical-observation; the cross-corpus *va-yera el-X* theophany-formula distribution is documentary. The Gen 46:29 deployment is the chapter-singular reunion-as-theophany application. → **OVERLAY** as a chapter-singular literary-observation. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the Niphal construction is morphologically explicit; (b) the cross-corpus *va-yera el-X* theophany-formula distribution is exhaustively verifiable; (c) the verbatim-coincidence between the theophany-formula and the reunion-deployment is grammatically transparent; (d) the literary observation is documented across mainstream scholarship (Sarna, Alter, Cassuto, Westermann). // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.v. *ra'ah*; BDB pp. 906-909; TDOT XIII:208-242; NIDOTTE 3:1007-1015; Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 p. 316; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 161; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 p. 601; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 267; Cassuto *Commentary on the Book of Genesis* II 1964 / ET 1974; on the va-yera-el-X theophany-formula: J. Barr *The Semantics of Biblical Language* 1961; on Gen 18:1 and the three-visitors theophany: G. von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972; on the Niphal-of-ra'ah in the theophany-register: G. Vanoni 'Sehen' TLOT.

terms.partOfSpeech: verb (qal cohortative 1cs 'let me die') + definite-article + noun (pa'am 'this time / this very occasion'); the cohortative + emphatic-particle death-readiness statement
terms.literal: amutah ha-pa'am — now let me die; the cohortative-of-mut + emphatic ha-pa'am 'this time' death-readiness statement
terms.standardEnglish: now let me die (ASV/KJV); I can die now (NJPS modernized); I can die now (NRSV); now I can die (Alter)
terms.wohChoice: now let me die (ASV-baseline; the cycle's Gen 45:28 → 46:30 death-readiness arc closure documented in commentary; sibling-link to the existing overlay `va-techi-ruach-yaaqov-spirit-revival-chayah-arc-gen45`)
terms.rationale: **Gen 46:30 stages Ya'aqov's response to seeing Yosef alive: *va-yomer Yisra'el el-Yosef amutah ha-pa'am acharei re'oti et-paneikha ki odkha chai* ('and Yisra'el said unto Yosef, Now let me die, since I have seen thy face, that thou art yet alive'). The construction combines the cohortative *amutah* ('let me die' — the volitive 1cs of *mut* 'to die') with the emphatic particle *ha-pa'am* ('this time / this very moment'). The verse directly echoes Gen 45:28: *va-yomer Yisra'el rav od Yosef beni chai elkhah ve-er'ennu be-terem amut* ('and Yisra'el said, It is enough; Yosef my son is yet alive: I will go and see him before I die'). The two statements bracket the chapter-transition Gen 45 → 46 with a death-readiness arc: at Gen 45:28 Ya'aqov resolves to go-and-see-the-son-before-dying; at Gen 46:30 Ya'aqov declares himself ready-to-die-now-that-he-has-seen-the-son.** // **The construction.** The cohortative *amutah* (Qal of *mut* with the volitive *-ah* ending) names the 1cs's-own-desire-to-die — not a wish for death-as-relief (the suicidal register), but a stated-readiness-to-die now that the chapter's-foundational-purpose has been completed. The construction is psychologically-precise: Ya'aqov is not despairing but rather expressing-completed-purpose. The emphatic *ha-pa'am* ('this time / this very occasion') intensifies the cohortative: not just 'let me die' (generic), but 'let me die this very moment'. The construction names the moment of completed-purpose. // **The Gen 45:28 → 46:30 arc.** The two statements bracket the chapter-transition with a precise death-readiness arc: // **(a) Gen 45:28** — the future-oriented resolve: *elkhah ve-er'ennu be-terem amut* ('I will go and see him before I die'). The statement names a present-resolve oriented toward a future-seeing; the deathward-trajectory is acknowledged but deferred until the seeing has happened. // **(b) Gen 46:30 (here)** — the completed-purpose statement: *amutah ha-pa'am acharei re'oti et-paneikha* ('now let me die, since I have seen thy face'). The statement names a present-readiness oriented toward a past-completed seeing; the deathward-trajectory is now accepted because the seeing has happened. The arc therefore traces: resolve → going → seeing → readiness. The chapter-46 verse is the resolution-of-the-Gen-45 resolve. // **The chapter's affective-pivot architecture.** The Gen 46:30 deployment is the chapter's final-affective-statement before the Pharaoh-audience-instructions begin (vv 31-34). The chapter's affective-architecture: // (a) Vv 1-4 — the divine-encouragement at Be'er-Sheva: the deity authorizes the descent and promises the return. The patriarch is in vision-receiving mode. // (b) V 29 — the reunion-as-theophany: Yosef shows himself to Ya'aqov; the falling-on-the-neck embrace; the prolonged weeping. The reunion is staged in theophanic-lexical register (governed by the sibling overlay `va-yera-elav-reunion-as-theophany-lexical-echo-gen46`). // (c) V 30 (here) — the death-readiness statement: the patriarch declares the chapter's-purpose-completed; he can die now. The statement closes the cycle's emotional arc that began at Gen 37:34 with the *tarof toraf* belief (Ya'aqov's grief-rending on receiving the bloodied tunic). The Gen 37:34 → 45:28 → 46:30 arc traces the patriarch's emotional-trajectory from grief through resolve to completion. // **Bidirectional sibling-link to the existing overlay `va-techi-ruach-yaaqov-spirit-revival-chayah-arc-gen45`.** The Gen 46:30 death-readiness statement is paired with the chapter-45 spirit-revival arc closure at v 27. The two entries jointly track the cycle's affective-pivots across the chapter-transition: the Gen 45:26 fainting-of-the-heart → Gen 45:27 spirit-revival → Gen 45:28 resolve-to-see → Gen 46:30 readiness-to-die. The two entries form a bidirectional sibling-pair: the chapter-45 entry tracks the revival; the chapter-46 entry tracks the post-reunion death-readiness. Both rationales cross-reference the other by id. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific death-readiness statement; the cycle's Gen 45:28 → 46:30 arc closure is the wider context; the sibling-link to the existing chapter-45 overlay is bidirectional. → **OVERLAY** with sibling-link wired. // The claim_type is *direct* because (a) the construction is morphologically explicit (cohortative + emphatic-particle); (b) the Gen 45:28 / 46:30 lexical-link is HB-internal-explicit (the same verbal-root *mut* in two distinctive constructions); (c) the cycle's affective-arc is documented across mainstream scholarship (Sarna, Alter, Sternberg, Fokkelman, Westermann). // **Scholarly literature.** HALOT s.vv. *mut*, *pa'am*; BDB pp. 559 (mut), 822-823 (pa'am); Joüon-Muraoka §114 (the cohortative); Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 316-317; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 p. 161; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 601-602; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 p. 267; on the cycle's Gen 45:28 / 46:30 death-readiness arc: M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; G. W. Coats *From Canaan to Egypt* CBQMS 4, 1976; on the broader Yosef-cycle affective architecture: R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1.

terms.rationale: **Gen 46 continues the cycle-wide Ya'aqov/Yisra'el name-alternation pattern that the chapter-45 deployment at v 28 inaugurated. The chapter-46 distribution: v 1 *va-yissa Yisra'el ve-khol asher-lo* (the action-of-departure: Yisra'el); v 2a *va-yomer Elohim le-Yisra'el be-mar'ot ha-laylah* (the divine-address opener: Yisra'el); v 2b *va-yomer Ya'aqov Ya'aqov* (the doubled-call by the deity: Ya'aqov); v 2c *va-yomer hineni* (the response: identity-marker dropped, just *hineni*); v 5a *va-yaqom Ya'aqov mi-Be'er Shava* (the rising-from-Be'er-Sheva: Ya'aqov); v 5b *va-yisu vnei-Yisra'el et-Ya'aqov avihem* (the carrying-by-the-sons: collective *bnei Yisra'el* + father Ya'aqov); v 8 *ve-eleh shmot bnei-Yisra'el ha-ba'im Mitzraymah Ya'aqov u-vanav* (the genealogy-opener: collective *bnei Yisra'el* + father Ya'aqov). The chapter's distribution is the cycle's densest single-chapter alternation-cluster: the patriarch is Yisra'el in the action-of-departure register and in the people-named-collective register, and Ya'aqov in the divine-address (the doubled-call) and in the genealogy-of-his-own-line register.** // **The pattern's structural-logic.** The chapter-46 distribution follows a recognizable structural-logic: // **(a) Yisra'el in action-of-departure register (vv 1, 5b).** When the patriarch is acting in the covenantal-determined register — taking-the-journey-with-all-that-he-has, being-carried-by-the-sons-collective — the Yisra'el-name marks the covenantal-determination dimension. // **(b) Yisra'el in the people-named-collective register (vv 5b, 8).** When the genealogical-tribal-line is being named collectively — *bnei Yisra'el* — the Yisra'el-name marks the covenantal-tribal identity (Yisra'el-as-eponym of the twelve-tribe federation). // **(c) Yisra'el in the divine-address-opener (v 2a).** The narrator's framing of the divine-address uses Yisra'el — naming the deity as speaking-to-the-covenantal-patriarch. // **(d) Ya'aqov in the doubled-call (v 2b).** The deity itself addresses the patriarch by the older Ya'aqov-name. The literary force: the deity speaks not to the elevated-Yisra'el but to the patriarchal-aetiology Ya'aqov — the deity addresses the patriarch's pre-Penuel identity. The shift from Yisra'el (narrator's frame) to Ya'aqov (divine address) within the same verse is one of the chapter's most-marked literary-features. // **(e) Ya'aqov in the action-of-rising (v 5a) and in the genealogy-of-his-own-line (v 8).** The Ya'aqov-name marks the patriarch as the immediate-actor and the genealogical-source: the patriarch rises from Be'er-Sheva (Ya'aqov-the-acting-individual); the patriarch is the source of the seventy-souls genealogy (Ya'aqov-the-genealogical-founder). // **The cycle-wide alternation pattern.** The chapter-46 distribution is the cycle's continuation of the alternation pattern that runs from Gen 32:29 (the Penuel renaming) through Gen 50:25 (Yosef's deathbed-statement to the brothers). The cycle's principal name-shift moments: Gen 32:29 (the Penuel renaming); Gen 35:10 (the Beit-El P-source-doublet renaming); Gen 37 (the cycle's opening, Ya'aqov-default); Gen 43:6, 8, 11 (Yisra'el-cluster at the second-journey decision); Gen 45:25-28 (the Gen 45 acceptance-pivot at v 28, governed by the sibling overlay); Gen 46:1-2-5-8 (here); Gen 47:27-31 (the post-settlement Yisra'el-cluster); Gen 48:2 (the *va-yitchazzeq Yisra'el* deathbed-strengthening); Gen 49:1-2 (the deathbed-blessings Ya'aqov / Yisra'el alternation). The pattern is one of the corpus's most-studied source-critical and literary observations. // **Bidirectional sibling-link to the existing overlay `yaaqov-yisrael-name-shift-yosef-cycle-acceptance-v28`.** The chapter-46 continuation of the pattern is paired with the chapter-45 acceptance-pivot. The two entries jointly track the cycle's name-shift pattern across the chapter-transition Gen 45 → 46. The chapter-45 entry governs the v 28 acceptance-pivot; this entry governs the chapter-46 distribution (vv 1, 2a, 2b, 5, 8). Both rationales cross-reference the other by id. The two entries flag the broader cycle-wide pattern as a future cycle-wide central-candidate when Gen 46-50 is processed; the cumulative pattern across Gen 32-50 may justify promotion to a central entry. // **Overlay housing.** Chapter-specific continuation of the cycle-wide name-shift pattern; the sibling-link to the existing chapter-45 overlay is bidirectional. The cycle-wide pattern is documented as a future central-candidate. → **OVERLAY** with sibling-link wired and promotion-seed flagged. // The claim_type is *inferred* because (a) the chapter-46 name-distribution is grammatically and textually explicit (the two names are uncontested in their distribution); (b) but the literary-and-source-critical observation of the alternation-pattern is interpretive rather than grammatical; (c) the cycle-wide pattern's interpretation is documented across mainstream named scholarship (Sarna, Alter, Westermann, von Rad, Brueggemann, Friedman) but admits both source-critical and literary readings; (d) the WoH proper-name convention preserves the source's name on the surface; the interpretive observation is documented in the rationale. // **Scholarly literature.** Sarna *JPS Genesis* 1989 pp. 311-314; Westermann *Genesis 37-50* 1986 pp. 153-161; Hamilton *NICOT Genesis 18-50* 1995 pp. 587-602; Alter *The Five Books of Moses* 2004 pp. 266-267; on the cycle's Ya'aqov/Yisra'el alternation pattern: G. von Rad *Genesis* OTL 1972 pp. 401-405; W. Brueggemann *Genesis* Interpretation 1982 pp. 348-355; J. P. Fokkelman *Narrative Art in Genesis* SSN 17, 1975; on the source-critical readings of the alternation: J. Wellhausen *Prolegomena* 1883; S. R. Driver *Introduction to the Literature of the OT* 1913; R. E. Friedman *The Bible with Sources Revealed* 2003; on the literary readings: M. Sternberg *The Poetics of Biblical Narrative* 1985 pp. 285-308; R. Alter *The Art of Biblical Narrative* 1981 ch. 1.
